• Requires 6 months of MDT

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain the role of the 'monthly pulse' dose in the WHO leprosy management protocol.
back:
• 600 mg of Rifampicin administered once a month
• Must be taken under direct supervision of a healthcare provider
• Ensures adherence to the most potent bactericidal component

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the WHO-recommended duration of treatment for Paucibacillary (PB) versus Multibacillary (MB) leprosy.
back:
• PB duration: 6 months of treatment
• MB duration: 12 months of treatment
• Both are administered using standardized blister packs

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Identify the primary pharmacological reason Clofazimine is added to the multibacillary (MB) regimen but traditionally omitted from the paucibacillary (PB) regimen.
back:
• MB requires three drugs to prevent resistance due to high bacterial load
• Clofazimine provides added bactericidal activity and suppresses Lepra reactions

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: In the WHO MDT blister pack for Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy, the drug intended for daily, self-administered use is [___].
back:
• Dapsone (100 mg daily for adults)
• Inhibits folate synthesis in Mycobacterium leprae
• Must be completed within a 6 to 9-month window

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A patient on MDT for leprosy develops acute inflammation, edema of existing lesions, and new nerve tenderness. Name the reaction and the primary treatment.
back:
• Type 1 Lepra Reaction (Reversal Reaction)
• Management: High-dose oral corticosteroids (Prednisolone)
• Continue MDT without interruption

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain how a positive slit-skin smear at any site affects the WHO leprosy classification regardless of the number of skin lesions.
back:
• Automatically classifies the patient as Multibacillary (MB)
• Mandates the 12-month triple-drug MDT regimen
• Indicates a higher bacterial index and transmission risk

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the clinical presentation and pharmacological management of Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL) compared to Reversal Reactions.
back:
• ENL (Type 2): Systemic symptoms, painful nodules; treated with Thalidomide or Clofazimine
• Type 1: Localized inflammation; treated primarily with Corticosteroids

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Identify the biochemical mechanism of action of Dapsone in the treatment of leprosy.
back:
• Competitive inhibitor of dihydropteroate synthase
• Blocks the synthesis of dihydrofolic acid
• Structurally analogous to para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA)

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: The WHO standard Multidrug Therapy (MDT) for paucibacillary leprosy consists of Rifampicin and [___] administered over a 6-month period.
back:
• Dapsone
• Rifampicin is given as a monthly supervised dose
• Dapsone is self-administered daily.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A 35-year-old male with 8 hypopigmented anaesthetic patches and a positive skin smear is diagnosed with Multibacillary (MB) leprosy. The required duration of WHO standard MDT is [___].
back:
• 12 months
• MB is defined as >5 skin lesions or positive skin smears
• Regimen includes Rifampicin, Dapsone, and Clofazimine.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain the role of Clofazimine in the management of Multibacillary (MB) leprosy beyond its bacteriostatic action.
back:
• Exerts anti-inflammatory effects
• Reduces the frequency and severity of Type 2 lepra reactions (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum)
• Causes characteristic brownish skin discoloration.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the WHO classification criteria for Paucibacillary (PB) versus Multibacillary (MB) leprosy.
back:
• PB: 1–5 skin lesions and negative skin smears at all sites
• MB: >5 skin lesions OR positive skin smear at any site.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Which specific MDT component is administered as a 600 mg single monthly supervised dose in both PB and MB regimens?
back:
• Rifampicin
• It is the most potent bactericidal component
• Ensures treatment adherence through supervised monthly pulses.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: In the management of Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (Type 2 reaction), the drug of choice for severe cases that are refractory to steroids is [___].
back:
• Thalidomide
• Strongly contraindicated in pregnancy due to severe teratogenicity
• Inhibits TNF-alpha activity.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A patient on MDT for leprosy presents with a sudden onset of painful, red nodules on the limbs and high-grade fever. Identify the complication and the first-line pharmacotherapy.
back:
• Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (Type 2 Reaction)
• Management: Continue MDT, administer NSAIDs for mild cases, or Corticosteroids for severe cases.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain the mechanism of action by which Dapsone achieves its bacteriostatic effect against Mycobacterium leprae.
back:
• Competitively inhibits the enzyme dihydropteroate synthase
• Acts as a structural analog of p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA)
• Prevents bacterial folic acid synthesis.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the management of a Type 1 (Reversal) reaction with a Type 2 (ENL) reaction regarding MDT.
back:
• In both reactions, WHO MDT should be continued without interruption
• Type 1 requires corticosteroids for nerve involvement
• Type 2 may require Thalidomide or Clofazimine.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: What is the WHO recommendation for the use of Rifampicin, Dapsone, and Clofazimine in a pregnant patient diagnosed with leprosy?
back:
• Standard MDT is safe during pregnancy
• Treatment must be continued to prevent permanent disability
• No evidence of teratogenicity for these three drugs.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: According to WHO protocols, the standard triple therapy for multibacillary leprosy consists of rifampin, dapsone, and [___].
back:
• Clofazimine
• Used to prevent the emergence of dapsone resistance
• Recommended for all patients with a positive skin smear

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A 30-year-old male with leprosy begins a new drug regimen. Two days later, he presents with jaundice and decreased hemoglobin. A peripheral smear shows Heinz bodies. The drug most likely responsible is [___].
back:
• Dapsone
• Triggers hemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency
• Acts as a folate synthesis inhibitor similar to sulfonamides

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain the mechanism of action of dapsone against Mycobacterium leprae.
back:
• Competitive inhibition of dihydropteroate synthase
• Prevents the synthesis of folate
• Structurally related to p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA)

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the WHO-recommended drug regimens for paucibacillary versus multibacillary leprosy.
back:
• Paucibacillary: Dapsone + Rifampin
• Multibacillary: Dapsone + Rifampin + Clofazimine
• Multibacillary is defined by a positive skin smear

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Identify the most prominent dermatologic adverse effect associated with chronic clofazimine use.
back:
• Discoloration of the skin and conjunctivae
• Ranges from red to brownish-black
• Due to drug storage in reticuloendothelial tissues

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) is an inflammatory reaction occurring during dapsone therapy for lepromatous leprosy that is suppressed by [___].
back:
• Thalidomide
• Helps manage the sudden release of antigens from dying bacilli
• Clofazimine also provides some protection against this reaction

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A patient with multiple skin nodules and a positive skin smear for M. leprae is prescribed a 12-month course of triple therapy. This indicates a diagnosis of [___] leprosy.
back:
• Multibacillary leprosy
• Requires the addition of Clofazimine to Rifampin and Dapsone
• Usually associated with lepromatous presentations

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: How does rifampin carry out its biological function in the management of leprosy?
back:
• Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
• Highly bactericidal against M. leprae
• Prevents the selection of dapsone-resistant mutants

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast dapsone with standard sulfonamides regarding their accumulation and half-life in leprosy patients.
back:
• Dapsone half-life: 1–2 days (much longer than typical sulfonamides)
• Dapsone exhibits significant tissue retention
• Retained in skin, muscle, liver, and kidneys

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Name the two primary components of the standard WHO regimen for paucibacillary leprosy.
back:
• Rifampin
• Dapsone
• Regimen used for cases with lower organism burdens

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: For the management of Multibacillary (MB) leprosy, the WHO-recommended standard Multidrug Therapy (MDT) consists of Rifampicin, Dapsone, and [___].
back:
● Clofazimine
● Administered for 12 months
● Prevents drug resistance and ensures bacterial clearance.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A 35-year-old male presents with six hypopigmented skin lesions and a positive slit-skin smear for acid-fast bacilli. According to WHO classification, this patient should be treated for [___].
back:
● Multibacillary (MB) Leprosy
● Requires 3-drug MDT (Rifampicin, Dapsone, Clofazimine)
● Treatment duration is 12 months.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain the mechanism by which Dapsone exerts its anti-leprotic effect against Mycobacterium leprae.
back:
● Inhibits folate synthesis
● Acts as a structural analog/competitive antagonist of p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA)
● Inhibits dihydropteroate synthase.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the WHO treatment regimens for Paucibacillary (PB) versus Multibacillary (MB) leprosy in terms of drug composition.
back:
● PB Regimen: 2 drugs (Rifampicin + Dapsone)
● MB Regimen: 3 drugs (Rifampicin + Dapsone + Clofazimine)
● Both use Rifampicin as the bactericidal core.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Specify the administration frequency of Rifampicin in the WHO standard MDT for leprosy.
back:
● Once monthly
● Administered as a supervised dose (600 mg)
● Essential for high bactericidal activity.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A characteristic side effect of Clofazimine that often leads to poor patient compliance is [___].
back:
● Reddish-brown skin discoloration
● May also cause conjunctival discoloration
● Reversible upon drug discontinuation.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A patient undergoing leprosy treatment develops jaundice and anemia. Laboratory tests reveal Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. The likely causative agent is [___].
back:
● Dapsone
● Causes dose-dependent hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
● Can also cause methemoglobinemia.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Detail the molecular target of Rifampicin in the treatment of Mycobacterium leprae.
back:
● Binds to the beta subunit of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
● Inhibits bacterial RNA synthesis
● Highly bactericidal against M. leprae.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the total duration of WHO MDT for Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy and Multibacillary (MB) leprosy.
back:
● PB Duration: 6 months total
● MB Duration: 12 months total
● Consistent across adults and children (with adjusted doses).

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Identify the WHO-recommended prophylactic measure for healthy contacts of a newly diagnosed leprosy patient.
back:
● Single-dose Rifampicin (SDR)
● Administered as post-exposure prophylaxis
● Reduces the risk of developing leprosy in contacts.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: According to WHO criteria, Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy is clinically distinguished from Multibacillary (MB) leprosy by the presence of [___] skin lesions.
back:
• 1 to 5 skin lesions
• Slit-skin smears must be negative at all sites
• Involves only one nerve trunk.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A patient presents with 8 anaesthetic, hypopigmented patches and a positive slit-skin smear. Identify the WHO classification and the standard duration of therapy.
back:
• Classification: Multibacillary (MB) Leprosy
• Duration: 12 months of Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT)
• Criteria: >5 lesions or positive smears.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain the mechanism by which Dapsone exerts its bacteriostatic effect against Mycobacterium leprae.
back:
• Competitively inhibits dihydropteroate synthase
• Acts as a structural analog of PABA
• Blocks the synthesis of folate required for nucleic acid production.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the drug composition of the WHO Paucibacillary (PB) regimen with the Multibacillary (MB) regimen for adults.
back:
• PB Regimen: Rifampicin and Dapsone only
• MB Regimen: Rifampicin, Dapsone, and Clofazimine
• Clofazimine is added for its effect on high bacterial loads.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: List the three drugs in the MB-MDT regimen and identify which component is administered as a supervised monthly dose.
back:
• Rifampicin: 600 mg once monthly (Supervised)
• Clofazimine: 300 mg once monthly (Supervised) + 50 mg daily
• Dapsone: 100 mg daily (Self-administered).

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: The WHO-recommended agent in leprosy therapy that is notorious for causing reversible red-to-brown skin discoloration is [___].
back:
• Clofazimine
• It is a phenazine dye that accumulates in reticuloendothelial tissues
• May also cause gastrointestinal intolerance.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A leprosy patient on MDT develops sudden onset of painful, erythematous subcutaneous nodules, fever, and arthralgia. Identify the reaction and the primary drug for severe cases.
back:
• Type 2 Lepra Reaction (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum/ENL)
• Treatment: Prednisolone (Corticosteroids)
• Thalidomide is an alternative for severe, steroid-resistant cases.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain why Rifampicin is considered the most critical component of the WHO leprosy Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT).
back:
• Potent bactericidal activity against M. leprae
• Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
• Effectively 'sterilizes' the patient within a few doses to prevent transmission.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Distinguish between Type 1 (Reversal) and Type 2 (ENL) lepra reactions based on their immunological hypersensitivity classification.
back:
• Type 1: Type IV Hypersensitivity (Delayed/Cell-mediated)
• Type 2: Type III Hypersensitivity (Immune complex-mediated)
• Type 1 causes nerve tenderness; Type 2 causes systemic vasculitis.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: How is the total duration of WHO MDT for Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy different from Multibacillary (MB) leprosy?
back:
• PB Leprosy: 6 months of treatment
• MB Leprosy: 12 months of treatment
• Both are completed within a maximum timeframe (e.g., 9 months for PB).

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: According to the WHO classification, leprosy is categorized as Multibacillary (MB) if there are more than [___] anesthetic skin lesions.
back:
• Five (5) skin lesions
• Any case with a positive skin smear is also classified as MB leprosy.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A 35-year-old male presents with 8 anesthetic nodules and thickened ulnar nerves. The standard WHO Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) for this patient must include [___], Dapsone, and Clofazimine.
back:
• Rifampicin
• This is the regimen for Multibacillary (MB) leprosy.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain the biological function of Rifampicin within the WHO Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) for leprosy.
back:
• Acts as a potent bactericidal agent
• Kills 99.9% of Mycobacterium leprae within days
• Allows for significantly shortened treatment durations.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the standard treatment duration for Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy and Multibacillary (MB) leprosy under WHO guidelines.
back:
• PB Leprosy: 6 months (Rifampicin + Dapsone)
• MB Leprosy: 12 months (Rifampicin + Dapsone + Clofazimine).

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Identify the drug used specifically to suppress Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL) or Type 2 Lepra reactions.
back:
• Thalidomide
• High-dose corticosteroids are an alternative if Thalidomide is unavailable.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Patients must be screened for [___] deficiency before starting the standard MDT component Dapsone due to the risk of hemolytic anemia.
back:
• Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency
• Dapsone is a sulfone that causes oxidative stress in erythrocytes.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A patient with 3 hypoesthetic skin patches is started on MDT. Two weeks later, the patches become red and swollen with new neuritis. This likely represents a [___].
back:
• Type 1 Lepra Reaction (Reversal Reaction)
• It is a delayed-type hypersensitivity (T-cell mediated) response.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain the role of Clofazimine in the management of leprosy beyond its direct antimicrobial activity.
back:
• Acts as a phenazine dye with anti-inflammatory properties
• Helps prevent and manage Type 2 (ENL) reactions during chronic therapy.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the pathophysiology of Type 1 (Reversal) reactions and Type 2 (ENL) reactions in leprosy.
back:
• Type 1: Type IV hypersensitivity (cellular immunity change)
• Type 2: Type III hypersensitivity (immune-complex mediated).

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Identify the specific side effect of Clofazimine involving the skin and eyes that patients should be counseled on before starting MB therapy.
back:
• Reddish-brown to brownish-black skin discoloration
• Discoloration of the conjunctivae.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: According to standard WHO protocols for leprosy, the three-drug regimen for multibacillary disease includes Rifampin, Dapsone, and [___].
back:
• Clofazimine
• It is a phenazine dye
• Standard for patients with positive smears at any site
• Used to prevent drug resistance and relapse

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A patient undergoing leprosy treatment presents with sudden onset jaundice, fatigue, and dark urine. Blood tests confirm methemoglobinemia and hemolysis. Identify the most likely culprit drug.
back:
• Dapsone
• Risk is highest in G6PD-deficient patients
• Can also cause Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL)
• Methemoglobinemia is common but rarely clinical

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the primary biochemical mechanism of action of Dapsone with that of Clofazimine in leprosy management.
back:
• Dapsone: Inhibits folate synthesis (dihydropteroate synthase)
• Clofazimine: Phenazine dye; mechanism is unclear; involves DNA binding
• Dapsone is bacteriostatic; Clofazimine is weakly bactericidal

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A 30-year-old presents with hypopigmented skin patches and a positive acid-fast smear. Contrast the standard drug combinations for this patient versus those with a negative smear.
back:
• Smear Positive (Multibacillary): Rifampin + Dapsone + Clofazimine
• Smear Negative (Paucibacillary): Rifampin + Dapsone only
• MB requires longer therapy (up to 12 months)

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Identify the primary hepatic metabolic process responsible for the elimination of Dapsone and its relevance to inter-patient variability.
back:
• Acetylation via N-acetyltransferase
• Similar to Isoniazid metabolism
• Excreted in urine as glucuronide or sulfonate conjugates
• Dosing requires adjustment in renal failure

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: In the WHO classification of leprosy for treatment purposes, 'Multibacillary' status is confirmed by a [___] smear from any site.
back:
• Positive
• Any site including skin or nasal mucosa
• Dictates the addition of Clofazimine to the regimen
• Associated with higher organism burden

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: During leprosy treatment, a patient develops painful subcutaneous nodules and fever. Identify the complication and the drug specifically indicated to suppress this reaction.
back:
• Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL)
• Suppressed by Thalidomide
• Occurs most commonly in lepromatous leprosy
• Represents a reaction to dying bacilli

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain the biological rationale for using combination therapy (MDT) rather than Dapsone monotherapy in WHO leprosy protocols.
back:
• Prevents emergence of drug-resistant M. leprae strains
• Large parasite populations readily select for resistant mutants
• MDT reduces treatment duration and relapse rates
• Ensures efficacy against potentially dapsone-resistant organisms

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the typical elimination half-lives of Dapsone and Clofazimine in human tissues.
back:
• Dapsone: 1–2 days
• Clofazimine: Approximately 2 months
• Clofazimine is highly lipophilic and stored in RE tissues
• Dapsone requires daily dosing; Clofazimine accumulates slowly

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Which standard antileprotic agent is known to cause a harmless but prominent reddish-brown discoloration of the skin and conjunctivae?
back:
• Clofazimine
• Due to its nature as a phenazine dye
• Discoloration occurs as crystals accumulate in phagocytic cells
• Reversible upon discontinuation, though slow to resolve

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Under the WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) guidelines, the paucibacillary (PB) protocol requires the patient to self-administer a 100 mg daily dose of [___] for exactly six months.
back: * Dapsone * Bacteriostatic agent that inhibits bacterial folate synthesis * Standard PB therapy duration is 6 months * Self-administered daily by the patient to maintain effective therapeutic blood levels.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A 35-year-old male presents with 7 anesthetic skin lesions and a positive acid-fast bacilli slit-skin smear. Identify the WHO classification and the recommended duration of therapy.
back: * Multibacillary (MB) leprosy * Recommended treatment duration: 12 months * Standard regimen involves Rifampicin, Dapsone, and Clofazimine * Clinical diagnosis is based on positive slit-skin smears and multiple anesthetic lesions.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Describe the biochemical mechanism of action of Rifampicin in the multidrug treatment of leprosy.
back: * Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase * Blocks transcription by binding specifically to the beta-subunit * Bactericidal against leprosy bacilli * Essential for rapid bacterial killing and reducing the risk of drug resistance.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the standard WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) for Paucibacillary (PB) versus Multibacillary (MB) leprosy in terms of drug count and duration.
back: * PB: 2 drugs (Rifampicin, Dapsone) given for a 6-month duration * MB: 3 drugs (Rifampicin, Dapsone, Clofazimine) given for 12 months * PB protocol requires negative slit-skin smears.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: State the standard monthly supervised dose of Rifampicin used in the treatment of both paucibacillary and multibacillary leprosy.
back: * 600 mg Rifampicin * Administered once every 28 days under direct medical supervision * Applied in both PB and MB protocols * Key for preventing the emergence of resistant leprosy strains.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: In the classification of leprosy for WHO MDT purposes, a case exhibiting only 1 to 5 hypopigmented skin lesions and negative skin smears is designated as [___].
back: * Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy * Requires a two-drug regimen including Rifampicin and Dapsone * Treatment duration is exactly 6 months * Characterized clinically by five or fewer hypopigmented lesions.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A patient undergoing treatment for multibacillary leprosy presents with reddish-brown skin discoloration and dry skin (ichthyosis). Name the causative drug and its storage property.
back: * Clofazimine * A highly lipophilic phenazine dye * Stored within the reticuloendothelial system and macrophages * Causes characteristic reddish-brown skin discoloration and potentially significant conjunctival hyperpigmentation.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain the biological mechanism of Thalidomide when used to manage Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL) reactions during leprosy therapy.
back: * Suppresses tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) production * Modulates cellular cytokine response * Specifically used to treat Type 2 Lepra reactions like Erythema Nodosum Leprosum * Contraindicated in pregnancy due to extreme teratogenicity.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Distinguish between the slit-skin smear findings associated with Paucibacillary (PB) versus Multibacillary (MB) leprosy according to WHO definitions.
back: * Paucibacillary (PB): Slit-skin smear must be negative at all tested sites * Multibacillary (MB): Slit-skin smear is positive at any anatomical site * Smear results guide therapy intensity.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Identify the primary metabolic toxicity of Dapsone that results in Heinz body formation and anemia in susceptible patients.
back: * Oxidative hemolysis and anemia * Occurs primarily in patients with Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency * Results in Heinz body formation and methemoglobinemia * Mandatory screening before initiating therapy.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: The primary anti-leprosy agent that acts as a structural analog of p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) to inhibit folate synthesis is [___].
back:
• Dapsone
• Acts as a folate synthesis antagonist.
• Bacteriostatic against M. leprae.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A 30-year-old male with lepromatous leprosy begins WHO multi-drug therapy (MDT). One week later, he presents with sudden onset of fever, painful subcutaneous nodules, and arthralgia. This reaction is likely [___].
back:
• Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (Type 2 Lepra Reaction)
• Occurs primarily in lepromatous leprosy.
• Managed with Thalidomide or corticosteroids.

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the WHO-recommended Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) regimens for Paucibacillary (PB) versus Multibacillary (MB) leprosy.
back:
• Paucibacillary: Rifampin + Dapsone (for 6 months).
• Multibacillary: Rifampin + Dapsone + Clofazimine (for 12 months).

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A leprosy patient with G6PD deficiency presents with pallor and dark urine shortly after starting therapy. Contrast the likely drug cause of this reaction with the drug that causes skin discoloration.
back:
• Hemolysis cause: Dapsone (oxidative stress in G6PD deficiency).
• Skin discoloration cause: Clofazimine (reddish-brown to black pigmentary changes).

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Identify the specific role and standard WHO frequency of Rifampin administration in the treatment of leprosy.
back:
• Role: Most potent bactericidal agent against M. leprae.
• Frequency: 600 mg administered once monthly (supervised).

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: According to standard WHO protocols, leprosy is classified as [___] if a skin smear is positive from any site of infection.
back:
• Multibacillary (MB) leprosy
• Requires triple drug therapy (Rifampin, Dapsone, Clofazimine).
• Standard treatment duration is 12 months.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Penicillins inhibit bacterial growth by covalently binding to [___] and halting the transpeptidation reaction of cell wall synthesis.
back:
• Penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)
• This blocks cross-linking of peptidoglycan
• Leads to cell wall instability and autolysin-mediated lysis.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: An 8-year-old child presents with permanent yellowish-brown discoloration of the teeth and enamel hypoplasia. Which antibiotic class, if used in early childhood, is the likely cause?
back:
• Tetracyclines
• They chelate calcium in newly formed bone and teeth
• Contraindicated in pregnancy and children under 8 years.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain how Vancomycin carries out its biological function in inhibiting cell wall synthesis.
back:
• Binds firmly to the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of nascent peptidoglycan
• Inhibits transglycosylase to prevent chain elongation
• Prevents cross-linking, weakening the cell wall.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the binding dynamics and resulting effects of Aminoglycosides versus Tetracyclines on the 30S ribosomal subunit.
back:
• Aminoglycosides: Irreversible binding; cause mRNA misreading and block initiation (Bactericidal).
• Tetracyclines: Reversible binding; block aminoacyl-tRNA from entering the A-site (Bacteriostatic).

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Name the enzyme inhibited by Sulfonamides and explain the competitive nature of this interaction.
back:
• Dihydropteroate synthase
• Sulfonamides are structural analogs of p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA)
• They competitively inhibit the first step of folate synthesis.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Fluoroquinolones block bacterial DNA synthesis by primarily inhibiting [___] in Gram-negative bacteria.
back:
• DNA gyrase (Topoisomerase II)
• Prevents the relaxation of positively supercoiled DNA
• Required for normal transcription and replication.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A 24-year-old athlete treated for a respiratory infection develops acute pain and a palpable gap in the posterior ankle. Which antibiotic class was likely used?
back:
• Fluoroquinolones
• Associated with tendinitis and tendon rupture
• Risk increases with age, renal insufficiency, or corticosteroid use.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the biochemical activation required for Metronidazole to exert its toxic effects on anaerobic pathogens.
back:
• Requires non-enzymatic chemical reduction of its nitro group
• Reduction is catalyzed by reduced ferredoxin in anaerobic cells
• Reactive products damage bacterial DNA and proteins.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the primary toxicities of Gentamicin and Streptomycin within the inner ear.
back:
• Gentamicin: Primarily vestibulotoxic (vertigo, ataxia) and nephrotoxic.
• Streptomycin: Primarily vestibulotoxic; often causes irreversible vertigo and loss of balance.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the idiosyncratic, dose-independent hematologic toxicity specifically associated with Chloramphenicol use.
back:
• Aplastic anemia
• Usually irreversible and potentially fatal
• Distinct from the dose-related, reversible bone marrow suppression.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: The benzimidazole class of drugs, such as mebendazole and albendazole, exert their antihelminthic effect primarily by inhibiting [___].
back:
• Microtubule synthesis
• Binds to β-tubulin to prevent polymerization
• Results in impaired glucose uptake and parasite death

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient being treated for Onchocerca volvulus with ivermectin develops fever, headache, and a papular rash 24 hours after the first dose. This reaction is primarily caused by [___].
back:
• Release of proteins/antigens from dying microfilariae
• Termed a Mazotti-like reaction
• Often managed with corticosteroids if severe

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the cellular mechanism by which Praziquantel induces paralysis and dislodgment in trematodes like Schistosoma.
back:
• Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium ions
• Induces massive muscle contraction
• Leads to tegumental damage, paralysis, and detachment from host tissues

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the drug of choice for neurocysticercosis with the drug of choice for intestinal tapeworms regarding their pharmacokinetic interaction with corticosteroids.
back:
• Albendazole (Neurocysticercosis): Bioavailability is increased by dexamethasone
• Praziquantel (Tapeworms): Bioavailability is markedly reduced (up to 50%) by corticosteroids

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the neuromuscular mechanism by which Pyrantel pamoate causes the expulsion of Ascaris lumbricoides.
back:
• Acts as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent
• Stimulates acetylcholine release and inhibits cholinesterase
• Causes spastic paralysis; worms are then expelled by host peristalsis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: In the treatment of lymphatic filariasis, doxycycline acts as a macrofilaricide by targeting [___], an intracellular bacterial symbiont of the parasite.
back:
• Wolbachia species
• Essential for filarial survival and reproduction
• Loss of symbiont leads to sterility and eventual adult worm death

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient with a heavy load of Loa loa is treated with diethylcarbamazine and develops retinal hemorrhages and encephalopathy. These severe adverse effects are attributed to [___].
back:
• Host inflammatory response to antigens from rapidly killed microfilariae
• Risk increases with microfilarial load (>2500/mL)
• May require pretreatment with albendazole or apheresis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the specific ionic mechanism and physiological consequence of Ivermectin in susceptible nematodes.
back:
• Targets glutamate-gated chloride channels
• Intensifies GABA-mediated transmission
• Induces hyperpolarization resulting in flaccid paralysis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Distinguish between the primary clinical risks of short-term (1-3 days) versus long-term (months) Albendazole therapy.
back:
• Short-term: Minimal risks (mild GI distress, headache)
• Long-term (Hydatid/Cysticercosis): Hepatotoxicity (elevated enzymes), alopecia, and bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia)

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: State the most critical contraindication for using Thiabendazole and why it is no longer a first-line agent.
back:
• Contraindication: Pregnancy and liver/renal disease
• Rationale: Extremely high toxicity (SJS, liver failure) compared to better-tolerated agents like ivermectin/albendazole

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Benzimidazoles like Albendazole exert their primary antihelminthic effect by binding to parasite β-tubulin, which directly inhibits [___].
back:
• Microtubule polymerization/synthesis.
• Leads to impaired glucose uptake.
• Results in depletion of glycogen stores and parasite death.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient treated for Onchocerciasis develops fever, pruritus, and tender lymphadenopathy 24 hours after a dose of Ivermectin. These findings are characteristic of the [___].
back:
• Mazzotti reaction.
• Caused by the host immune response to dying microfilariae.
• Managed with corticosteroids or antihistamines.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the mechanism by which Praziquantel induces tegumental damage and paralysis in trematodes.
back:
• Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium ions.
• Induces strong muscular contraction and spastic paralysis.
• Causes tegumental vacuolization and dislodgement from host tissues.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the effect of concomitant corticosteroid administration on the bioavailability of Praziquantel versus Albendazole in the management of neurocysticercosis.
back:
• Praziquantel: Bioavailability is significantly decreased by corticosteroids.
• Albendazole: Bioavailability is increased by corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone), enhancing clinical efficacy.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary physiological effect of Pyrantel pamoate on the nematode neuromuscular junction.
back:
• Acts as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent.
• Induces persistent activation of nicotinic receptors.
• Causes spastic paralysis, leading to expulsion of the worm.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: In the treatment of lymphatic filariasis, Doxycycline acts indirectly by targeting [___], an obligate intracellular bacterial symbiont.
back:
• Wolbachia.
• Bacterial death leads to sterility and death of adult filarial worms.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A 40-year-old patient on high-dose Albendazole for hydatid disease presents with hair loss and a low white cell count. These adverse effects indicate [___].
back:
• Alopecia and Bone Marrow Suppression (Pancytopenia).
• More common with long-term therapy.
• Requires monitoring of blood counts and liver enzymes.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the mechanism by which Diethylcarbamazine facilitates the clearance of microfilariae from the host circulation.
back:
• Immobilizes microfilariae by altering their surface structure.
• Displaces them from tissues into the circulation.
• Makes them more susceptible to destruction by host phagocytes.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast Mebendazole and Albendazole in terms of their systemic absorption when targeting tissue-based helminths.
back:
• Mebendazole: Very poorly absorbed (<10%); absorption is not significantly affected by food.
• Albendazole: Erratically absorbed; systemic absorption is significantly enhanced by a fatty meal.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Name the most severe and potentially fatal dermatological adverse effect associated with Thiabendazole therapy.
back:
• Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
• This risk, along with irreversible liver failure, makes it less preferred than Ivermectin.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: The primary mechanism of action for benzimidazoles like albendazole is the inhibition of [___] synthesis via binding to β-tubulin.
back:
- Microtubule synthesis.
- Prevents polymerization of tubulin dimers.
- Disrupts glucose uptake and microtubule-dependent intracellular transport.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient treated for onchocerciasis with ivermectin develops fever, headache, pruritus, and hypotension within 24 hours. Identify the likely reaction and its pathophysiology.
back:
- Mazzotti reaction.
- Caused by the rapid killing of microfilariae.
- Result of the release of parasitic antigens and subsequent host immune response.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain how Praziquantel induces paralysis and dislodgement of trematodes and cestodes.
back:
- Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium ions.
- Triggers strong muscular contraction followed by spastic paralysis.
- Causes tegumental damage, leading to parasite disintegration.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the physiologic state of the worm following treatment with Ivermectin versus Praziquantel.
back:
- Ivermectin: Induces flaccid paralysis by intensifying GABA-mediated inhibitory signals.
- Praziquantel: Induces spastic paralysis by increasing calcium influx.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the indirect mechanism by which Doxycycline exerts anti-filarial effects against Wuchereria bancrofti.
back:
- Targets Wolbachia, an intracellular bacterial symbiont.
- Depletion of Wolbachia causes sterility in adult worms.
- Eventually leads to the death of the adult filarial parasite.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Praziquantel increases the permeability of trematode cell membranes to [___], resulting in rapid contraction and paralysis.
back:
- Calcium ions (Ca2+).
- Leads to spastic contraction.
- Facilitates host immune clearance of the parasite.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A child being treated for a common pinworm infection (Enterobius vermicularis) receives a drug that acts as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker. Identify the drug and its primary side effects.
back:
- Pyrantel pamoate.
- Mild GI upset (nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps).
- Transient dizziness or headache.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe how Diethylcarbamazine facilitates the clearance of microfilariae by the host immune system.
back:
- Immobilizes microfilariae by altering their surface structure.
- Displaces parasites from tissues into the circulation.
- Enhances recognition and destruction by host immune defenses.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the metabolic consequences of microtubule inhibition by Albendazole in intestinal nematodes.
back:
- Prevents polymerization of tubulin dimers into microtubules.
- Inhibits microtubule-dependent glucose absorption.
- Depletes glycogen stores, resulting in metabolic exhaustion and parasite death.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary contraindication for Praziquantel use in the treatment of cysticercosis.
back:
- Ocular cysticercosis.
- Inflammation from dying larvae can cause permanent eye damage.
- Requires ophthalmologic clearance before therapy.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Albendazole and other benzimidazoles exert their antihelminthic effects by primarily inhibiting [___].
back:
• Microtubule synthesis
• Binds to β-tubulin to prevent polymerization
• Blocks glucose uptake in parasites
• Results in parasite immobilization and death

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A 35-year-old patient undergoing long-term high-dose therapy for hydatid disease develops a low white blood cell count. This drug-induced toxicity is [___].
back:
• Bone marrow suppression (Pancytopenia)
• Occurs during prolonged Albendazole use
• Requires regular blood count monitoring
• Often accompanied by elevated liver enzymes

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the mechanism of action of Praziquantel in the treatment of schistosome infections.
back:
• Increases calcium permeability of cell membranes
• Causes strong muscular contraction and paralysis
• Leads to tegumental damage and dislodgement
• Parasites are subsequently destroyed by host defenses

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the risks of treating Taenia solium infection with Niclosamide versus Praziquantel.
back:
• Niclosamide: Kills adults only; released eggs may hatch, theoretically increasing cysticercosis risk
• Praziquantel: Kills both adults and larval stages
• Praziquantel is preferred for active neurocysticercosis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: How does Pyrantel Pamoate achieve the expulsion of Ascaris lumbricoides?
back:
• Acts as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker
• Induces release of acetylcholine and inhibits cholinesterase
• Causes spastic paralysis of the worm
• Parasites are expelled live by normal peristalsis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Ivermetin paralyzes nematodes and arthropods by intensifying [___]-mediated neurotransmission.
back:
• γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)
• Targets glutamate-gated chloride channels
• Increases membrane permeability to chloride ions
• Results in hyperpolarization and muscle paralysis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient treated for Strongyloides develops dizziness, hallucinations, and later, fatal Stevens-Johnson syndrome. These severe toxicities are associated with [___].
back:
• Thiabendazole
• Significantly more toxic than other benzimidazoles
• Can cause irreversible liver failure
• Also associated with severe neuropsychiatric symptoms

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the indirect mechanism by which Doxycycline acts as a macrofilaricidal agent against Wuchereria bancrofti.
back:
• Targets and kills intracellular Wolbachia bacteria
• Wolbachia is an essential endosymbiont for filarial survival
• Results in sterility and eventual death of adult worms
• Superior to drugs targeting only microfilariae

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the absorption and systemic activity of Mebendazole versus Albendazole.
back:
• Mebendazole: <10% absorbed; active mainly against intraluminal parasites
• Albendazole: Variable absorption (increased by fatty meals)
• Albendazole: Rapidly converted to active sulfoxide metabolite for systemic/tissue activity

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary adverse reaction seen during the treatment of Onchocerciasis with Ivermectin.
back:
• Mazzotti reaction
• Caused by host response to dying microfilariae
• Symptoms: Fever, headache, rash, hypotension, and lymphadenopathy
• Usually requires corticosteroid management in severe cases

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Benzimidazoles like albendazole and mebendazole primarily exert their antihelminthic effect by inhibiting [___] synthesis in nematodes.
back:
*   Microtubule polymerization
*   Binds to β-tubulin to prevent dimer formation
*   Blocks glucose uptake in the parasite
*   Leads to parasite immobilization and death

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient being treated for Onchocerca volvulus with ivermectin develops fever, pruritus, and tender lymphadenopathy. Identify this clinical reaction and its cause.
back:
*   Mazzotti reaction
*   Caused by host immune response to antigens released from dying microfilariae
*   Symptoms peak 2 days post-treatment
*   Managed with corticosteroids if severe

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism by which Praziquantel induces spastic paralysis in trematodes and cestodes.
back:
*   Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium ions
*   Triggers massive calcium influx
*   Causes immediate muscular contraction followed by paralysis
*   Results in parasite detachment from host tissues

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the neuromuscular mechanisms of action between Pyrantel Pamoate and Piperazine in the treatment of Ascaris lumbricoides.
back:
*   Pyrantel: Acts as a nicotinic agonist and cholinesterase inhibitor causing spastic paralysis.
*   Piperazine: Acts as a GABA agonist at the myoneural junction causing flaccid paralysis.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the unique indirect mechanism by which Doxycycline acts as a macrofilaricide against Wuchereria bancrofti.
back:
*   Kills Wolbachia (intracellular bacterial symbionts)
*   Deprives the filarial parasite of essential survival factors
*   Leads to sterility and eventual death of adult worms

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: For the radical cure of Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale, the drug of choice targeting dormant liver hypnozoites is [___].
back:
*   Primaquine
*   The only agent effective against hypnozoites
*   Requires screening for G6PD deficiency before initiation
*   Prevents clinical relapse of malaria

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient with neurocysticercosis is prescribed Albendazole and Dexamethasone concurrently. What is the clinical rationale for this combination?
back:
*   Dexamethasone reduces inflammation caused by dying cysticerci
*   Prevents seizures and intracranial hypertension
*   Increases plasma concentrations of the active metabolite, albendazole sulfoxide

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: How does Diethylcarbamazine facilitate the clearance of microfilariae from the host's tissues?
back:
*   Immobilizes microfilariae by altering surface structures
*   Displaces them from tissues into the general circulation
*   Increases susceptibility to host immune destruction via phagocytosis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Distinguish between the adverse effects of Albendazole seen in short-term versus long-term (e.g., hydatid disease) therapy.
back:
*   Short-term (1-3 days): Generally asymptomatic; mild GI distress.
*   Long-term (months): Hepatotoxicity (elevated LFTs), alopecia, and bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia).

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary toxicities that restrict the clinical use of Thiabendazole compared to other benzimidazoles.
back:
*   Neuropsychiatric symptoms (hallucinations, dizziness)
*   Severe gastrointestinal distress (nausea, vomiting)
*   Risk of irreversible liver failure
*   Rare, fatal Stevens-Johnson syndrome

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: The primary mechanism of action for Albendazole involves the inhibition of [___] polymerization by binding to β-tubulin.
back:
• Inhibits microtubule synthesis.
• Prevents parasite glucose uptake.
• Leads to gradual immobilization and eventual death of the helminth.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient undergoing treatment for Onchocerciasis with Ivermectin develops fever, pruritus, and tender lymphadenopathy. This reaction is primarily due to [___].
back:
• Host inflammatory response to dying microfilariae (Mazzotti reaction).
• Managed with corticosteroids or antihistamines.
• Not a direct drug toxicity.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the physiological mechanism by which Praziquantel induces the dislodgement of schistosomes from the mesenteric vessels.
back:
• Increases cell membrane permeability to Calcium ions.
• Induces strong muscular contraction and spastic paralysis.
• Causes vacuolization and disintegration of the parasite tegument.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the neuromuscular effects of Pyrantel pamoate with Ivermectin on intestinal nematodes.
back:
• Pyrantel: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker (ACh release/cholinesterase inhibition) causing spastic paralysis.
• Ivermectin: Potentiates GABA-mediated inhibitory signals causing flaccid paralysis.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Name the specific adverse effect requiring monitoring during long-term Albendazole therapy for hydatid cysts (Echinococcosis).
back:
• Hepatotoxicity (elevated liver enzymes).
• Bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia).
• Monitoring: Periodic CBC and liver function tests.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Diethylcarbamazine acts by [___] microfilariae, allowing host immune mechanisms to destroy the parasite.
back:
• Immobilizing the microfilariae.
• Altering their surface structures.
• Displacing them from tissue to accessible areas for host defense.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient being treated for Giardiasis experiences severe vomiting and flushing after consuming a glass of wine. This drug's mechanism of action involves [___].
back:
• Reduction to reactive intermediates in anaerobic cells.
• DNA damage and biochemical disruption.
• Drug: Metronidazole (Disulfiram-like reaction).

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the indirect mechanism by which Doxycycline acts as a macrofilaricidal agent against Wuchereria bancrofti.
back:
• Targets Wolbachia, an intracellular bacterial symbiont.
• Kills the bacteria essential for filarial survival.
• Results in adult worm sterility and death.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Distinguish between the safety profiles of the benzimidazoles Mebendazole and Thiabendazole.
back:
• Mebendazole: Very safe; poorly absorbed with minimal systemic toxicity.
• Thiabendazole: Highly toxic; risk of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and irreversible liver failure.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: List the most severe central nervous system (CNS) adverse effect associated with Diethylcarbamazine in patients with high Loa loa microfilarial loads.
back:
• Encephalopathy.
• Retinal hemorrhages.
• Often associated with fever and headache due to massive parasite destruction.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: The primary biochemical mechanism by which benzimidazoles, such as Albendazole and Mebendazole, exert their antihelminthic effect is through the inhibition of [___].
back:
• Microtubule synthesis
• This involves binding to fungal β-tubulin
• Resulting in structural disruption and cell death

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A 30-year-old traveler returning from West Africa receives Ivermectin for Onchocerciasis. Within 24 hours, he develops high fever, generalized pruritus, and tender lymphadenopathy. This clinical presentation is known as the [___].
back:
• Mazzotti reaction
• Caused by the host immune response to proteins released from dying microfilariae
• Managed with corticosteroids if severe

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the role of calcium permeability in the mechanism of action of Praziquantel against trematodes and cestodes.
back:
• Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium
• Leads to rapid calcium influx
• Causes massive muscle contraction and spastic paralysis of the worm

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the drug-drug interaction effect of concomitant corticosteroid use on the bioavailability of Albendazole versus Praziquantel in neurocysticercosis therapy.
back:
• Albendazole: Dexamethasone increases its active sulfoxide metabolite levels
• Praziquantel: Corticosteroids significantly decrease its plasma concentrations
• Clinical significance: Albendazole is often preferred for brain cysts

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary neuromuscular effect of Pyrantel Pamoate that results in the expulsion of Ascarids from the host GI tract.
back:
• Acts as a neuromuscular blocking agent
• Stimulates acetylcholine release and inhibits cholinesterase
• Causes spastic paralysis; worms are expelled by normal peristalsis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: In the treatment of lymphatic filariasis, Doxycycline acts indirectly as a macrofilaricide by targeting the intracellular bacterial symbiont [___].
back:
• Wolbachia
• Essential for the survival and reproduction of the filarial worms
• Depletion leads to sterility and eventual death of adult worms

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient with refractory Strongyloidiasis is prescribed Thiabendazole. Despite its efficacy, the drug is rarely used now due to its potential for [___] and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
back:
• Irreversible liver failure
• Thiabendazole is significantly more toxic than Ivermectin or Albendazole
• Neuropsychiatric symptoms are also common side effects

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the physiological mechanism by which Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) clears microfilariae from the host circulation.
back:
• Immobilizes microfilariae and alters their surface structure
• Makes parasites susceptible to host phagocytosis
• Does not directly kill adult worms rapidly

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Distinguish between the typical adverse effect profile of short-term Albendazole use (1-3 days) and the risks associated with long-term use (e.g., in hydatid disease).
back:
• Short-term: Mild GI distress, headache, dizziness
• Long-term: Hepatotoxicity (elevated LFTs), pancytopenia, and reversible alopecia
• Requirement: Monitor blood counts and liver function regularly

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the rare but serious cardiac adverse effect requiring EKG monitoring during the administration of Sodium Stibogluconate for Leishmaniasis.
back:
• QT interval prolongation
• Can lead to dangerous arrhythmias
• Other effects: T-wave changes and muscle pain

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: The primary bacteriostatic drug in the WHO leprosy protocol that inhibits the enzyme [___] to block folate synthesis is Dapsone.
back:
• Dihydropteroate synthase
• Acts as a structural analog of p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA)
• Essential component of Multidrug Therapy (MDT) to prevent resistance

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A 40-year-old on leprosy treatment develops dark skin pigmentation and nausea. Laboratory findings show drug crystals in phagocytic cells. Which medication is responsible?
back:
• Clofazimine
• Phenazine dye that accumulates in the reticuloendothelial system
• Side effect: Reversible reddish-brown skin and conjunctival discoloration

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain the mechanism by which Rifampicin provides a diagnostic contrast to Dapsone regarding their bacterial killing rates.
back:
• Rifampicin: Highly bactericidal (kills 99.9% of bacilli in one dose)
• Dapsone: Primarily bacteriostatic
• Rifampicin targets RNA polymerase; Dapsone targets folate synthesis

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A patient has 3 anesthetic skin lesions, while another has 10. Contrast the specific WHO-recommended drug regimens and treatment durations for these two cases.
back:
• 3 lesions (Paucibacillary): Rifampicin + Dapsone for 6 months
• 10 lesions (Multibacillary): Rifampicin + Dapsone + Clofazimine for 12 months
• Multibacillary requires triple therapy and longer duration

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Which pharmacological agent is used to suppress the severe Type 2 reaction (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum) seen in lepromatous leprosy patients?
back:
• Thalidomide
• Potent anti-inflammatory used when corticosteroids are insufficient
• Standard MDT must be continued during the reaction

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: According to WHO diagnostic criteria, a patient is classified as having Multibacillary (MB) leprosy if they present with more than [___] skin lesions.
back:
• Five (5) lesions
• MB is also diagnosed if skin smears are positive at any site
• Requires 12 months of triple-drug therapy

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: A patient starting MDT for leprosy presents with fatigue, jaundice, and a significant drop in hemoglobin. This clinical scenario most likely indicates a deficiency in which enzyme?
back:
• Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD)
• Dapsone causes oxidative stress and acute hemolysis in deficient individuals
• Heinz bodies are often seen on peripheral smear

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Explain the biological rationale for adding Clofazimine to the drug regimen for Multibacillary (MB) leprosy but not for Paucibacillary (PB) cases.
back:
• MB has a massive organism burden (up to 10^10 bacilli)
• Third drug prevents selection of dapsone-resistant mutants
• Clofazimine also suppresses ENL reactions common in high-burden cases

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Contrast the physiological metabolic loops inhibited by Dapsone and Rifampicin within the Mycobacterium leprae organism.
back:
• Dapsone: Folate synthesis loop (competitive PABA antagonism)
• Rifampicin: Protein synthesis initiation (DNA-dependent RNA polymerase inhibition)
• MDT blocks two distinct essential survival pathways simultaneously

category: Explain standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of leprosy
front: Identify the biochemical class to which the anti-leprosy drug Clofazimine belongs.
back:
• Phenazine dye
• Highly lipophilic molecule
• Stored extensively in skin and reticuloendothelial tissues

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: The benzimidazole class of antihelminthics, including albendazole and mebendazole, primarily exert their effect by inhibiting [___] synthesis in nematodes.
back:
• Microtubule synthesis inhibition
• Binds to parasite β-tubulin
• Prevents glucose uptake and depletes glycogen stores

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A 30-year-old patient being treated for Onchocerciasis develops fever, pruritus, and tender lymphadenopathy 24 hours after the first dose of Ivermectin. This reaction is primarily caused by [___].
back:
• Mazzotti-like reaction
• Triggered by the rapid release of antigens from dying microfilariae
• Managed with antihistamines or corticosteroids if severe

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the specific mechanism by which Praziquantel induces paralysis and dislodgement of schistosomes and cestodes.
back:
• Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium
• Induces spastic muscular contraction and paralysis
• Results in sucker detachment from the host's vessel walls

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the neuromuscular mechanisms of Pyrantel Pamoate and Piperazine in the treatment of Ascariasis, explaining why they should not be co-administered.
back:
• Pyrantel: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker (spastic paralysis)
• Piperazine: GABA agonist causing hyperpolarization (flaccid paralysis)
• Co-administration causes pharmacological antagonism as they have opposite effects at the myoneural junction

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the systemic adverse effects associated with Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) use in patients with high Loa loa worm burdens.
back:
• Fever, papular rash, and arthralgia (antigen release)
• Retinal hemorrhages
• Encephalopathy (rare but life-threatening complication)

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Pyrantel pamoate acts as a [___] blocking agent that causes spastic paralysis in susceptible helminths like pinworms and ascarids.
back:
• Neuromuscular blocking agent
• Triggers excessive release of acetylcholine
• Inhibits cholinesterase

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient on a 6-month course of Albendazole for hydatid disease requires regular monitoring of [___] due to potential cumulative toxicity.
back:
• Liver function tests (risk of hepatotoxicity)
• Complete blood counts (risk of pancytopenia/agranulocytosis)
• Monitor monthly during prolonged therapy

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the indirect mechanism of action of Doxycycline when used in the treatment of lymphatic filariasis or onchocerciasis.
back:
• Kills Wolbachia (obligate intracellular bacterial symbiont)
• Disrupts the symbiosis required for worm survival
• Leads to sterility and eventual death of adult female worms

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the safety profiles of Iodoquinol and Paromomycin when used as luminal amebicides.
back:
• Iodoquinol: Risk of neurotoxicity and optic neuropathy with prolonged use; contains iodine
• Paromomycin: Aminoglycoside; minimal absorption but can accumulate in renal failure

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: State the primary mechanism of action and the specific species targeted by Metrifonate.
back:
• Mechanism: Organophosphate cholinesterase inhibition (paralyzes adult worms)
• Target: Schistosoma haematobium
• Note: Not available in the USA; ineffective against S. mansoni

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Albendazole and mebendazole primarily exert their antihelminthic effect by inhibiting [___] synthesis in nematodes.
back:
• Microtubule. These drugs bind to β-tubulin, preventing polymerization into microtubules.
• This disruption inhibits essential glucose uptake and transport.
• This eventually leads to parasite immobilization and death.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A 30-year-old male is treated for onchocerciasis with ivermectin. Within 24 hours, he develops fever, headache, and a severe pruritic rash. Explain the pathophysiology of this reaction.
back:
• Mazzotti reaction.
• Host inflammatory response to antigens released from dying microfilariae.
• It is not direct drug toxicity.
• Symptoms include fever, tachycardia, rash, and lymphadenopathy.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the specific ion-channel mechanism by which Praziquantel causes paralysis in schistosomes and cestodes.
back:
• Increases cell membrane permeability to Calcium ions.
• Results in massive worm contraction and tegumental damage.
• Leads to rapid paralysis, dislodgement, and death of schistosomes.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: In a clinical setting for Ascariasis, contrast the physiological type of paralysis induced by Pyrantel pamoate with that induced by Piperazine.
back:
• Pyrantel Pamoate: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker causing spastic paralysis via ACh release and cholinesterase inhibition.
• Piperazine: GABA agonist causing hyperpolarization and flaccid paralysis at the myoneural junction.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary ionic/neurotransmitter mechanism of action of Ivermectin in paralyzing nematodes.
back:
• Intensifies γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-mediated transmission in peripheral nerves.
• Causes hyperpolarization and paralysis of the nematode.
• Prevents release of microfilariae from the uteri of adult female worms.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: The most significant dose-related adverse effect of [___] used in neurocysticercosis is a symptomatic inflammatory reaction resulting in headache, seizures, and meningismus.
back:
• Praziquantel.
• Reaction is caused by proteins released from dying parasites in the brain.
• It is typically managed by co-administration of corticosteroids to reduce inflammation.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient with suspected neurocysticercosis is prescribed Albendazole. Name a drug class or specific medication that, if co-administered, increases the plasma levels of its active metabolite.
back:
• Dexamethasone or Praziquantel.
• These medications increase the bioavailability of albendazole sulfoxide.
• This interaction enhances therapeutic efficacy against tissue-dwelling larval stages.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the cellular mechanism by which Doxycycline provides macrofilaricidal activity against Wuchereria bancrofti.
back:
• Targets Wolbachia, an essential intracellular bacterial endosymbiont of the parasite.
• Bacterial depletion inhibits microfilarial production and causes female sterility.
• Eventually results in the death of adult macrofilariae.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Distinguish the adverse effect profiles between short-term use and long-term (e.g., Hydatid disease) Albendazole therapy.
back:
• Short-term: Generally well-tolerated with mild GIT upset or headache.
• Long-term: Risk of hepatotoxicity (elevated enzymes), alopecia, and bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia).

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Mention the specific severe toxicities that strictly limit the clinical use of Thiabendazole compared to newer benzimidazoles.
back:
• High systemic toxicity including nausea, dizziness, and neuropsychiatric symptoms.
• Potential for irreversible liver failure.
• Rare reports of fatal Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Benzimidazoles like albendazole and mebendazole exert their antihelminthic effect by specifically inhibiting [___] synthesis in nematodes.
back:
* Microtubule synthesis
* Prevents polymerization of tubulin
* Disrupts parasite glucose uptake and intracellular transport

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A 35-year-old male with neurocysticercosis is started on praziquantel. Shortly after, he develops severe headache, vomiting, and meningismus. These symptoms primarily result from [___].
back:
* Inflammatory response to dying larvae
* Release of parasite antigens into host tissues
* Exacerbated by immune recognition of destroyed organisms

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the mechanism by which Pyrantel pamoate causes expulsion of intestinal nematodes.
back:
* Acts as a neuromuscular blocking agent
* Stimulates release of acetylcholine and inhibits cholinesterase
* Results in spastic paralysis of the worm
* Facilitates expulsion via normal host peristalsis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the physiological targets and resulting effects of Ivermectin and Pyrantel pamoate on nematode movement.
back:
* Ivermectin: Intensifies GABA-mediated transmission; causes flaccid paralysis.
* Pyrantel pamoate: Targets nicotinic receptors/cholinesterase; causes spastic paralysis.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the systemic 'Mazzotti-like' reaction frequently seen during the treatment of Onchocerciasis with Ivermectin.
back:
* Host immune response to dying microfilariae
* Symptoms: Fever, headache, pruritus, and lymphadenopathy
* Intensity correlates with skin microfilarial load

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Praziquantel's efficacy against trematodes and cestodes is based on its ability to increase cell membrane permeability to [___], leading to contraction and paralysis.
back:
* Calcium ions ($Ca^{2+}$)
* Causes rapid vacuolization of the parasite tegument
* Results in parasite dislodgment and death

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient being treated for Loa loa with Diethylcarbamazine develops high fever, papular rash, and joint pain on the first day. This reaction is best described as [___].
back:
* Allergic response to released parasite proteins
* Triggered by the rapid destruction of microfilariae
* Can include retinal hemorrhage or encephalopathy in heavy infections

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: How does Doxycycline act as a macrofilaricidal agent against Wuchereria bancrofti despite being a traditional antibacterial antibiotic?
back:
* Targets intracellular Wolbachia bacteria
* Wolbachia is an essential bacterial symbiont for filarial survival
* Killing the bacteria leads to sterility and death of adult worms

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the primary adverse effects of short-term versus long-term (e.g., for hydatid disease) Albendazole therapy.
back:
* Short-term: Mild GI distress and headache.
* Long-term: Hepatotoxicity (elevated enzymes), alopecia, and bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia).

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Name the primary severe adverse effects of Thiabendazole that have led to its replacement by ivermectin or other benzimidazoles.
back:
* High systemic toxicity
* Potential for irreversible liver failure
* Risk of fatal Stevens-Johnson syndrome

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Benzimidazoles like albendazole exert their antihelminthic effects against nematodes primarily by inhibiting [___].
back:
• Binding to parasite beta-tubulin to inhibit microtubule synthesis
• Prevents polymerization of tubulin dimers into microtubules
• Disrupts essential parasite cellular processes including glucose uptake and energy metabolism
• Eventually leads to parasite immobilization and death

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient with Onchocerca volvulus infection develops fever, headache, and severe pruritus shortly after receiving a standard oral dose of ivermectin. This clinical presentation is most likely due to [___].
back:
• The Mazzotti reaction
• Occurs due to rapid killing of microfilariae and release of parasite antigens
• Triggers a host inflammatory response
• Managed with corticosteroids in severe cases to limit systemic inflammation

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the primary mechanism by which praziquantel causes paralysis and dislodgement of trematodes and cestodes.
back:
• Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium ions
• Induces marked contraction and subsequent spastic paralysis
• Causes detachment of worms from host tissues
• Leads to tegumental vacuolization and damage, allowing host immune destruction

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the clinical utility of albendazole versus mebendazole based on their systemic bioavailability.
back:
• Albendazole: Higher absorption (increased by fatty meals); reaches systemic tissues/CSF; choice for hydatid disease and neurocysticercosis
• Mebendazole: Minimal absorption (<10%); remains primarily within the gut lumen
• Primarily used for intestinal nematodes like Ascaris or pinworms

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Summarize the neuromuscular effects of pyrantel pamoate on susceptible intestinal helminths.
back:
• Acts as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent
• Stimulates release of acetylcholine and inhibits cholinesterase
• Causes spastic paralysis of the parasite
• Results in immobilization and subsequent expulsion of live worms by host peristalsis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: The drug of choice for treating Loa loa and Wuchereria bancrofti, which acts by immobilizing microfilariae through surface structure alteration, is [___].
back:
