category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the primary clinical indication and major adverse effect of the anthelminthic Bithionol.
back:
• Indication: Alternative for Fascioliasis (sheep liver fluke) and Paragonimiasis.
• Adverse Effect: Skin rashes and photosensitivity.
• Mechanism: Unknown, likely interferes with oxidative phosphorylation.
• Note: Not widely available in the USA.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The benzimidazole class of antihelminthics, including Albendazole and Mebendazole, exerts its primary effect by inhibiting [___].
back:
• Microtubule synthesis
• Binds to β-tubulin to prevent polymerization
• Blocks glucose uptake and depletes glycogen stores

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A shepherd presents with a large, unilocular cyst in the liver containing 'daughter cysts' on CT. The primary drug of choice used to treat this infection, often as an adjunct to surgery, is [___].
back:
• Albendazole
• Used for Echinococcus granulosus (Hydatid disease)
• Often given for 1–6 months to reduce cyst viability

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism by which Ivermectin induces paralysis in nematodes such as Strongyloides stercoralis.
back:
• Intensifies GABA-mediated neurotransmission
• Increases chloride channel permeability
• Causes hyperpolarization of the nerve/muscle cell
• Results in flaccid paralysis and death

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast Albendazole and Praziquantel in the management of neurocysticercosis regarding their interaction with concomitant corticosteroids.
back:
• Albendazole: Preferred; serum levels are increased by dexamethasone
• Praziquantel: Levels are decreased by up to 50% when given with corticosteroids

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: List the primary clinical indications for Diethylcarbamazine citrate in the treatment of filarial infections.
back:
• Wuchereria bancrofti (Lymphatic filariasis)
• Brugia malayi
• Loa loa (Loiasis)
• Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Praziquantel acts against trematodes and cestodes by increasing the cell membrane permeability to [___].
back:
• Calcium ions (Ca2+)
• Causes massive influx leading to muscle contraction
• Results in paralysis, dislodgement, and death

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient with Onchocerciasis (River Blindness) experiences high fever, hypotension, and bronchospasm after the first dose of treatment. This reaction is known as the [___].
back:
• Mazzotti reaction
• Caused by host immune response to dying microfilariae
• Treated with corticosteroids

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Describe the pharmacodynamic action of Pyrantel pamoate at the helminthic myoneural junction.
back:
• Acts as a neuromuscular blocking agent
• Stimulates nicotinic receptors and inhibits cholinesterase
• Results in spastic paralysis and expulsion of parasites

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the clinical utility of Mebendazole and Albendazole in terms of their systemic absorption and tissue penetration.
back:
• Mebendazole: Very low absorption (<10%); used mainly for intraluminal parasites (e.g., whipworm)
• Albendazole: Better systemic absorption/tissue penetration; preferred for tissue cysts (e.g., Hydatid, Cysticercosis)

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the specific fluke infection for which Bithionol is utilized as a primary alternative to Triclabendazole.
back:
• Fasciola hepatica (Sheep liver fluke)
• Administered orally after meals on alternate days
• Also used for Paragonimiasis

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The primary mechanism of action of benzimidazoles, such as albendazole and mebendazole, is the inhibition of [___] synthesis within the parasite.
back:
• Microtubule synthesis
• Binds to β-tubulin to prevent polymerization
• Results in impaired glucose uptake and parasite death

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 29-year-old Peruvian man presents with an incidental finding of a 10-cm fluid-filled liver cyst containing smaller daughter cysts. The most appropriate pharmacological treatment for this condition is [___].
back:
• Albendazole
• Diagnosis: Hydatid disease (Echinococcus granulosus)
• Inhibits microtubule synthesis in tissue stages
• Often used as an adjunct to surgery or aspiration

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Describe the physiological process by which Praziquantel causes the detachment and death of schistosomes (flukes).
back:
• Increases cell membrane permeability to Calcium
• Induces strong muscular contraction and spastic paralysis
• Causes vacuolization and disintegration of the parasite tegument

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient with onchocerciasis receives Ivermectin, while another with pinworms receives Pyrantel pamoate. Contrast the resulting muscular states (paralysis types) induced in their respective parasites.
back:
• Ivermectin: Flaccid paralysis (potentiates GABA-mediated inhibitory signals)
• Pyrantel pamoate: Spastic paralysis (induces ACh release and inhibits cholinesterase)

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Mention the primary clinical drug used for onchocerciasis and its specific effectiveness across different parasite life stages.
back:
• Ivermectin
• Microfilaricidal: Rapidly kills microfilariae in skin and eyes
• Not effectively macrofilaricidal: Does not kill adult worms but blocks microfilarial release

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: In the treatment of lymphatic filariasis and tropical eosinophilia, the drug [___] is considered the standard treatment of choice.
back:
• Diethylcarbamazine (DEC)
• Immobilizes microfilariae and alters their surface structure
• Facilitates host immune-mediated destruction of parasites

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient with neurocysticercosis begins albendazole therapy and suddenly develops severe headaches and seizures. Identify the underlying cause and the required adjunctive medication.
back:
• Cause: Inflammatory response to dying tissue larvae
• Adjunctive drug: Corticosteroids (e.g., Dexamethasone)
• Reduces inflammation and intracranial pressure during larval death

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which Doxycycline achieves a 'macrofilaricidal' effect in the treatment of lymphatic filariasis.
back:
• Kills Wolbachia, an intracellular bacterial symbiont of the worm
• Depletion of Wolbachia leads to sterility in adult females
• Results in gradual death of the adult filarial worms

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the metabolic targets and clinical utility of Niclosamide versus Praziquantel in the management of cestodes (tapeworms).
back:
• Niclosamide: Inhibits oxidative phosphorylation/ATPase; active only against luminal adult worms
• Praziquantel: Increases calcium permeability; active against luminal adults and tissue larvae (cysticercosis)

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the characteristic adverse reaction associated with the rapid death of microfilariae during treatment of Onchocerca or Loa loa.
back:
• Mazzotti-like reaction
• Symptoms: Fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, and tachycardia
• Mechanism: Immune response to antigens released from dying microfilariae

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The primary mechanism of action for benzimidazoles like Albendazole and Mebendazole involves the inhibition of [___] synthesis in susceptible helminths.
back:
• Inhibition of microtubule synthesis.
• Specifically binds to parasite β-tubulin.
• Prevents microtubule polymerization, leading to parasite immobilization and death.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 29-year-old shepherd presents with a large liver cyst identified as Echinococcus granulosus. To optimize the systemic absorption of the prescribed Albendazole for this tissue-based infection, the drug must be administered with [___].
back:
• A fatty meal.
• Fat significantly increases the erratic oral bioavailability of albendazole sulfoxide.
• Important for treating systemic/tissue infections rather than intraluminal ones.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the pharmacodynamic mechanism by which Pyrantel pamoate facilitates the expulsion of Ascaris lumbricoides.
back:
• Acts as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent.
• Induces persistent release of acetylcholine and inhibits cholinesterase.
• Results in spastic paralysis of the worm, which is then expelled by peristalsis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the drug-drug interaction effect of concurrent corticosteroid use on Praziquantel versus Albendazole in the treatment of neurocysticercosis.
back:
• Corticosteroids decrease the plasma bioavailability of Praziquantel.
• Corticosteroids increase the plasma levels of Albendazole sulfoxide.
• This makes Albendazole often preferred for neurocysticercosis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the drug of choice for Onchocerciasis (river blindness) and the specific immunologic reaction often triggered by the rapid death of microfilariae.
back:
• Drug: Ivermectin.
• Reaction: Mazzotti reaction.
• Symptoms: Fever, pruritus, headache, and lymphadenopathy due to dying microfilariae.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The antihelminthic agent that acts by increasing the cell membrane permeability to calcium, leading to paralysis and dislodgement of Schistosoma flukes, is [___].
back:
• Praziquantel.
• Induces parasite contraction followed by vacuolization.
• Drug of choice for all species of Schistosoma.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 10-year-old child presents with nocturnal perianal pruritus. If the Scotch tape test reveals Enterobius vermicularis eggs, what is the single-dose oral drug of choice that is available without a prescription?
back:
• Pyrantel Pamoate.
• Effectively cures pinworm in >95% of cases.
• Standard practice is to repeat the dose once after 2 weeks to prevent reinfection.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Describe the specialized role of Doxycycline in the management of lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti).
back:
• Acts indirectly by killing Wolbachia, an intracellular bacterial endosymbiont of the worm.
• Depletion of Wolbachia leads to sterility and death of adult female filarial worms.
• Offers significant macrofilaricidal activity.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the spectrum of activity of Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) and Ivermectin regarding adult filarial worms.
back:
• DEC: Microfilaricidal and often macrofilaricidal (kills adult worms).
• Ivermectin: Potently microfilaricidal but has no significant effect on adult worms (only blocks microfilarial release).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Which luminal antihelminthic is non-absorbable and acts by inhibiting oxidative phosphorylation in tapeworms such as Taenia saginata?
back:
• Niclosamide.
• Kills adult worms and scolex upon contact.
• Not effective against cysticercosis or hydatid disease as it remains in the gut lumen.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The broad-spectrum oral agent [___] acts against nematodes by inhibiting microtubule synthesis, making it the preferred drug for hydatid disease.
back:
* Albendazole.
* Rapidly metabolized in the liver to the active sulfoxide form.
* Systemic absorption increases significantly when administered with a fatty meal.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient with advanced AIDS presents with disseminated Strongyloides stercoralis infection (hyperinfection syndrome). The primary drug of choice for this condition is [___].
back:
* Ivermectin.
* Dosage: 200 mcg/kg daily for 2 days.
* Acts by intensifying GABA-mediated transmission, resulting in parasite paralysis and death.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the physiological mechanisms by which Ivermectin and Pyrantel pamoate induce paralysis in susceptible helminths.
back:
* Ivermectin: GABA agonist that causes flaccid paralysis.
* Pyrantel pamoate: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that induces spastic paralysis via acetylcholine release.
* Both facilitate the expulsion of parasites by the host.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient with multiple symptomatic parenchymal brain cysts is being started on therapy for neurocysticercosis. Contrast the clinical choice between Albendazole and Praziquantel regarding their interaction with adjunctive corticosteroids.
back:
* Albendazole: Preferred agent; corticosteroids (dexamethasone) increase its plasma levels.
* Praziquantel: Bioavailability is markedly reduced (up to 50%) by concurrent corticosteroid use.
* Albendazole also demonstrates superior subarachnoid penetration.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the therapeutic role of Diethylcarbamazine in the management of loiasis (Loa loa) and its primary mechanism against microfilariae.
back:
* Drug of choice for loiasis and tropical eosinophilia.
* Immobilizes microfilariae and alters their surface structure.
* Displaces parasites from tissues, making them susceptible to destruction by host defense mechanisms.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: In patients presenting with the classic 'creeping eruption' associated with cutaneous larva migrans, the first-line oral drug of choice is [___].
back:
* Albendazole.
* Ivermectin is a frequently used alternative.
* These agents stop the migration of hookworm larvae through the skin layers.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient being treated for Onchocerca volvulus with Ivermectin develops fever, hypotension, and lymphangitis within 24 hours of the first dose. Identify this reaction and the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
* Mazzotti-like reaction.
* Caused by the host immune response to the massive release of antigens from dying microfilariae.
* Severe cases may require treatment with corticosteroids.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Describe the indirect mechanism by which Doxycycline achieves macrofilaricidal activity against Wuchereria bancrofti.
back:
* Targets Wolbachia, an intracellular bacterial symbiont essential for filarial survival.
* Depletion of Wolbachia leads to sterility and eventual death of adult worms.
* Effective against adult worms where other drugs primarily target microfilariae.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the systemic absorption and primary clinical utility of Albendazole versus Mebendazole in treating helminthic infections.
back:
* Albendazole: Higher absorption; active sulfoxide metabolite reaches systemic tissues for hydatid disease and cysticercosis.
* Mebendazole: Minimal absorption (<10%); primarily limited to intraluminal parasites like pinworm or whipworm.
* Both inhibit microtubule synthesis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the drug of choice for the treatment of all species of Schistosomiasis and its specific effect on the parasite tegument.
back:
* Praziquantel.
* Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium, causing spastic paralysis.
* Leads to vacuolization and disintegration of the parasite tegument, resulting in death.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Albendazole is classified as a benzimidazole that kills parasites by binding to helminthic [___], thereby inhibiting microtubule polymerization.
back:
* Beta-tubulin
* Inhibits glucose uptake and ATP production
* Results in slow parasite immobilization and death.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient with Neurocysticercosis develops severe inflammation after starting albendazole. The drug typically co-administered to reduce this reaction while increasing albendazole plasma levels is [___].
back:
* Dexamethasone (Corticosteroid)
* Reduces host immune response to dying larvae
* Increases active albendazole sulfoxide concentrations.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the mechanism by which Ivermectin induces flaccid paralysis in nematodes like *Strongyloides stercoralis*.
back:
* Functions as a GABA agonist in parasite peripheral nerves
* Increases chloride ion permeability, causing hyperpolarization
* Results in paralysis and death of the nematode.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the clinical utility of Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) and Ivermectin in a patient diagnosed with *Onchocerca volvulus* (River Blindness).
back:
* DEC: No longer preferred; causes severe inflammatory (Mazzotti) reactions to rapidly dying microfilariae.
* Ivermectin: Drug of choice; kills microfilariae slowly and prevents their release from adult worms.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the specific trematode species for which Metrifonate serves as a low-cost alternative to praziquantel.
back:
* Schistosoma haematobium
* Not effective against S. mansoni or S. japonicum
* Acts by inhibiting parasite cholinesterase.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Praziquantel's ability to kill flukes and tapeworms is mediated by a rapid increase in the permeability of the parasite's cell membrane to [___].
back:
* Calcium ions (Ca2+)
* Causes tetanic contraction and vacuolization of the tegument
* Results in parasite detachment from host tissues.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient returning from South America presents with *Schistosoma mansoni* that is resistant to praziquantel. The specific alternative drug used only for this species is [___].
back:
* Oxamniquine
* Acts by inducing worm contraction and detachment
* Ineffective against S. haematobium or S. japonicum.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: In the context of *Taenia solium* (Pork tapeworm) infection, explain the mechanism of Niclosamide and the theoretical danger of using it for this specific species.
back:
* Mechanism: Inhibits oxidative phosphorylation/ATPase activity
* Danger: Kills adult worm but not eggs; released eggs can cause cysticercosis if they hatch in the host.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the absorption requirements and resulting distribution for Albendazole and Mebendazole.
back:
* Albendazole: High-fat meals increase absorption; distributes well to tissues (CSF/Hydatid cysts).
* Mebendazole: Minimal absorption (<10%); remains active primarily within the intestinal lumen.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the standard dosage and timing for repeating Pyrantel Pamoate in the treatment of pinworm infection.
back:
* Dosage: 11 mg/kg (max 1 g) single oral dose
* Timing: Repeated after 2 weeks
* Goal: To eliminate worms that matured from survivors of the first dose.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Benzimidazole drugs like albendazole and mebendazole exert their antihelminthic effect by inhibiting [___] synthesis in nematodes.
back:
Microtubule

*   Blocks glucose uptake in the parasite.
*   Leads to depletion of glycogen stores.
*   Results in parasite death and eventual expulsion.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 30-year-old patient presents with seizures and a CT scan showing multiple calcified parenchymal cysts. Identify the drug of choice and the rationale for co-administering corticosteroids.
back:
Albendazole

*   Primary drug of choice for neurocysticercosis.
*   Corticosteroids reduce the inflammatory response to dying larvae.
*   Steroid use prevents the exacerbation of neurological symptoms.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the physiological mechanism by which Praziquantel induces paralysis and dislodgement in trematodes like Schistosoma.
back:
Calcium ion permeability increase

*   Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium.
*   Causes marked contraction and spastic paralysis of parasite musculature.
*   Leads to vacuolization and disintegration of the parasite tegument.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the clinical utility and safety of Ivermectin versus Diethylcarbamazine specifically in the management of Onchocerciasis (River Blindness).
back:
Ivermectin is the first-line choice

*   Ivermectin: Safer microfilaricidal; blocks microfilarial release for months.
*   DEC: Can cause severe ocular inflammation and permanent blindness.
*   Ivermectin induces a much milder Mazzotti reaction.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Describe the specific neuromuscular action of Pyrantel Pamoate against intestinal nematodes like Ascaris lumbricoides.
back:
Neuromuscular blocking agent

*   Acts as a persistent nicotinic receptor agonist.
*   Causes spastic paralysis of the worm.
*   Facilitates expulsion of live worms via normal host peristalsis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The primary mechanism of action for Ivermectin involves intensifying inhibitory signaling mediated by [___] in the peripheral nerves of nematodes.
back:
Glutamate-gated chloride channels / GABA

*   Causes hyperpolarization of nerve and muscle cells.
*   Leads to flaccid paralysis of the parasite.
*   High safety margin as it doesn't cross the human blood-brain barrier.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 5-year-old child presents with perianal itching that worsens at night. Cellophane tape test confirms Enterobius vermicularis. Recommend the standard pharmacological regimen.
back:
Mebendazole or Pyrantel Pamoate

*   Single oral dose initially.
*   Repeat the same dose after exactly two weeks.
*   Household members should be treated concurrently to prevent reinfection.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: How does Doxycycline exert its macrofilaricidal activity against Wuchereria bancrofti despite not being a traditional anthelminthic?
back:
Targets Wolbachia endosymbionts

*   Kills the intracellular bacteria essential for parasite survival.
*   Leads to sterility and eventual death of adult macrofilariae.
*   Significantly reduces host inflammatory reactions.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the efficacy and clinical application of Niclosamide with Praziquantel in the treatment of Hymenolepis nana (dwarf tapeworm).
back:
Praziquantel is superior

*   Praziquantel: Kills both adult worms and the larval stages.
*   Niclosamide: Only active against the adult intestinal stage.
*   Praziquantel requires a single dose; Niclosamide requires a 7-day course.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Define the clinical features of the Mazzotti reaction associated with Diethylcarbamazine therapy.
back:
Acute inflammatory response

*   Symptoms: Fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and headache.
*   Signs: Pruritus, skin rash, and tender lymphadenopathy.
*   Pathophysiology: Caused by immune response to dying microfilarial proteins.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Benzimidazole antihelminthics like albendazole and mebendazole exert their primary effect by inhibiting [___] synthesis in nematodes.
back: • Microtubule synthesis inhibition • Binds to β-tubulin • Disruption of parasite glucose uptake and motility leads to death.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 30-year-old immigrant from Mexico presents with a new-onset seizure. MRI reveals a solitary parenchymal cyst. What is the preferred antihelminthic agent and the mandatory adjunct to prevent inflammatory complications?
back: • Preferred agent: Albendazole • Mandatory adjunct: Corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) • Corticosteroids reduce inflammation and edema caused by dying larvae.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which Ivermectin carries out its biological function of paralyzing nematodes and arthropods.
back: • Intensifies GABA-mediated signal transmission • Binds to glutamate-gated chloride channels • Causes hyperpolarization resulting in tonic paralysis of parasite muscles.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast Diethylcarbamazine and Ivermectin regarding their clinical application and safety in the treatment of Onchocerciasis (River Blindness).
back: • Ivermectin: Drug of choice; kills microfilariae without severe host inflammation • Diethylcarbamazine: Avoided due to severe Mazzotti reactions (inflammatory response to dying microfilariae).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Describe the specific ion-channel effect of Praziquantel on susceptible schistosomes and cestodes.
back: • Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium • Induces rapid contraction and spastic paralysis • Causes tegumental damage allowing host immune clearance.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Pyrantel pamoate acts as a [___] agent that induces release of acetylcholine and inhibits cholinesterase, resulting in spastic paralysis of intestinal nematodes.
back: • Neuromuscular blocking agent • Effective only against luminal organisms (poor absorption) • Primary indication: Ascariasis and Pinworm (Enterobius).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient on high-dose prednisone for COPD develops larvae in the stool. Identify the first-line treatment and the risk associated with this infection in immunocompromised hosts.
back: • First-line treatment: Ivermectin • Risk: Disseminated Strongyloidiasis (hyperinfection syndrome) • Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg daily for two days is standard.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Describe how Doxycycline carries out its indirect macrofilaricidal function against Wuchereria bancrofti and Onchocerca volvulus.
back: • Targets Wolbachia (intracellular bacterial symbionts) • Bacterial death deprives the filarial worm of essential metabolic factors • Results in sterility and slow death of adult worms.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast Niclosamide and Praziquantel regarding their effect on Taenia solium eggs and the associated risk of cysticercosis.
back: • Niclosamide: Kills adults but not eggs; theoretical risk of cysticercosis from released ova • Praziquantel: Kills adults and is active against larval cysticercosis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: State the primary clinical indication for Bithionol and its most frequently encountered class-specific adverse effect.
back: • Indication: Fascioliasis (Sheep liver fluke) or Paragonimiasis • Adverse effect: Gastrointestinal distress (nausea, diarrhea) occurs in up to 40% of patients.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Benzimidazoles such as Albendazole and Mebendazole primarily exert their antihelminthic effect by binding to parasite β-tubulin, which directly inhibits [___] synthesis.
back:
• Microtubule polymerization
• Leads to impaired glucose uptake and depletion of glycogen stores
• Results in parasite immobilization and death.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 35-year-old immigrant from Central America being treated for neurocysticercosis develops worsening neurologic symptoms including seizures and meningismus 24 hours after the first dose of Praziquantel. This clinical deterioration is caused by [___].
back:
• Inflammatory response to proteins released by dying larvae
• Often managed by pre-administration of corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone)
• Reduces CNS edema and seizure risk.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Describe the specific ion channel interaction that allows Ivermectin to induce flaccid paralysis in nematodes such as Strongyloides stercoralis.
back:
• Binds to glutamate-gated chloride channels
• Increases permeability to chloride ions
• Causes hyperpolarization of nerve or muscle cells, leading to parasite paralysis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the species-specific clinical utility of Metrifonate and Oxamniquine in the treatment of Schistosomiasis.
back:
• Metrifonate: Only effective against S. haematobium (bladder fluke)
• Oxamniquine: Only effective against S. mansoni (intestinal fluke)
• Praziquantel: Broad spectrum for all Schistosoma species.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the primary pharmacological reason Pyrantel pamoate is highly effective for intestinal nematodes like Ascaris but lacks utility for systemic tissue-invasive stages.
back:
• Poorly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract
• Acts locally as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent
• Expels worms from the lumen via spastic paralysis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: In the management of lymphatic filariasis, the drug [___] acts by both immobilizing microfilariae and altering their surface structure, making them more vulnerable to host phagocytosis.
back:
• Diethylcarbamazine
• Drug of choice for W. bancrofti, B. malayi, and Loa loa
• Can cause severe reactions due to antigen release.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient presents with a serpiginous, intensely pruritic skin eruption on the foot after walking barefoot on a tropical beach. The antihelminthic drug of choice for this condition targets [___].
back:
• Microtubule synthesis (Albendazole)
• Alternative: Ivermectin (Cl- channel opener)
• Diagnosis: Cutaneous larva migrans.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the role of targeting endosymbiotic bacteria in the management of filarial infections using Doxycycline.
back:
• Kills Wolbachia, an endosymbiont required for filarial fertility and survival
• Results in the sterility of adult female worms
• Provides indirect macrofilaricidal activity.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the biochemical targets of Praziquantel and Niclosamide in the treatment of adult tapeworm (cestode) infections.
back:
• Praziquantel: Increases Ca2+ permeability causing tetanic contraction and vacuolization
• Niclosamide: Inhibits oxidative phosphorylation/ATP generation
• Both are effective for beef, fish, and pork tapeworms.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Name the antihelminthic agent that is the drug of choice for most fluke (trematode) and tapeworm (cestode) infections but is specifically contraindicated in ocular cysticercosis.
back:
• Praziquantel
• Contraindicated because parasite destruction in the eye may cause irreparable inflammatory damage
• Use Albendazole for most neurocysticercosis cases instead.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The primary mechanism of benzimidazole derivatives like albendazole involves the inhibition of [___] synthesis, leading to parasite immobilization and death.
back:
• Microtubule synthesis
• Binds selectively to parasite β-tubulin
• Prevents glucose uptake and depletes glycogen stores

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 25-year-old traveler returning from Lake Malawi presents with hematuria and terminal dysuria. Microscopic examination of urine shows large eggs with terminal spines. Identify the drug of choice and its basic cellular effect.
back:
• Praziquantel
• Increases calcium permeability of parasite cell membranes
• Causes contraction and paralysis of the worm

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the neuro-muscular mechanism by which Ivermectin achieves parasite paralysis in Strongyloides stercoralis infections.
back:
• Intensifies GABA-mediated transmission
• Targets glutamate-gated chloride channels
• Causes hyperpolarization and flaccid paralysis of the nematode

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the clinical considerations of using Albendazole versus Praziquantel for neurocysticercosis, specifically regarding interaction with concurrent corticosteroids.
back:
• Albendazole: Preferred; blood levels increase with corticosteroids
• Praziquantel: Bioavailability decreases (up to 50%) with concurrent corticosteroids
• Both require steroids to limit inflammation from dying larvae

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Name the mechanism by which Pyrantel Pamoate causes expulsion of Ascaris lumbricoides from the host intestinal tract.
back:
• Neuromuscular blocking agent
• Acts as a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist
• Causes persistent depolarization and spastic paralysis

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: In the treatment of Loa loa (loiasis) and lymphatic filariasis, [___] is the first-line drug used to immobilize microfilariae and render them susceptible to host defense mechanisms.
back:
• Diethylcarbamazine (DEC)
• Synthetic piperazine derivative
• Immobilizes microfilariae and alters their surface structure

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient with a 10cm unilocular liver cyst is diagnosed with Echinococcus granulosus. Provide the drug of choice and the dietary instruction required for optimal systemic absorption.
back:
• Albendazole
• Take with a fatty meal (increases systemic absorption for tissue parasites)
• Used as an adjunct to surgical aspiration or resection

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Describe the unique indirect mechanism by which Doxycycline exerts macrofilaricidal activity against Wuchereria bancrofti.
back:
• Targets Wolbachia bacteria
• Wolbachia is an essential intracellular bacterial symbiont for filarial survival
• Kills endosymbionts, leading to sterility and death of adult worms

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast Mebendazole and Albendazole regarding their systemic absorption and suitability for treating extraintestinal (tissue) helminthic infections.
back:
• Mebendazole: Low absorption (<10%); used mainly for intraluminal parasites
• Albendazole: Variable absorption; metabolized to active sulfoxide; excellent tissue distribution for systemic/tissue infections

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: State the primary clinical indication and the major limitation of Niclosamide in tapeworm infections.
back:
• Indication: Taenia saginata (beef) and Diphyllobothrium latum (fish) tapeworms
• Limitation: Not effective against cysticercosis or hydatid disease

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The primary molecular mechanism of action for benzimidazoles such as Mebendazole and Albendazole involves the inhibition of [___] synthesis in parasitic nematodes.
back:
• Inhibition of microtubule synthesis.
• Binds to parasitic β-tubulin to prevent polymerization.
• Leads to impaired glucose uptake and eventual parasite death.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 25-year-old immigrant presents with new-onset seizures; imaging reveals multiple symptomatic parenchymal brain cysts confirmed as neurocysticercosis. The preferred drug of choice, which provides superior subarachnoid penetration compared to Praziquantel, is [___].
back:
• Albendazole.
• Often administered with corticosteroids to reduce inflammatory responses to dying larvae.
• Standard course: 400 mg twice daily for up to 21 days.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the biophysical changes induced by Praziquantel in schistosomes that facilitate their dislodgement from host vascular walls.
back:
• Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium ions.
• Induces immediate marked contraction and spastic paralysis of worm musculature.
• Causes tegumental vacuoles to form, leading to host immune destruction.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient in West Africa presents with significant microfilaremia of *Onchocerca volvulus* and suspected *Loa loa* co-infection. Contrast the safety considerations for using Ivermectin versus Diethylcarbamazine in this specific scenario.
back:
• Onchocerciasis: Ivermectin is the drug of choice; DEC is avoided due to severe Mazotti reactions.
• Loiasis: DEC is standard but dangerous in high burdens; Ivermectin can cause fatal encephalopathy in patients with high *Loa loa* counts.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Specify the neuromuscular effect of Pyrantel Pamoate that results in the mechanical expulsion of *Ascaris lumbricoides* from the human intestinal tract.
back:
• Acts as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent.
• Induces persistent activation of nicotinic receptors and inhibits cholinesterase.
• Causes spastic paralysis; worms lose attachment and are expelled by normal peristalsis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: In the treatment of large intestinal tapeworm infections like *Taenia saginata*, the luminal agent [___] acts by inhibiting oxidative phosphorylation, though it is notoriously ineffective against cysticercosis.
back:
• Niclosamide.
• Kills the scolex and proximal segments on contact.
• Not absorbed from the GIT; requires thorough chewing of tablets for efficacy.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A sheep farmer from an endemic region presents with right upper quadrant pain and is diagnosed with *Fasciola hepatica* (sheep liver fluke). Identify the specific antihelminthic required, as this fluke is traditionally resistant to Praziquantel.
back:
• Bithionol (or Triclabendazole).
• Bithionol dosage: 30–50 mg/kg on alternate days for 10–15 doses.
• Common adverse effects: Diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and photosensitivity.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient with lymphatic filariasis fails to clear adult *Wuchereria bancrofti* despite courses of Diethylcarbamazine. Describe the unique indirect mechanism by which Doxycycline exerts macrofilaricidal activity.
back:
• Targets *Wolbachia*, an essential intracellular bacterial symbiont of the filarial worms.
• Depletion of *Wolbachia* leads to sterility of female worms.
• Results in the gradual death of the adult macrofilariae.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Differentiate between Albendazole and Mebendazole regarding their systemic bioavailability and clinical preference for treating tissue-invasive helminthic infections.
back:
• Albendazole: Higher systemic absorption (enhanced by fatty meals); converted to active sulfoxide; preferred for tissue sites (hydatid cysts/neurocysticercosis).
• Mebendazole: Very low absorption (<10%); primarily used for intraluminal intestinal nematodes.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the specific schistosomal species targeted by Metrifonate and name the biochemical class to which this drug belongs.
back:
• Species: *Schistosoma haematobium* (Urinary schistosomiasis).
• Class: Organophosphate (Cholinesterase inhibitor).
• Mechanism: Paralyzes adult worms, causing them to drift into the lungs for destruction.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Benzimidazoles like Albendazole primarily exert their broad-spectrum effects by binding to beta-tubulin and inhibiting [___] synthesis.
back: Microtubule synthesis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient from an endemic region presents with cystic liver lesions and positive serology for Echinococcus granulosus. Identify the first-line antihelminthic drug used as an adjunct to surgery.
back: Albendazole.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Describe the biochemical mechanism by which Ivermectin causes flaccid paralysis in susceptible nematodes.
back: Intensifies GABA-mediated neurotransmission in peripheral nerves.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the alternative agents for Schistosoma mansoni versus Schistosoma haematobium when the first-line therapy (Praziquantel) is not an option.
back:
• S. mansoni: Oxamniquine.
• S. haematobium: Metrifonate.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Specify the ionic mechanism of action by which Praziquantel facilitates parasite dislodgement and death.
back: Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium, causing massive contraction and tegumental damage.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: In the management of strongyloidiasis and onchocerciasis, the primary drug of choice is [___].
back: Ivermectin.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 25-year-old patient is diagnosed with a beef tapeworm (Taenia saginata). Identify the standard single-dose oral agent used for eradication.
back: Praziquantel (or Niclosamide).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain how Doxycycline's target in filarial parasites differs from standard antihelminthic drugs.
back: Targets and kills Wolbachia (an intracellular bacterial symbiont), indirectly causing filarial death.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Distinguish the oral administration requirements for Albendazole when treating intestinal helminths versus tissue-invasive disease.
back:
• Intestinal: Empty stomach (limits systemic absorption).
• Tissue: Fatty meal (significantly increases bioavailability).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: State the primary mechanism of action of Pyrantel Pamoate against intestinal nematodes.
back: Neuromuscular blockade via stimulation of acetylcholine release and inhibition of cholinesterase, paralyzing the worm.

category: Classify antiprotozoal drugs
front: Chloroquine is classified chemically as a(n) [___] and exerts its primary lethal effect on erythrocytic parasites by preventing the detoxification of heme into hemozoin.
back:
● 4-aminoquinoline.
● It interferes with the parasite's ability to sequester toxic heme released during hemoglobin digestion.
● This leads to the buildup of free heme, which is toxic to Plasmodium.

category: Classify antiprotozoal drugs
front: A female patient presents with foul-smelling, greenish vaginal discharge and a 'strawberry cervix' on examination. The drug of choice acts by reacting with [___] inside the parasite to form toxic metabolites.
back:
● Reduced ferredoxin.
● The drug is Metronidazole (a nitroimidazole).
● Its metabolites are taken up into bacterial/protozoal DNA, causing strand breakage and cell death.

category: Classify antiprotozoal drugs
front: Explain the role of iron-catalyzed cleavage in the mechanism of action of Artemisinin-based compounds against Plasmodium falciparum.
back:
● Heme iron in the parasite food vacuole cleaves the drug's endoperoxide bridge.
● This reaction releases highly reactive free radicals.
● These radicals alkylate and damage essential parasite proteins and membranes.

category: Classify antiprotozoal drugs
front: Contrast the clinical roles of Paromomycin and Metronidazole in the management of a patient presenting with an active amebic liver abscess.
back:
● Metronidazole: A tissue amebicide used to kill trophozoites in the liver and intestinal wall.
● Paromomycin: A luminal amebicide used following tissue therapy to eliminate surviving cysts in the bowel lumen.

category: Classify antiprotozoal drugs
front: Identify the specific parasitic stage targeted by Primaquine to achieve a 'radical cure' in P. vivax and P. ovale infections.
back:
● Hepatic hypnozoites (dormant liver stages).
● Primaquine is the only available agent effective against these stages, preventing future clinical relapses.

category: Classify antiprotozoal drugs
front: The first-line agent for the treatment of visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar) in regions without high resistance levels is [___].
back:
● Sodium stibogluconate (or Meglumine antimoniate).
● These belong to the class of pentavalent antimonials.
● They are administered parenterally for 28 days.

category: Classify antiprotozoal drugs
front: A patient with advanced AIDS (CD4 < 50) and a history of sulfa allergy requires prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jiroveci. Name the antiprotozoal agent administered via inhalation for this purpose.
back:
● Pentamidine (nebulized).
● It is used monthly as an alternative to TMP-SMZ.
● It is also the drug of choice for early-stage West African Sleeping Sickness.

category: Classify antiprotozoal drugs
front: Explain the synergistic mechanism between the two components of the antimalarial combination Malarone.
back:
● Atovaquone: Disrupts mitochondrial electron transport at the cytochrome bc1 complex.
● Proguanil: Enhances the mitochondrial toxicity of atovaquone by collapsing the mitochondrial membrane potential.

category: Classify antiprotozoal drugs
front: Distinguish between the sites of action of Pyrimethamine and Sulfadoxine in the sequential inhibition of the protozoal folate pathway.
back:
● Sulfadoxine: Inhibits dihydropteroate synthase (competes with PABA).
● Pyrimethamine: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (prevents synthesis of tetrahydrofolic acid).
● Together, they block sequential metabolic steps.

category: Classify antiprotozoal drugs
front: Identify the two primary nitro-compounds used in the treatment of American Trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease).
back:
● Nifurtimox (a nitrofuran).
● Benznidazole (a nitroimidazole).
● Both agents act primarily by releasing reactive oxygen species and causing cellular damage.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The organophosphate antihelminthic agent used as an alternative for Schistosoma haematobium that acts via cholinesterase inhibition is [___].
back:
* Metrifonate
* Specifically active against S. haematobium
* Paralyzes adult worms causing transit to lungs for destruction
* Not effective against eggs, which continue to pass for months.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient being treated for sheep liver fluke (Fasciola hepatica) develops a severe skin rash after one week of therapy. This reaction is likely an immunologic response to antigens released from dying worms during treatment with [___].
back:
* Bithionol
* Alternative to triclabendazole for fascioliasis
* Also used against Paragonimus westermani
* Adverse effects include diarrhea, vomiting, and dizziness.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Describe the physiological mechanism by which Piperazine induces the expulsion of Ascaris lumbricoides from the gastrointestinal tract.
back:
* Blocks acetylcholine at the worm's myoneural junction
* Induces flaccid paralysis in the nematode
* Live worms are subsequently expelled by normal peristalsis
* Used exclusively for ascariasis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the impact of concomitant corticosteroid administration on the bioavailability of Albendazole versus Praziquantel in the management of neurocysticercosis.
back:
* Albendazole: Bioavailability increases with corticosteroids (dexamethasone)
* Praziquantel: Bioavailability decreases by up to 50%
* Albendazole is often preferred due to better subarachnoid penetration.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain why caution is required when administering Diethylcarbamazine to patients with heavy Loa loa microfilarial burdens (>2500/mL).
back:
* Risk of severe encephalopathy and retinal hemorrhage
* Caused by rapid destruction of massive microfilaria numbers
* Often requires prior apheresis or albendazole pretreatment
* Reaction is immunologic to released parasite proteins.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The tetrahydroquinoline derivative [___] is used as a specific alternative to praziquantel for Schistosoma mansoni but lacks activity against S. haematobium or S. japonicum.
back:
* Oxamniquine
* Active against mature and immature S. mansoni flukes
* Causes worm contraction and detachment from mesenteric venules
* Contraindicated during pregnancy.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient with strongyloidiasis requires treatment but has a history of severe hepatic disease. Among the benzimidazoles, [___] should be avoided due to its high risk of irreversible liver failure and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
back:
* Thiabendazole
* Significantly more toxic than albendazole or mebendazole
* Also acts as a chelating agent for metals
* Preferred alternatives are Ivermectin or Albendazole.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Outline the metabolic transformation and subsequent biological action of Metrifonate within the human host.
back:
* Undergoes nonenzymatic transformation to Dichlorvos
* Dichlorvos serves as the active antihelminthic metabolite
* Inhibits cholinesterase to paralyze adult Schistosoma haematobium
* Drug is well distributed to all tissues.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Distinguish the helminthic spectrum of Nitazoxanide from its more common protozoal indications (Giardia/Cryptosporidium).
back:
* Helminths: Active against Ascaris lumbricoides, Fasciola hepatica, and certain tapeworms
* Mechanism: Inhibits the pyruvate-ferredoxin oxidoreductase pathway
* Lacks the mutagenic potential seen in nitroimidazoles.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the dietary modification required to enhance the systemic absorption of Mebendazole for the treatment of tissue-dwelling larvae like Trichinella spiralis.
back:
* Administer with a fatty meal
* Increases baseline absorption, which is otherwise <10%
* Necessary to reach therapeutic levels in muscle tissue
* Rapidly converted to inactive metabolites in the liver.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The primary mechanism of action for benzimidazoles (e.g., albendazole and mebendazole) involves the selective inhibition of helminthic [___].
back:
• Microtubule synthesis
• Binds to β-tubulin to prevent polymerization
• Disrupts parasite glucose uptake and microtubule-dependent processes.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 29-year-old immigrant from Peru presents with an incidental 10 cm multiloculated 'daughter cyst' in the liver on CT scan. After ensuring no rupture, the drug of choice for medical management is [___].
back:
• Albendazole
• Treatment for Hydatid disease (Echinococcus granulosus)
• Often used as an adjunct to surgery or aspiration (PAIR procedure).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the specific ionic mechanism by which Praziquantel induces spastic paralysis and dislodgement in schistosomes and cestodes.
back:
• Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium ions
• Causes massive influx of Ca2+ into the parasite
• Results in immediate muscular contraction, spastic paralysis, and tegumental damage.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the pharmacokinetic impact of concomitant Dexamethasone administration on Praziquantel versus Albendazole when treating neurocysticercosis.
back:
• Praziquantel: Bioavailability is significantly decreased (up to 50%)
• Albendazole: Serum levels of the active metabolite (albendazole sulfoxide) are increased
• Clinical significance: Albendazole is often preferred for parenchymal cysts.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the primary neurotransmitter system targeted by Ivermectin to induce flaccid paralysis in nematodes.
back:
• Intensifies γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-mediated transmission
• Binds to glutamate-gated chloride channels
• Leads to hyperpolarization and flaccid paralysis of the worm.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: In the management of onchocerciasis (River Blindness), the microfilaricidal agent of choice that does not effectively kill adult worms is [___].
back:
• Ivermectin
• Standard dose: 150 mcg/kg orally
• Does not cause the severe Mazzotti reaction seen with older drugs.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: An AIDS patient presents with severe epigastric pain and larvae in the stool confirmed as *Strongyloides stercoralis*. Specify the first-line pharmacological treatment and its duration.
back:
• Ivermectin
• Dosage: 200 mcg/kg daily for 2 days
• Repeat courses may be needed in disseminated hyperinfection syndrome.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Describe how Diethylcarbamazine facilitates the destruction of microfilariae despite not being a direct toxin.
back:
• Immobilizes microfilariae by altering surface structure
• Displaces them from tissues to the circulation
• Increases susceptibility to host immune defense and phagocytosis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the influence of fatty meals on the oral absorption and clinical application of Mebendazole versus Albendazole.
back:
• Mebendazole: Very poorly absorbed (<10%); used primarily for intraluminal parasites
• Albendazole: Absorption significantly increased with fatty meals; essential for targeting tissue parasites like hydatid cysts.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the neuromuscular effect and specific biochemical target of Pyrantel Pamoate in the treatment of Ascariasis.
back:
• Neuromuscular blocking agent
• Target: Stimulates release of acetylcholine and inhibits cholinesterase
• Result: Spastic paralysis of the worm and subsequent expulsion by peristalsis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: In the management of the sheep liver fluke (*Fasciola hepatica*), the preferred alternative to triclabendazole is the halogenated phenol [___].
back:
• Bithionol.
• Acts by inhibiting the respiratory chain in the parasite.
• Administered orally on alternate days for 10–15 doses.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 40-year-old traveler develops jaundice and upper abdominal pain after consuming raw watercress. Stool microscopy identifies *Fasciola hepatica* eggs. Why should Praziquantel be avoided in this patient?
back:
• Praziquantel is notoriously ineffective against *Fasciola hepatica* even at high doses.
• Appropriate therapy requires Bithionol or Triclabendazole.
• Most other flukes respond well to Praziquantel.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the role of Doxycycline as an indirect macrofilaricidal agent against *Wuchereria bancrofti* and *Onchocerca volvulus*.
back:
• Targets *Wolbachia*, an obligatory intracellular bacterial symbiont of the filarial worms.
• Depletion of *Wolbachia* leads to adult worm sterility and death.
• Provides superior efficacy against adult worms compared to Ivermectin.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the pharmacokinetic impact of concomitant corticosteroid use (e.g., Dexamethasone) on the plasma levels of Albendazole versus Praziquantel.
back:
• Albendazole: Corticosteroids increase the plasma concentration of the active metabolite (albendazole sulfoxide).
• Praziquantel: Corticosteroids significantly decrease bioavailability by up to 50%.
• This makes Albendazole often preferred in neurocysticercosis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: How does Piperazine facilitate the expulsion of *Ascaris lumbricoides* from the human gastrointestinal tract?
back:
• Blocks acetylcholine at the parasite myoneural junction.
• Induces flaccid paralysis in the worm.
• Paralytic worms are subsequently expelled by normal host intestinal peristalsis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Unlike the flaccid paralysis induced by piperazine, Pyrantel pamoate causes spastic paralysis in nematodes by stimulating the release of [___] and inhibiting cholinesterase.
back:
• Acetylcholine (ACh).
• Acts as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent.
• Used for pinworm, ascaris, and hookworm infections.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient with Loiasis (*Loa loa*) presents with a very high microfilarial load (>2500/mL). Why is a course of Albendazole recommended prior to using Diethylcarbamazine (DEC)?
back:
• To prevent DEC-induced encephalopathy and severe allergic reactions.
• Albendazole is slower acting and kills microfilariae more gradually.
• Limits the massive release of parasite antigens into the circulation.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Describe the biochemical activation process and distribution of Albendazole required for systemic efficacy against tissue-based parasites.
back:
• Undergoes rapid, extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver.
• Converted to the active metabolite, albendazole sulfoxide.
• Distributes widely to bile, cerebrospinal fluid, and hydatid cysts.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the clinical spectrum of Oxamniquine with that of Praziquantel in the treatment of human Schistosomiasis.
back:
• Oxamniquine: Strictly limited to *Schistosoma mansoni* infections.
• Praziquantel: Broad-spectrum; drug of choice for *S. haematobium*, *S. mansoni*, and *S. japonicum*.
• Oxamniquine is an alternative when Praziquantel resistance is suspected.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: What is the primary contraindication for using Praziquantel to treat a patient with tissue-stage *Taenia solium* larvae?
back:
• Ocular cysticercosis.
• Destruction of the larvae within the eye can lead to irreversible inflammatory tissue damage.
• Praziquantel requires chewing avoidance due to its bitter, emetic taste.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The specific benzimidazole drug of choice for the treatment of Fasciola hepatica (sheep liver fluke) is [___].
back: Triclabendazole (Bithionol is an alternative).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 7-year-old with heavy Ascaris lumbricoides infection is prescribed an agent that causes flaccid paralysis by blocking acetylcholine at the myoneural junction. Identify the drug.
back: Piperazine.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism of action of Nitazoxanide in the treatment of Cryptosporidium parvum.
back: It acts as a prodrug whose active metabolite, tizoxanide, inhibits the pyruvate-ferredoxin oxidoreductase pathway, interfering with anaerobic energy metabolism.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the impact of Niclosamide and Praziquantel on the risk of Cysticercosis during the treatment of adult Taenia solium infections.
back:
• Praziquantel: Kills both adult worms and eggs.
• Niclosamide: Kills only adults; viable eggs released after segment digestion theoretically increase the risk of autoinfection/cysticercosis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the specific filarial species for which Diethylcarbamazine is highly effective because it kills both the microfilariae and the adult worms.
back: Mansonella streptocerca (it is also active against adult Loa loa).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The antihelminthic drug [___] is the treatment of choice for Intestinal Capillariasis when administered at a dosage of 400 mg daily for 10 days.
back: Albendazole.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A patient diagnosed with Gnathostomiasis requires a prolonged treatment course to ensure eradication. Specify the recommended drug and duration.
back: Albendazole, 400 mg twice daily for 3 weeks.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain why Thiabendazole has been largely replaced by Ivermectin or Albendazole for the treatment of Strongyloidiasis.
back: Thiabendazole is significantly more toxic, carrying risks of irreversible liver failure and fatal Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the treatment protocols for Albendazole in Ascariasis versus Microsporidial infections.
back:
• Ascariasis: Single 400 mg oral dose.
• Microsporidial: 400 mg twice daily for 2 weeks or longer.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: State the required oral dosing schedule for Bithionol in the treatment of pulmonary Paragonimiasis.
back: 30–50 mg/kg administered after meals on alternate days for 10–15 doses.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: The antifungal class that acts by binding directly to ergosterol and forming pores in the fungal cell membrane is [___].
back:
• Polyene macrolides
• Examples: Amphotericin B, Nystatin

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: A 35-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with meningitis. CSF shows encapsulated yeast on India Ink. Induction therapy involves Amphotericin B plus [___].
back:
• Flucytosine (5-FC)
• Synergistic effect prevents secondary resistance

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Explain the role of the Azole class in disrupting fungal cell membrane integrity.
back:
• Inhibits fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme 14α-demethylase
• Prevents the conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the systemic selectivity of Imidazoles (e.g., Ketoconazole) with Triazoles (e.g., Fluconazole).
back:
• Imidazoles: Lower selectivity; significant inhibition of mammalian P450 enzymes (steroid synthesis)
• Triazoles: Higher selectivity; fewer human endocrine side effects/drug interactions

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Identify the specific component of the fungal cell wall targeted by Echinocandins like Caspofungin.
back:
• β-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase
• Disrupts cell wall structural integrity, leading to cell death

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: The allylamine drug commonly used for onychomycosis that inhibits squalene epoxidase is [___].
back:
• Terbinafine
• Accumulates in keratin (keratophilic); fungicidal

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: A patient with neutropenia develops fever and pulmonary infiltrates with a 'halo sign.' Identify the current drug of choice from the triazole class.
back:
• Voriconazole
• Superior to Amphotericin B for invasive aspergillosis

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Describe the intracellular activation process required for Flucytosine to exert its antifungal effect.
back:
• Taken up by cytosine permease
• Converted to 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) by cytosine deaminase
• Inhibits DNA and RNA synthesis

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the clinical use and toxicity limitations of Nystatin compared to Amphotericin B.
back:
• Amphotericin B: IV for systemic infections; high nephrotoxicity
• Nystatin: Topical/oral rinse for mucocutaneous infections; too toxic for parenteral use

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Identify the primary mechanism by which Griseofulvin inhibits the growth of dermatophytes.
back:
• Interferes with microtubule function
• Disrupts assembly of the mitotic spindle

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Amphotericin B is a polyene macrolide that exerts its fungicidal effect by binding to [___] in the fungal cell membrane, creating pores that cause intracellular content leakage.
back:
* Ergosterol.
* Exploits lipid differences between fungal (ergosterol) and mammalian (cholesterol) membranes.
* Results in rapid cell death.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: A patient with advanced AIDS presents with headache and positive India ink staining in the CSF. Identify the systemic pyrimidine analog used in combination induction therapy for this condition.
back:
* Flucytosine (5-FC).
* Synergizes with Amphotericin B for Cryptococcal meningitis.
* Narrow spectrum: limited to Cryptococcus and some Candida species.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Explain the role of the 14α-demethylase enzyme inhibition in the antifungal action of the azole drug class.
back:
* Azoles inhibit fungal cytochrome P450 enzymes.
* Specifically block conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol.
* Disrupts membrane permeability and fungal cell growth.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the pharmacological profile and selectivity of the systemic imidazoles (e.g., Ketoconazole) with the newer triazoles (e.g., Fluconazole).
back:
* Imidazoles: Lower selectivity; frequently inhibit mammalian P450, causing more drug interactions and steroid synthesis issues.
* Triazoles: Higher selectivity for fungal P450; improved safety profile; mainstay of systemic therapy.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Identify the specific component of the fungal cell wall targeted by the echinocandin class (e.g., Caspofungin, Micafungin).
back:
* β(1–3)-glucan.
* Drugs inhibit β-glucan synthase.
* Leads to cell wall disruption and lysis; active against Candida and Aspergillus.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: The allylamine drug [___] is highly effective for onychomycosis because it is keratophilic and inhibits squalene epoxidase, leading to ergosterol deficiency.
back:
* Terbinafine.
* Kills dermatophytes by causing toxic squalene accumulation.
* Used primarily for mucocutaneous infections.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: A neutropenic patient being treated for invasive aspergillosis reports transient blurring and altered color perception 30 minutes after each dose. Identify the most likely drug.
back:
* Voriconazole.
* Visual disturbances occur in up to 30% of patients.
* Triazole of choice for invasive aspergillosis.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Describe the intracellular metabolic conversion required for Flucytosine to exert its antifungal effect while sparing human cells.
back:
* Taken up by fungal cytosine permease.
* Converted to 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) by cytosine deaminase (absent in humans).
* Metabolites inhibit DNA (via FdUMP) and RNA synthesis.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Contrast conventional Amphotericin B deoxycholate with Liposomal Amphotericin B regarding their therapeutic index and toxicity.
back:
* Conventional: Limited by dose-dependent nephrotoxicity (azotemia) and infusion reactions.
* Liposomal: Higher therapeutic index; lipid vehicle reduces nonspecific binding to human cell membranes, sparing kidneys.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Identify the polyene antifungal restricted to topical use for mucocutaneous candidiasis due to its high systemic toxicity.
back:
* Nystatin.
* Mechanism identical to Amphotericin B.
* Used for oral thrush (swish and swallow) and vaginal candidiasis.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: The four primary pharmacological classes of systemic antifungal drugs used for the treatment of systemic infections are polyenes, antimetabolites, azoles, and [___].
back:
• Echinocandins
• Includes: Caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin
• Act by disrupting the fungal cell wall rather than the cell membrane.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: A patient with invasive aspergillosis is treated with a drug that inhibits 14α-sterol demethylase. Classify this drug and identify the current preferred agent for this clinical condition.
back:
• Class: Triazole (sub-class of Azoles)
• Preferred Agent: Voriconazole
• Notes: Replaced amphotericin B and itraconazole as the primary treatment for aspergillosis.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Explain the difference in the biological target between polyene antifungals and azole antifungals regarding the fungal cell membrane.
back:
• Polyenes (e.g., Amphotericin B): Bind directly to ergosterol to form ion-leaking pores.
• Azoles: Inhibit the synthesis of ergosterol by blocking fungal cytochrome P450 enzymes (14α-sterol demethylase).

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the chemical classification and typical clinical usage of imidazoles versus triazoles within the azole class.
back:
• Imidazoles (e.g., Ketoconazole, Clotrimazole): Two nitrogen atoms in the ring; mostly limited to topical use due to poor selectivity.
• Triazoles (e.g., Fluconazole, Voriconazole): Three nitrogen atoms; higher selectivity and preferred for systemic therapy.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: The echinocandin class of antifungals is classified by its unique ability to target which specific component of the fungal cell?
back:
• Target: β(1–3)-glucan
• Mechanism: Inhibition of β-glucan synthase
• Result: Disruption of the fungal cell wall (not the membrane).

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Griseofulvin and terbinafine are classified as [___] systemic drugs used for the treatment of mucocutaneous fungal infections.
back:
• Oral systemic drugs
• Used primarily for dermatophytoses and onychomycosis
• Terbinafine is an allylamine; Griseofulvin is a separate fungistatic class.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: A patient with cryptococcal meningitis receives induction therapy with a pyrimidine analog that inhibits DNA/RNA synthesis. Identify the classification and the specific drug used in this synergistic combination.
back:
• Class: Antimetabolite
• Drug: Flucytosine (5-FC)
• Usage: Always used in combination (usually with Amphotericin B) to prevent the rapid development of resistance.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Describe the biochemical step inhibited by allylamines (e.g., terbinafine) compared to the step inhibited by azoles in the ergosterol biosynthetic pathway.
back:
• Allylamines: Inhibit squalene epoxidase (an early step, leading to toxic squalene accumulation).
• Azoles: Inhibit 14α-sterol demethylase (a later step, blocking lanosterol conversion to ergosterol).

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Contrast Nystatin and Amphotericin B regarding their clinical classification for systemic versus topical administration.
back:
• Nystatin: Polyene used only topically (skin, mouth, vagina) because it is too toxic for systemic use.
• Amphotericin B: Polyene used intravenously for life-threatening systemic mycoses (broadest spectrum).

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Which specific triazoles are classified as having clinical activity against the agents of mucormycosis (Zygomycosis)?
back:
• Posaconazole
• Isavuconazole
• Note: These are the first azoles with significant activity against these molds; Fluconazole/Voriconazole lack this activity.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: To increase the systemic bioavailability of Albendazole for the treatment of tissue-bound parasites, the medication should be administered with a [___].
back:
* A fatty meal
* Significantly enhances the absorption of the drug into the systemic circulation
* Necessary to achieve therapeutic levels in cysts or neurologic tissues
* Contrast with administration on an empty stomach for intraluminal parasites

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
coreConcept: Loiasis management in high microfilarial burden
front: A patient with loiasis and a microfilarial load exceeding 2500 parasites/mL is at high risk for encephalopathy if treated with Diethylcarbamazine. State the preferred initial drug to safely lower the parasite burden.
back:
* Albendazole
* Provides a slower, better-tolerated reduction of microfilaremia
* Minimizes the risk of severe systemic inflammatory reactions or neurologic complications associated with rapid microfilarial death

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the physiological mechanism by which Metrifonate achieves its therapeutic effect against Schistosoma haematobium.
back:
* Acts as an organophosphate cholinesterase inhibitor
* Paralyzes adult worms, causing them to dislodge from the vesical plexus
* Displaced worms are passively carried to the lungs and subsequently killed by host defenses

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the effect of concomitant corticosteroid administration on the plasma concentrations of Albendazole versus Praziquantel during the treatment of neurocysticercosis.
back:
* Albendazole: Dexamethasone increases its active sulfoxide plasma levels
* Praziquantel: Corticosteroids decrease its bioavailability by up to 50%
* Clinically significant for determining drug choice in symptomatic brain cyst management

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify the group of GABA-modulating medications that should be avoided in patients receiving Ivermectin to prevent the potential risk of neurotoxicity.
back:
* Benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and valproic acid
* These agents potentiate the drug’s GABA-mediated signaling effects
* Prevents excessive central nervous system depression or potential drug penetration into the CNS
