category: Discuss drugs used for systemic mycotic infections
front: Identify the three echinocandins currently available for the parenteral treatment of systemic fungal infections.
back:
* Caspofungin, Micafungin, and Anidulafungin.
* These are large cyclic peptides linked to long-chain fatty acids.
* They are available only in intravenous formulations for systemic use.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Amphotericin B exerts its fungicidal effect by binding to [___] in the fungal cell membrane, forming pores that lead to the leakage of intracellular contents.
back:
* Ergosterol
* Forms transmembrane channels/pores
* Causes lethal leakage of ions (K+) and macromolecules

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient being treated for invasive aspergillosis reports transient blurring and changes in color perception immediately following each intravenous dose. These symptoms are characteristic of [___].
back:
* Voriconazole
* Occurs in ~30% of patients
* Generally resolves within 30 minutes; non-permanent

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain the role of $\beta(1,3)$-D-glucan synthase inhibition in the mechanism of action of the echinocandins (e.g., caspofungin).
back:
* Blocks synthesis of $\beta(1,3)$-D-glucan, an essential cell wall component
* Disrupts fungal cell wall structural integrity
* Results in osmotic instability and fungal cell death

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) penetration and oral bioavailability of Fluconazole with that of Itraconazole.
back:
* Fluconazole: High bioavailability (>90%); excellent CSF penetration (>70%)
* Itraconazole: Variable, pH-dependent bioavailability; poor CSF penetration (<1%)

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the specific enzyme inhibited by Terbinafine and the toxic metabolite that subsequently accumulates in the fungal cell.
back:
* Enzyme: Squalene epoxidase
* Metabolite: Squalene (toxic accumulation)
* Leads to ergosterol deficiency and membrane disruption

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Flucytosine is selectively toxic to fungi because it is converted into [___] by the fungal enzyme cytosine deaminase, an enzyme absent in human cells.
back:
* 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU)
* Inhibits DNA (via FdUMP) and RNA (via FUTP) synthesis
* Often used synergistically with Amphotericin B

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Following induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis, a patient develops rising serum creatinine, profound hypokalemia, and magnesium wasting. The most likely causative agent is [___].
back:
* Amphotericin B
* Causes renal tubular injury and decreased perfusion
* Requires sodium loading/saline hydration to mitigate risk

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: How do fungi commonly develop resistance to the azole class of medications (e.g., fluconazole)?
back:
* Mutations in the 14-$\alpha$-demethylase gene (ERG11)
* Increased expression of multidrug efflux pumps (CDR/MDR)
* Alterations in the ergosterol biosynthetic pathway

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Distinguish between the clinical application routes for Nystatin and Amphotericin B despite their similar polyene structures.
back:
* Nystatin: Restricted to topical/mucosal use (e.g., thrush) due to extreme systemic toxicity
* Amphotericin B: Administered intravenously for systemic life-threatening mycoses

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the broadest-spectrum triazole currently used for the treatment of invasive mucormycosis (Zygomycosis).
back:
* Posaconazole (or Isavuconazole)
* First azole with significant activity against Mucorales
* Requires high-fat meals for optimal oral absorption

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: The primary mechanism of action for Amphotericin B involves binding to [___] in the fungal cell membrane, resulting in the formation of artificial pores and leakage of intracellular contents.
back:
* Ergosterol
* This binding alters membrane permeability
* Leads to leakage of ions and macromolecules
* Resulting in fungicidal activity

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient receiving high-dose Flucytosine for cryptococcal meningitis develops a significant drop in absolute neutrophil count and hemoglobin. This adverse effect is primarily attributed to the metabolic conversion of the drug to [___].
back:
* 5-fluorouracil (5-FU)
* Occurs via intestinal flora or fungal enzymes
* Causes dose-dependent bone marrow suppression
* Leading to anemia and leukopenia

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which azole antifungals (e.g., Fluconazole) inhibit fungal growth.
back:
* Inhibition of fungal cytochrome P450 enzymes
* Specifically targets 14α-demethylase
* Blocks conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol
* Disrupts fungal cell membrane structure

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the mechanism of action and primary site of fungal cell disruption between Echinocandins (e.g., Caspofungin) and Polyene Macrolides (e.g., Amphotericin B).
back:
* Echinocandins: Inhibit β(1,3)-D-glucan synthase, disrupting the fungal cell wall
* Polyenes: Bind ergosterol, creating pores in the cell membrane
* Contrast: Echinocandins target the wall; Polyenes target the membrane

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: State the clinical rationale for utilizing lipid-based formulations of Amphotericin B over the conventional deoxycholate formulation.
back:
* Significantly reduced nephrotoxicity
* Lower incidence of infusion-related reactions
* Allows for higher therapeutic dosing
* Preferential binding to fungal ergosterol over human cholesterol

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Terbinafine exerts its antifungal effect by inhibiting the enzyme [___], leading to toxic accumulation of squalene and deficiency of ergosterol.
back:
* Squalene epoxidase
* Blocks the first step of ergosterol biosynthesis
* Causes fungal cell death via squalene toxicity
* Highly effective for dermatophytoses

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient treated for invasive aspergillosis with Voriconazole complains of seeing "bright spots" and blurred vision 30 minutes after each dose. Identify the cause and management of these symptoms.
back:
* Voriconazole-induced visual disturbances
* Occurs in up to 30% of patients
* Management: Reassurance, as symptoms are transient
* Typically resolves within 30 minutes

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Describe the biochemical synergy observed between Amphotericin B and Flucytosine in the treatment of Cryptococcus neoformans.
back:
* Amphotericin B creates membrane pores
* Enhances entry of Flucytosine into the fungal cell
* Flucytosine disrupts DNA/RNA synthesis
* Combined effect facilitates more rapid fungal clearance

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Distinguish between Itraconazole and Fluconazole regarding their cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) penetration and primary clinical uses.
back:
* Itraconazole: Poor CSF penetration; used for endemic mycoses (e.g., Histoplasma)
* Fluconazole: Excellent CSF penetration (>70%); used for cryptococcal meningitis
* Bioavailability: Itraconazole is pH-dependent; Fluconazole is high and pH-independent

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Specify the antifungal class and specific agent considered the first-line treatment for invasive aspergillosis.
back:
* Class: Triazoles
* Agent: Voriconazole
* Superior efficacy compared to conventional amphotericin B
* Available in both oral and IV formulations

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Albendazole and mebendazole belong to the benzimidazole class, which exert their primary antihelminthic effect by inhibiting [___] synthesis in nematodes.
back:
● Microtubule synthesis inhibition.
● Bind to parasite β-tubulin to prevent polymerization.
● Leads to impaired glucose uptake and parasite death.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A 24-year-old traveler returning from West Africa presents with localized pruritic swellings ('Calabar swellings') and a visible worm migrating across the conjunctiva. The drug of choice is [___].
back:
● Diethylcarbamazine (DEC).
● Effectively kills microfilariae and adult Loa loa worms.
● Often requires antihistamine/corticosteroid co-administration to limit allergic reactions.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which Praziquantel causes the paralysis and death of schistosomes and cestodes.
back:
● Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium.
● Causes immediate strong contraction and spastic paralysis of the worm musculature.
● Triggers vacuolization and disintegration of the parasite tegument.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast the clinical utility and safety profile of Ivermectin versus Diethylcarbamazine in the treatment of Onchocerca volvulus (Onchocerciasis).
back:
● Ivermectin: Drug of choice; microfilaricidal only; safer profile with fewer ocular inflammatory reactions.
● Diethylcarbamazine: No longer used for onchocerciasis due to severe risk of Mazzotti reactions and permanent eye damage.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Mention the primary mechanism and the drug of choice for treating Strongyloides stercoralis (threadworm) infection.
back:
● Drug: Ivermectin.
● Mechanism: Intensifies GABA-mediated transmission in peripheral nerves, causing nematode paralysis and death.
● Dosing: 200 mcg/kg daily for two days.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: The primary medical therapy for [___] disease involves long-term high-dose Albendazole, often as an adjunct to surgical aspiration or the PAIR procedure.
back:
● Hydatid disease (Echinococcus granulosus).
● Dosing: 400 mg twice daily for at least one month.
● Efficacy: More active against E. granulosus than E. multilocularis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: A child presents with nocturnal perianal pruritus. Scotch tape test reveals Enterobius vermicularis eggs. Identify an effective over-the-counter neuromuscular blocking agent used for treatment.
back:
● Pyrantel pamoate.
● Mechanism: Acts as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker, inducing persistent activation of nicotinic receptors.
● Result: Causes worm paralysis followed by expulsion from the gut.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: How does Doxycycline exert its antihelminthic effect in patients with lymphatic filariasis or onchocerciasis?
back:
● Targets Wolbachia, an intracellular bacterial endosymbiont of the worms.
● Loss of Wolbachia leads to sterility and eventual death of the adult macrofilariae.
● Reduces microfilaria production and disease progression.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Contrast Albendazole and Praziquantel regarding their pharmacokinetics when co-administered with corticosteroids in the treatment of neurocysticercosis.
back:
● Albendazole: Plasma levels of active sulfoxide metabolite are increased by dexamethasone.
● Praziquantel: Bioavailability is significantly decreased (up to 50%) by corticosteroids.
● Clinical impact: Albendazole is usually preferred for neurocysticercosis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action, clinical uses, adverse effects of anthelminthic drugs
front: Identify a major limitation of Niclosamide in the treatment of Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) infections.
back:
● Kills adult worms but has no effect on ova.
● Viable eggs released in the gut could theoretically cause cysticercosis.
● Praziquantel or Albendazole are often preferred due to this risk.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Micafungin is known to cause clinically significant drug-drug interactions, specifically resulting in the increased serum concentrations of [___] and sirolimus.
back: Nifedipine and cyclosporine.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient receiving high-dose Amphotericin B for Cryptococcal meningitis develops cardiac arrhythmias and muscle weakness. Explain the specific renal pathophysiology causing the severe potassium and magnesium wasting seen in this patient.
back:
*   Increased renal tubular permeability leading to tubular injury.
*   Induction of distal renal tubular acidosis (RTA).
*   Direct toxic effect on the distal tubule causing severe electrolyte leakage.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Describe the unique spectrum of action that distinguishes Posaconazole from earlier triazoles like Fluconazole and Voriconazole regarding the treatment of Zygomycetes.
back:
*   It is the first azole with significant activity against agents of mucormycosis (Rhizopus, Absidia).
*   Possesses the broadest spectrum of the azole family.
*   Used primarily as salvage therapy for invasive aspergillosis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
coreConcept: Azole Tissue Distribution and Clinical Utility
front: Contrast the therapeutic rationale for selecting Itraconazole over Fluconazole in a patient with Blastomycosis versus a patient with fungal central nervous system (CNS) involvement.
back:
*   Itraconazole: Drug of choice for dimorphic fungi (Blastomyces, Histoplasma) but has poor CNS penetration.
*   Fluconazole: Lower activity against dimorphic fungi but high CSF-to-serum ratio (>0.7), making it the drug of choice for fungal meningitis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the pharmacodynamic rationale for the clinical practice of 'sodium loading' (administering saline infusions) prior to the delivery of Amphotericin B.
back:
*   Attenuates the reversible prerenal component of renal failure.
*   Decreases drug-induced renal vasoconstriction and ischemia.
*   Reduces the overall severity of drug-induced azotemia.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: To minimize the risk of dose-dependent bone marrow toxicity, peak serum concentrations of the pyrimidine analog [___] should be monitored and maintained below 100 mcg/mL.
back: Flucytosine (5-FC).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient stabilized on Warfarin for atrial fibrillation is prescribed Voriconazole for aspergillosis. Predict the likely change in the patient's International Normalized Ratio (INR) and state the underlying mechanism.
back:
*   INR will increase (increased bleeding risk).
*   Mechanism: Voriconazole is a potent inhibitor of mammalian CYP3A4 enzymes.
*   This results in decreased hepatic metabolism and accumulation of Warfarin.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain why Griseofulvin therapy for Tinea unguium (nail infection) must be continued for several months to achieve clinical cure, despite the drug being well-absorbed.
back:
*   The drug only binds to and protects newly forming keratin.
*   It provides no effect on currently infected tissue.
*   Treatment must continue until infected nails are entirely replaced by drug-protected new growth.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the hepatic metabolic profiles of Griseofulvin and Terbinafine, specifically regarding their interaction with the Cytochrome P450 system.
back:
*   Griseofulvin: Induces hepatic microsomal enzymes and can increase the metabolism of drugs like Warfarin.
*   Terbinafine: Inhibits squalene epoxidase rather than P450 enzymes; it does not significantly induce or inhibit the P450 system.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the primary clinical indications for the newly licensed triazole, Isavuconazonium sulfate, distinguishing its spectrum from standard Fluconazole.
back:
*   Invasive aspergillosis and invasive mucormycosis.
*   Distinction: Unlike Fluconazole, Isavuconazole is active against molds and filamentous fungi.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: To attenuate the reversible prerenal component of Amphotericin B-induced nephrotoxicity, clinicians frequently administer a concurrent intravenous infusion of [___].
back:
- Normal saline (sodium loading)
- Increases renal blood flow
- Reduces the incidence and severity of azotemia.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A transplant recipient on Cyclosporine develops candidemia. After starting an echinocandin, his liver enzymes begin to rise sharply. This interaction is most likely associated with the use of [___].
back:
- Caspofungin
- Combination with Cyclosporine increases hepatic aminotransferases
- This specific pairing should generally be avoided.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain how gastric environment and food intake affect the bioavailability of oral Itraconazole capsules.
back:
- Absorption is increased by food
- Requires low gastric pH (acidic) for solubility
- Bioavailability is markedly reduced by proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the efficacy of Fluconazole and Posaconazole against filamentous fungi such as *Aspergillus* and the agents of Mucormycosis.
back:
- Fluconazole: Zero activity against molds or *Aspergillus*
- Posaconazole: Broad spectrum; active against *Aspergillus* and is the first azole active against Mucormycosis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: State the primary toxic metabolite responsible for the dose-limiting bone marrow suppression seen during Flucytosine therapy.
back:
- 5-fluorouracil (5-FU)
- Converted by fungal enzymes or intestinal flora
- Causes reversible anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: The polyene macrolide [___] is too toxic for parenteral administration and is strictly used topically or as an oral 'swish and swallow' for localized candidal suppression.
back:
- Nystatin
- Negligible absorption from skin or gastrointestinal tract
- Indicated for oropharyngeal thrush and intertriginous candidiasis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient being treated for invasive aspergillosis reports seeing flashes of light, blurring, and changes in color perception shortly after each drug infusion. Identify the agent.
back:
- Voriconazole
- Occurs in ~30% of patients
- Visual disturbances are transient and usually resolve within 30 minutes.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain why a 1 mg 'test dose' is often administered intravenously before starting a full therapeutic course of Amphotericin B Deoxycholate.
back:
- Gauges severity of immediate infusion-related reactions
- Identifies risk for fever, chills, and hypotension
- Helps determine the necessary premedication strategy (e.g., corticosteroids).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the physical formulation of Amphotericin B Deoxycholate (Fungizone) with Liposomal Amphotericin B (AmBisome).
back:
- Fungizone: Colloidal suspension of micelles
- AmBisome: Drug packaged into small lipid spheres (liposomes)
- Liposomal forms allow higher dosing with significantly less nephrotoxicity.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Mention the rare but serious organ-specific toxicity that necessitates baseline and periodic monitoring when prescribing oral Terbinafine.
back:
- Hepatotoxicity (Serious liver injury)
- Although rare, it requires monitoring of liver function tests (LFTs)
- May occur regardless of prior liver health.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: To attenuate the reversible prerenal component of nephrotoxicity during conventional Amphotericin B administration, clinicians often routinely administer [___] infusions.
back:
• Normal saline (sodium loading).
• Improves renal perfusion and decreases the risk of drug-induced renal tubular injury.
• Useful when daily doses cannot be reduced.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A diabetic patient with ketoacidosis presents with necrotic nasal lesions and fungal hyphae invading blood vessels. Among the triazole class, identify the specific agent indicated for this condition.
back:
• Posaconazole.
• It is the first triazole with significant activity against the agents of mucormycosis (Mucoraceae).
• Also used for salvage therapy in invasive aspergillosis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain the role of dietary intake in the clinical efficacy of oral Griseofulvin for the treatment of dermatophytosis.
back:
• Absorption is significantly improved when taken with fatty foods.
• As an insoluble drug, fat increases its systemic bioavailability.
• Facilitates the drug's deposition in newly forming keratin.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the drug interaction profiles of Caspofungin and Micafungin regarding their concurrent use with the immunosuppressant Cyclosporine.
back:
• Caspofungin: Avoid combination due to significantly increased risk of elevated liver enzymes.
• Micafungin: Safe for use, though it may slightly increase Cyclosporine blood levels without same hepatic risk.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Why is systemic Ketoconazole frequently associated with gynecomastia and loss of libido in male patients?
back:
• Non-selective inhibition of mammalian cytochrome P450 enzymes.
• Interferes with the synthesis of human steroid hormones, specifically testosterone and cortisol.
• Triazoles are preferred as they are more fungal-selective.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: The newest triazole agent, [___], is currently licensed for the treatment of both invasive aspergillosis and invasive mucormycosis.
back:
• Isavuconazonium sulfate (Isavuconazole).
• It is a water-soluble prodrug with high bioavailability.
• Offers a broad spectrum similar to posaconazole with better tolerability than voriconazole.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient being treated for pulmonary tuberculosis is started on Itraconazole for Histoplasmosis but fails to achieve clinical cure. Identify the likely pharmacokinetic interaction responsible.
back:
• Rifampin (a potent CYP450 inducer) significantly reduces Itraconazole bioavailability.
• Leads to subtherapeutic antifungal serum levels.
• Itraconazole absorption is also dependent on low gastric pH.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Describe the physiological basis of the primary dose-limiting toxicity associated with Flucytosine therapy.
back:
• Bone marrow suppression (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia).
• Caused by the metabolic conversion of the drug to 5-fluorouracil (a toxic antineoplastic) by intestinal flora.
• Requires monitoring of peak serum concentrations.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the pharmacodynamic nature (cidal vs. static) of Polyenes and Azoles against most fungal pathogens.
back:
• Polyenes: Fungicidal; they create physical pores in the cell membrane causing immediate leakage.
• Azoles: Fungistatic; they inhibit ergosterol synthesis, which arrests growth but does not kill immediately.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Which azole is considered the drug of choice for the treatment of invasive aspergillosis due to its superior efficacy and survival rates compared to Amphotericin B?
back:
• Voriconazole.
• It is also active against fluconazole-resistant species like Candida krusei.
• Exhibits high oral bioavailability and good tissue distribution.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: The newest triazole agent, [___], is an orally bioavailable prodrug used for the treatment of both invasive aspergillosis and invasive mucormycosis.
back:
• Isavuconazole (Isavuconazonium sulfate)
• Broad-spectrum activity similar to posaconazole
• Better tolerated than voriconazole with no specific food requirements
• Half-life is approximately 130 hours

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient receiving an intravenous echinocandin for esophageal candidiasis develops significantly elevated liver enzymes shortly after starting Cyclosporine. Identify the antifungal agent most likely responsible.
back:
• Caspofungin
• Concomitant use with cyclosporine increases the risk of hepatic enzyme elevation
• This specific combination is generally contraindicated
• Most common side effects are otherwise minor GI symptoms

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain why the serum concentration of Itraconazole decreases significantly when it is co-administered with Rifampin.
back:
• Rifampin is a potent inducer of hepatic CYP3A4 enzymes
• It increases the metabolic clearance of itraconazole
• Results in subtherapeutic antifungal levels and potential treatment failure
• Bioavailability is also affected by gastric pH and food

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the clinical use of Clotrimazole troches with Nystatin suspension for the management of oropharyngeal thrush.
back:
• Clotrimazole troches are pleasant-tasting alternatives to nystatin
• Both are used to suppress local candidal infections topically
• Nystatin is a polyene; Clotrimazole is an imidazole azole
• Minimal systemic absorption occurs for both routes

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: To maintain a safe therapeutic window and prevent bone marrow suppression, peak serum levels of Flucytosine should not exceed which specific concentration?
back:
• 100 mcg/mL
• Levels above this threshold increase the risk of anemia and leukopenia
• Therapeutic range is typically 50–100 mcg/mL
• Monitoring is vital in patients with renal insufficiency

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
coreConcept: Ketoconazole Selective Toxicity and Steroid Inhibition
front: Unlike newer triazoles, the imidazole antifungal [___] is distinguished by its significant inhibitory effect on mammalian steroid synthesis.
back:
• Ketoconazole
• It is less selective for fungal P450 than triazoles
• Systemic use is now restricted due to adrenal and gonadal steroid inhibition
• No longer recommended for minor skin or nail infections

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A ward nurse is instructed to use soap and water rather than alcohol-based hand rubs after cleaning a room previously occupied by a patient with Clostridium difficile. Provide the pharmacological rationale.
back:
• Alcohol-based hand rubs are ineffective against fungal and bacterial spores
• C. difficile is a spore-forming organism
• Physical washing is required for mechanical removal of spores
• Prevents cross-contamination in healthcare settings

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
coreConcept: Amphotericin B Nephrotoxicity and Electrolyte Wasting
front: Explain the specific physiological mechanism leading to severe potassium and magnesium wasting during prolonged Amphotericin B therapy.
back:
• Amphotericin B induces renal tubular injury
• This leads to an irreversible component of nephrotoxicity
• Results in renal tubular acidosis and direct loss of ions
• Occurs most frequently with cumulative doses exceeding 4 grams

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the drug-drug interaction profiles of Anidulafungin and Micafungin.
back:
• Micafungin increases serum levels of sirolimus, nifedipine, and cyclosporine
• Anidulafungin has no clinically significant drug-drug interactions
• Both are intravenous-only echinocandins targeting beta-glucan synthase
• Neither requires dose adjustment for hepatic impairment

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Which systemic triazole is characterized by high water solubility, nearly 100% oral bioavailability, and excellent penetration into the cerebrospinal fluid (>70%)?
back:
• Fluconazole
• Agent of choice for cryptococcal meningitis secondary prophylaxis
• Elimination is primarily renal via glomerular filtration
• Least impact on hepatic microsomal enzymes among the azoles

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: To attenuate the prerenal component of [___]-induced nephrotoxicity, clinicians prioritize aggressive intravenous hydration with normal saline (sodium loading).
back:
* Amphotericin B
* Saline helps decrease drug-induced renal vasoconstriction.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A male patient being treated for a systemic fungal infection develops gynecomastia and loss of libido. This pathophysiology is linked to the drug's non-selective inhibition of host [___] synthesis.
back:
* Cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes
* Specifically inhibits mammalian testosterone and cortisol production.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain the role of fungal cytosine deaminase in the selective activation of Flucytosine (5-FC).
back:
* It converts 5-FC to the active antimetabolite 5-fluorouracil.
* Human cells lack this enzyme, preventing host cell DNA synthesis inhibition.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast conventional Amphotericin B deoxycholate with its liposomal formulation regarding their safety profiles.
back:
* Conventional: High affinity for human cholesterol, leading to severe renal damage.
* Liposomal: Reduced binding to human membranes, allowing higher doses with lower nephrotoxicity.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Describe the pharmacological reason why Terbinafine remains effective in fungal nail infections long after the medication is discontinued.
back:
* It is highly lipophilic and keratophilic.
* It accumulates in newly forming keratin structures (skin and nails).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Unlike most other systemic azoles which undergo hepatic metabolism, [___] is primarily eliminated unchanged by the kidneys.
back:
* Fluconazole
* Requires dosage adjustment in patients with renal failure.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient on Rifampin for tuberculosis is diagnosed with Histoplasmosis. Why is Itraconazole likely to fail as a co-therapy in this individual?
back:
* Rifampin is a potent CYP3A4 inducer.
* It significantly lowers Itraconazole serum levels below the therapeutic range.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism by which Echinocandins (e.g., Caspofungin) cause osmotic lysis of fungal cells.
back:
* Noncompetitive inhibition of 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase.
* This prevents cell wall polymer cross-linking, causing structural failure.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast Fluconazole and Itraconazole regarding their clinical utility in treating fungal meningitis.
back:
* Fluconazole: Excellent CNS penetration (>70% of serum levels).
* Itraconazole: Negligible CNS penetration; generally ineffective for meningitis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Name the specific oral antifungal agent that is noted for inducing a disulfiram-like reaction when ingested with alcohol.
back:
* Griseofulvin
* Patients must be warned to avoid alcohol during therapy.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Flucytosine (5-FC) is converted intracellularly into the active metabolite [___], which is incorporated into fungal RNA, leading to the inhibition of protein synthesis.
back:
• Fluorouridine triphosphate (FUTP)
• Interferes with RNA function and translation
• Fungal specificity relies on cytosine deaminase
• Used primarily with Amphotericin B to prevent resistance

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient being treated for systemic candidiasis with Amphotericin B deoxycholate develops profound muscle weakness and cardiac arrhythmias. These findings are most likely secondary to [___].
back:
• Renal tubular injury
• Causes severe potassium (K+) and magnesium (Mg2+) wasting
• May manifest as renal tubular acidosis
• Partially attenuated by sodium loading with saline

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which Candida species develop clinical resistance to the echinocandin class (e.g., Caspofungin).
back:
• Point mutations in Fks subunits
• Alters the target enzyme 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase
• Reduces the binding affinity of the drug
• Increasingly common in Candida glabrata infections

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the clinical utility of Itraconazole and Fluconazole in a patient presenting with fungal meningitis, focusing on blood-brain barrier penetration.
back:
• Fluconazole: Excellent CSF penetration (>70%); drug of choice for meningitis.
• Itraconazole: Negligible CSF penetration (<1%); inappropriate for CNS infections.
• Itraconazole is preferred for Histoplasma and Blastomyces tissue infections.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Define the therapeutic role and metabolic activation of the triazole Isavuconazonium sulfate.
back:
• Water-soluble prodrug of Isavuconazole
• Rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma esterases
• Approved for invasive Aspergillosis and Mucormycosis
• Offers better tolerability than Voriconazole

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Concomitant administration of Caspofungin and the immunosuppressant [___] is contraindicated because it significantly increases the risk of elevated hepatic aminotransferases.
back:
• Cyclosporine
• Leads to transient liver enzyme elevations
• Requires careful monitoring or drug substitution
• Avoided to prevent drug-induced hepatitis

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A 40-year-old male on oral Terbinafine for onychomycosis experiences drug-induced fungal cell death. This occurs primarily due to the toxic intracellular accumulation of [___].
back:
• Squalene
• Caused by inhibition of squalene epoxidase
• Leads to membrane disruption
• Simultaneously decreases ergosterol synthesis

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain the pharmacokinetic principle that allows Griseofulvin to protect skin from new dermatophyte infection despite its poor activity against existing fungal elements.
back:
• Binds avidly to newly synthesized keratin
• Deposits in maturing hair, skin, and nails
• Provides a barrier resistant to fungal invasion
• Requires long-term therapy (weeks to months)

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the treatment selection between Fluconazole and Echinocandins (e.g., Anidulafungin) for a critically ill patient with candidemia.
back:
• Echinocandins: First-line for severe candidemia or ICU patients.
• Fluconazole: Reserved for stable patients with sensitive isolates.
• Echinocandins target the cell wall; Fluconazole targets the membrane.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the primary clinical management steps required to mitigate the 'immediate' infusion-related toxicities of conventional Amphotericin B.
back:
• Slowing the infusion rate
• Premedication with antipyretics and antihistamines
• Use of a 1mg intravenous test dose
• Addition of corticosteroids to the infusion

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: The oral absorption of the broad-spectrum azole [___] is significantly improved when taken with high-fat meals.
back: • Posaconazole • Food maximizes systemic exposure • Essential for preventing breakthrough fungal infections in high-risk patients

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient with invasive mucormycosis is prescribed Isavuconazonium sulfate. Identify the active drug released and the clinical advantage of this prodrug salt.
back: • Active drug: Isavuconazole • Benefit: Water-soluble prodrug formulation • Allows high bioavailability and supports both oral and intravenous administration

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain how the inclusion of the carrier molecule cyclodextrin in newer Itraconazole formulations alters its pharmacological profile.
back: • Enhances aqueous solubility of the lipophilic drug • Markedly improves bioavailability over original capsules • Utilized in both oral liquid and IV preparations

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast Micafungin and Anidulafungin regarding their metabolism and potential for clinically significant drug-drug interactions.
back: • Micafungin: Increases levels of nifedipine and sirolimus; hepatically metabolized • Anidulafungin: Degraded non-enzymatically in blood; minimal drug interactions • Both are IV-only echinocandins

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the pharmacological consequence of co-administering Rifampin with Itraconazole and the underlying enzyme interaction.
back: • Effect: Drastic reduction in Itraconazole serum levels • Mechanism: Rifampin strongly induces CYP3A4 enzymes • Result: Potential failure of antifungal therapy

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: To minimize bone marrow toxicity and the risk of resistance, peak serum concentrations of Flucytosine should be maintained between [___] mcg/mL.
back: • 50 and 100 mcg/mL • Measured 1–2 hours after an oral dose • Monitored via therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A clinician chooses to avoid systemic Ketoconazole for a simple dermatophyte infection in favor of a newer triazole. Provide the primary safety rationale based on enzyme selectivity.
back: • Poor selectivity for fungal vs. mammalian P450 • High risk of inhibiting human testosterone and cortisol synthesis • Elevated risk of drug-induced clinical hepatitis

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Analyze the mechanism and clinical significance of emerging Echinocandin (e.g., Caspofungin) resistance in specific yeast species.
back: • Target: FKS gene mutations in Candida glabrata • Significance: Occurs after prolonged exposure in immunocompromised hosts • Critically limits treatment options for invasive candidiasis

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Distinguish between the underlying pathophysiology of 'Immediate' and 'Cumulative' renal toxicities associated with intravenous Amphotericin B.
back: • Immediate: Cytokine-mediated rigors and hypotension • Cumulative: Direct tubular injury and renal vasoconstriction • Prevention: Saline loading mitigates the cumulative azotemia

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the primary organ toxicity associated with systemic Terbinafine therapy and the required laboratory monitoring.
back: • Hepatic toxicity (Hepatotoxicity) • Monitoring: Baseline and periodic liver function tests (LFTs) • Warning: Use is contraindicated in patients with chronic or active liver disease

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Amphotericin B exerts its fungicidal effect by binding to [___] in the fungal cell membrane, leading to the formation of aqueous pores and lethal ion leakage.
back: • Ergosterol • Causes formation of transmembrane pores • Results in leakage of intracellular K+ and macromolecules • Direct damage to cell membrane integrity

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient receiving treatment for invasive aspergillosis with a triazole drug reports a transient flickering effect and altered color perception shortly after each dose. Identify the drug.
back: • Voriconazole • Visual disturbances occur in ~30% of patients • Symptoms include blurring and altered color perception • Typically reversible within 30–60 minutes

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain the difference in the primary cellular targets of Flucytosine versus the Triazole class of antifungal medications.
back: • Flucytosine: Nucleic acid synthesis (DNA and RNA inhibition) • Triazoles: Cell membrane synthesis (inhibits 14α-demethylase/ergosterol production) • Intracellular vs. Membrane targets

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A transplant recipient requires systemic antifungal therapy. Contrast the renal risk of Amphotericin B deoxycholate with that of Caspofungin.
back: • Amphotericin B: High risk of nephrotoxicity (azotemia, K+/Mg2+ wasting, distal RTA) • Caspofungin: Minimal renal toxicity; generally safe in renal impairment • Echinocandins have superior safety profiles

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the specific biochemical step and target enzyme inhibited by Terbinafine in the ergosterol biosynthetic pathway.
back: • Squalene epoxidase inhibition • Prevents conversion of squalene to squalene epoxide • Causes accumulation of toxic squalene • Resulting deficiency in ergosterol membrane component

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: In the pharmacological management of invasive aspergillosis, the triazole agent [___] is currently considered the first-line drug of choice due to superior efficacy over amphotericin B.
back: • Voriconazole • Replaced amphotericin B as standard induction therapy • Broad spectrum against molds and dimorphic fungi • Better survival outcomes in clinical trials

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient on chronic Warfarin therapy is prescribed Itraconazole for Histoplasmosis. Predict the effect on the patient's Prothrombin Time (PT/INR).
back: • Increased INR (risk of bleeding) • Itraconazole is a potent inhibitor of CYP3A4 • Reduces metabolism of Warfarin • Leads to increased plasma concentration of the anticoagulant

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain the pharmacodynamic basis for adding Flucytosine to Amphotericin B induction therapy for Cryptococcal meningitis.
back: • Synergy: Amphotericin-induced membrane damage increases Flucytosine uptake • Prevents emergence of Flucytosine resistance • Results in more rapid sterilization of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the physiological mechanism by which Amphotericin B induces hypokalemia versus how it induces normocytic normochromic anemia.
back: • Hypokalemia: Direct pore formation in renal tubules causing ion leakage • Anemia: Reduced erythropoietin production due to damaged renal tubular cells • Both reflect cumulative renal tubular toxicity

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Which structural component of the fungal cell, absent in mammalian cells, is targeted by the Echinocandin class (e.g., Anidulafungin)?
back: • β(1,3)-D-glucan • Synthesized by glucan synthase enzyme • Structural integrity of the cell wall is lost • Selective toxicity due to absence in human cells

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: To mitigate the prerenal component of Amphotericin B nephrotoxicity, clinicians typically administer [___] infusions concurrently with the drug.
back:
• Normal saline (Sodium loading).
• It attenuates the reversible component of renal failure associated with decreased renal perfusion.
• Sodium loading is standard clinical practice to reduce azotemia.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient being treated for invasive aspergillosis reports transient blurring and changes in color brightness occurring 30 minutes after each dose. Identify the drug responsible and the appropriate clinical response.
back:
• Voriconazole.
• These visual disturbances occur in ~30% of patients.
• No action is required as they are transient and resolve without treatment discontinuation.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain the role of the cyclodextrin carrier in newer formulations of Itraconazole.
back:
• It serves as a carrier molecule in oral liquid and IV preparations.
• Significantly enhances the drug's aqueous solubility and bioavailability compared to standard capsules.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the impact of high-fat meals on the absorption of Voriconazole versus Posaconazole.
back:
• Voriconazole: Absorption is decreased by food; must be taken on an empty stomach.
• Posaconazole: Absorption is significantly improved when taken with high-fat meals.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the specific clinical scenario where Caspofungin is licensed for use against Aspergillus species.
back:
• It is licensed only as salvage therapy.
• It is used in patients who have failed to respond to or are intolerant of Amphotericin B, rather than as primary therapy.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Isavuconazonium sulfate is the water-soluble [___] of Isavuconazole, uniquely licensed for both invasive aspergillosis and mucormycosis.
back:
• Prodrug.
• 186 mg of the sulfate is equivalent to 100 mg of the active isavuconazole base.
• It is available in both oral and IV formulations.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient on Itraconazole capsules for Histoplasmosis shows subtherapeutic drug levels despite compliance. He concurrently takes Omeprazole for GERD. Explain the pharmacological reason for this failure.
back:
• Itraconazole capsules require an acidic medium (low gastric pH) for absorption.
• Omeprazole (a PPI) increases gastric pH, which reduces Itraconazole's bioavailability and efficacy.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the primary molecular mechanism by which Candida glabrata develops resistance to Echinocandins.
back:
• Mutations in the Fks subunits of the target enzyme complex.
• This leads to an altered β(1–3)-glucan synthase with significantly reduced binding affinity for the drug.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast Micafungin and Anidulafungin regarding their potential for hepatic enzyme-mediated drug-drug interactions.
back:
• Micafungin: Can increase levels of nifedipine, cyclosporine, and sirolimus.
• Anidulafungin: Does not undergo significant hepatic metabolism and is relatively free of major drug interactions.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the critical monitoring parameter for a patient receiving prolonged Flucytosine therapy to prevent dose-limiting toxicity.
back:
• Peak serum concentrations.
• Levels must be maintained below 100 mcg/mL to avoid bone marrow toxicity (anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: In the management of vulvovaginal candidiasis, the topical imidazole [___] is commonly used over-the-counter due to its minimal systemic absorption and high local efficacy.
back:
• Clotrimazole (or Miconazole)
• Disrupts fungal cell membrane ergosterol synthesis
• Available as creams or vaginal suppositories
• Minimal adverse effects beyond local irritation

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient receiving systemic Amphotericin B develops profound muscle weakness and cardiac arrhythmias. Lab results show potassium of 2.1 mEq/L and magnesium of 1.0 mEq/L. Explain the pathophysiology of these findings.
back:
• Drug-induced renal tubular injury
• Increased permeability of the distal tubule membrane
• Results in severe distal wasting of K+ and Mg2+
• Leads to hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Describe the molecular mechanism of Echinocandin resistance (e.g. Caspofungin) commonly observed in clinical isolates of Candida glabrata.
back:
• Mutations in FKS1 or FKS2 genes
• Alters subunits of 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase
• Reduces the binding affinity of the drug
• Leads to higher MICs and treatment failure

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A renal transplant recipient on Cyclosporine develops Candidemia. Contrast the choice between Micafungin and Voriconazole regarding the specific risk of drug-drug interactions.
back:
• Voriconazole: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; dangerously elevates Cyclosporine levels
• Micafungin: Minimal CYP450 interaction; safer for calcineurin inhibitor regimens
• Micafungin avoids life-threatening immunosuppressant toxicity

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the critical physiological step required for the optimal oral absorption of Itraconazole capsules.
back:
• Acidic gastric environment (low pH)
• Absorption is significantly impaired by PPIs or H2 blockers
• Bioavailability is improved when taken with food
• Oral solution is less pH-dependent than capsules

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: During high-dose systemic antifungal therapy, the physician must monitor [___] and serum creatinine twice weekly to detect renal tubular wasting and potential acute kidney injury.
back:
• Potassium and Magnesium levels
• Detects distal tubular damage early
• Prevents life-threatening hypokalemic arrhythmias
• Often necessitates aggressive electrolyte supplementation

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient with alcoholic cirrhosis and invasive aspergillosis requires systemic therapy. Why might Isavuconazole be selected over Voriconazole in this scenario?
back:
• Lower incidence of drug-induced hepatotoxicity
• No dose adjustment required for mild-to-moderate cirrhosis
• Better overall tolerability profile
• Predictable linear pharmacokinetics

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Describe the specific ionic pathophysiology of the 'Type 1 Renal Tubular Acidosis' seen with chronic polyene use.
back:
• Pore formation in the distal tubular membrane
• Massive back-diffusion of hydrogen ions (H+)
• Inability to maintain the acidic urinary gradient
• Results in systemic metabolic acidosis

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the primary route of elimination for Fluconazole with that of all other systemic triazoles (e.g. Itraconazole, Voriconazole).
back:
• Fluconazole: Excreted unchanged by the kidneys (Renal)
• Other Triazoles: Extensively metabolized by the liver (Hepatic)
• Fluconazole requires adjustment for creatinine clearance
• Fluconazole reaches higher therapeutic levels in urine

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Name the systemic triazole antifungal that is strictly contraindicated in patients with symptomatic heart failure due to its negative inotropic properties.
back:
• Itraconazole
• Carries a black box warning for heart failure
• Can exacerbate ventricular dysfunction and pulmonary edema
• Discontinue if signs of CHF develop

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: [___] are a class of antiretrovirals that act as competitive inhibitors of reverse transcriptase and require intracellular activation via three phosphorylation steps to become active triphosphates.
back:
Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs).
- Examples include Abacavir, Emtricitabine, and Zidovudine.
- Act as DNA chain terminators upon incorporation into viral DNA.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: A 25-year-old patient presents with fever and cough during an influenza outbreak. If treatment is initiated within 48 hours, which class of antivirals is most appropriate to inhibit the spread of the infection within the respiratory tract?
back:
Neuraminidase Inhibitors.
- Examples: Oseltamivir (oral), Zanamivir (inhaled), Peramivir (IV).
- Mechanism: Prevents the release of progeny virions by inhibiting viral neuraminidase.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Explain the role of HIV Protease Inhibitors (PIs) in the viral life cycle and their impact on virion maturation.
back:
- Target: HIV protease enzyme.
- Mechanism: Prevent post-translational cleavage of Gag-Pol polyproteins.
- Outcome: Production of immature, noninfectious viral particles that cannot infect new cells.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
coreConcept: HIV Entry and Fusion Inhibitor Contrast
front: A patient with multi-drug resistant HIV is failing a standard NNRTI/NRTI regimen. Contrast the specific targets of Fusion Inhibitors versus CCR5 Co-receptor Antagonists in this scenario.
back:
- Fusion Inhibitors (e.g., Enfuvirtide): Bind to the gp41 subunit of the viral envelope to block viral entry.
- CCR5 Antagonists (e.g., Maraviroc): Bind to the host CCR5 receptor to prevent gp120 binding.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Categorize the anti-Hepatitis C agent Velpatasvir based on its specific viral protein target.
back:
NS5A Inhibitor.
- Part of direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens.
- Interferes with viral replication and assembly.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: [___] is an L-valyl ester prodrug of ganciclovir that provides significantly improved oral bioavailability for the treatment of CMV retinitis.
back:
Valganciclovir.
- Rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases in the intestine and liver to active ganciclovir.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: A 35-year-old female patient is found to be co-infected with both HIV and Hepatitis B (HBV). Which class of agents is clinically preferred due to dual activity against both viruses?
back:
Nucleoside/Nucleotide Analogs.
- Specifically Tenofovir, Lamivudine, and Emtricitabine.
- Caution: Interruption can lead to severe acute exacerbations of Hepatitis B.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: In the setting of a transplant patient with CMV infection resistant to Ganciclovir (UL97 mutation), explain how Foscarnet achieves its antiviral effect.
back:
- Classification: Inorganic pyrophosphate analog.
- Mechanism: Directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase by blocking the pyrophosphate binding site.
- Does not require activation by viral kinases (UL97).

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Contrast the mechanism of action of first-generation Adamantanes versus Neuraminidase inhibitors in treating Influenza A.
back:
- Adamantanes (Amantadine/Rimantadine): Block the M2 proton ion channel to inhibit viral uncoating.
- Neuraminidase Inhibitors (Oseltamivir): Inhibit the enzyme site to prevent viral release from host cells.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Identify the primary mechanism and classification of the anti-HIV drug Raltegravir.
back:
- Class: Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitor (INSTI).
- Mechanism: Inhibits the integration of reverse-transcribed HIV DNA into the host cell chromosome.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Antifungals that act by inhibiting the synthesis of β(1–3)-glucan, resulting in disruption of the fungal cell wall, belong to the class [___].
back:
• Echinocandins
• Includes Caspofungin, Micafungin, and Anidulafungin
• Only available in parenteral formulations.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: A 45-year-old transplant patient presents with progressive pulmonary infiltrates. A diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis is made. The first-line azole of choice for this condition is [___].
back:
• Voriconazole
• Replaced Amphotericin B and Itraconazole as standard of care
• Inhibits 14α-sterol demethylase.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Explain the biochemical role of flucytosine (5-FC) upon its intracellular conversion to 5-fluorouracil in fungal cells.
back:
• Converted to 5-FU by cytosine deaminase
• 5-FU metabolite FdUMP inhibits thymidylate synthase (blocks DNA synthesis)
• 5-FU metabolite FUTP inhibits RNA synthesis.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the mechanisms of action between polyene macrolides (Amphotericin B) and azole derivatives regarding the fungal cell membrane.
back:
• Polyenes: Bind to ergosterol to form membrane pores (fungicidal)
• Azoles: Inhibit ergosterol synthesis by blocking cytochrome P450-dependent 14α-demethylase (fungistatic).

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Identify the primary therapeutic target of the allylamine drug terbinafine in fungal sterol biosynthesis.
back:
• Inhibits squalene epoxidase
• Prevents synthesis of lanosterol from squalene
• Causes accumulation of toxic squalene.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: The primary oral drug used for the treatment of onychomycosis, which acts as a keratophilic and fungicidal agent, is [___].
back:
• Terbinafine
• Superior cure rates compared to Griseofulvin
• Requires 12-week course for toenail infections.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: A patient with cryptococcal meningitis is started on combination therapy. Why is flucytosine typically avoided as a monotherapy in this setting?
back:
• Development of secondary resistance occurs rapidly
• Synergistic effect required with Amphotericin B
• Prevents treatment failure in severe infections.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Describe the specific advantage of Fluconazole over other azoles for the treatment of fungal central nervous system (CNS) infections.
back:
• High cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) penetration
• Achieves >70% of serum concentrations in CSF
• Superior solubility and low protein binding.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the imidazole and triazole classes of systemic antifungal drugs based on their enzymatic selectivity.
back:
• Imidazoles (e.g. Ketoconazole): Less selective; high inhibition of human CYP450
• Triazoles (e.g. Fluconazole): Highly selective; minimal effect on mammalian steroid synthesis.

category: Classify antifungal drugs
front: Name the specific sterol found in fungal cell membranes that serves as the target for Polyene macrolides.
back:
• Ergosterol
• Analogous to cholesterol in mammalian membranes
• Binding creates leakage of intracellular ions.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: The [___] class of antiretroviral drugs, which includes Raltegravir and Dolutegravir, prevents the final step of provirus integration into the host cell chromosome.
back:
Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors (INSTIs).
- Binds to viral integrase.
- Interferes with DNA strand transfer.
- Blocks integration of HIV DNA into host genome.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: A patient with advanced AIDS presents with blurred vision and retinal opacities. Fundoscopy confirms CMV retinitis. Identify the two primary guanosine analogs used as first-line therapy for this condition.
back:
Valganciclovir (oral) and Ganciclovir (IV).
- Both target CMV DNA polymerase.
- Valganciclovir is the L-valyl ester prodrug of ganciclovir.
- Requires viral kinase UL97 for activation.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Explain the biochemical activation required for nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) to exert their antiviral effect in HIV-infected cells.
back:
Intracytoplasmic phosphorylation by host cellular kinases to a triphosphate form.
- Competitively inhibits reverse transcriptase.
- Acts as a substrate for viral DNA.
- Causes premature chain termination.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Contrast the adamantanes (Amantadine/Rimantadine) and neuraminidase inhibitors (Oseltamivir/Zanamivir) regarding their viral targets and influenza strain spectrum.
back:
Adamantanes: Target M2 proton channel; active against Influenza A only.
- Neuraminidase Inhibitors: Target viral neuraminidase (sialic acid analogs); active against Influenza A and B.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Categorize the direct-acting antiviral (DAA) agents used in chronic Hepatitis C treatment based on their specific nonstructural (NS) protein targets.
back:
NS3/4A Protease Inhibitors (e.g., Simeprevir).
- NS5A Replication/Assembly Inhibitors (e.g., Ledipasvir).
- NS5B RNA-dependent RNA Polymerase Inhibitors (e.g., Sofosbuvir).

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: [___] is a 36-amino-acid peptide fusion inhibitor that blocks HIV entry into the cell by binding to the gp41 subunit of the viral envelope glycoprotein.
back:
Enfuvirtide.
- Only parenterally administered antiretroviral.
- Prevents conformational changes required for membrane fusion.
- Lacks cross-resistance with other classes.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: An HIV-positive patient on combination therapy develops central obesity, a 'buffalo hump,' and insulin resistance. Which drug class is most classically associated with these morphologic derangements?
back:
Protease Inhibitors (PIs).
- Associated with lipodystrophy and fat redistribution.
- Examples: Atazanavir, Darunavir, Ritonavir.
- Common inhibitors of CYP3A4.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Describe the specific functions of the Hepatitis B (HBV) DNA polymerase inhibited by the nucleoside analog Entecavir.
back:
Base priming.
- Reverse transcription of the negative strand.
- Synthesis of the positive strand of HBV DNA.
- Competitively inhibits the polymerase enzyme.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Contrast Nonnucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs) with Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) regarding their binding sites and activation requirements.
back:
NNRTIs: Bind allosterically (near distinct site); do not require phosphorylation.
- NRTIs: Bind at the active site (competitively); require intracellular phosphorylation to triphosphate form.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Identify the two primary agents classified for the prevention or treatment of severe Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in high-risk infants.
back:
Palivizumab: Humanized monoclonal antibody for prevention.
- Ribavirin: Aerosolized guanosine analog for treatment of severe disease.
- Palivizumab targets the RSV F surface protein.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: The anti-retroviral agent [___] acts specifically as a CCR5 co-receptor antagonist, preventing viral entry into host CD4+ cells.
back:
• Maraviroc
• Requires tropism testing (active only against CCR5-tropic strains)
• Blocks gp120 interaction with host CCR5

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: An HIV-infected patient is screened for the HLA-B*5701 allele before starting a specific NRTI. The presence of this allele significantly increases the risk of a fatal hypersensitivity reaction to [___].
back:
• Abacavir
• Reaction presents with fever, rash, and GI symptoms
• Rechallenge is strictly contraindicated

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Explain the intracellular activation pathway required for Acyclovir to inhibit viral DNA synthesis.
back:
• Step 1: Monophosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase (selectivity)
• Step 2: Di- and triphosphorylation by host cell kinases
• Step 3: Competes with dGTP to inhibit viral DNA polymerase and cause chain termination

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Contrast the specific viral targets and spectrum of activity between Neuraminidase inhibitors (e.g., Oseltamivir) and Adamantanes (e.g., Amantadine).
back:
• Neuraminidase Inhibitors: Target viral release/budding; active against Influenza A and B
• Adamantanes: Target M2 proton channel (uncoating); active against Influenza A only; high resistance rates

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Identify the primary mechanism of action for the HIV Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitor (INSTI) class, such as Raltegravir.
back:
• Blocks the viral integrase enzyme
• Prevents the integration of reverse-transcribed HIV DNA into the host cell chromosome
• Inhibits the formation of the provirus

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: The direct-acting antiviral (DAA) [___] is classified as an NS5B polymerase inhibitor and is used as a backbone for interferon-free Hepatitis C therapy.
back:
• Sofosbuvir
• Acts as a chain terminator by targeting the HCV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalytic site
• Effective across all HCV genotypes

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: A patient with CMV retinitis receives a drug that does not require viral kinase activation but is associated with severe nephrotoxicity and electrolyte wasting (hypocalcemia). Identify the drug.
back:
• Foscarnet
• Mechanism: Inorganic pyrophosphate analog; directly inhibits DNA/RNA polymerase
• Used for ganciclovir-resistant CMV or acyclovir-resistant HSV

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Describe the physiological rationale behind using 'Ritonavir boosting' in HIV protease inhibitor (PI) regimens.
back:
• Ritonavir is a potent inhibitor of cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4)
• It increases the serum levels and half-life of other PIs (e.g., Atazanavir, Lopinavir)
• Result: Lower pill burden and improved resistance barrier

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Contrast Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) and Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs) regarding their binding site and activation requirements.
back:
• NRTIs: Bind to the active site; require intracellular phosphorylation to triphosphate form
• NNRTIs: Bind to an allosteric site (non-competitive); do not require phosphorylation

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Which three oral agents are used in the treatment of chronic Hepatitis B (HBV) that also possess intrinsic activity against HIV?
back:
• Tenofovir
• Lamivudine
• Emtricitabine
• Caution: Discontinuation can cause life-threatening HBV flares

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: The oral L-valyl ester prodrug of acyclovir, which achieves serum levels comparable to those of intravenous acyclovir, is [___].
back:
• Valacyclovir
• Converted via first-pass hepatic hydrolysis.
• Provides 3–5 times higher bioavailability than oral acyclovir.
• Used for HSV and VZV infections.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: A 35-year-old HIV-positive patient with a CD4 count of 45 presents with progressive vision loss and yellow-white retinal opacitates. The first-line oral agent used for both induction and maintenance of this condition is [___].
back:
• Valganciclovir
• It is the L-valyl ester prodrug of ganciclovir.
• Targeted against Cytomegalovirus (CMV).
• Major side effect is reversible myelosuppression.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Explain the biochemical activation required for Acyclovir to selectively inhibit DNA synthesis in virus-infected cells.
back:
• Initial phosphorylation to monophosphate by viral-specified Thymidine Kinase.
• Subsequent di- and tri-phosphorylation by host cell enzymes.
• Competes with dGTP for viral DNA polymerase and acts as a chain terminator.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Contrast the binding site and activation requirements of Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) versus Non-nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs).
back:
• NRTIs: Bind to the catalytic site, require intracellular phosphorylation to be active.
• NNRTIs: Bind to an allosteric site near the catalytic center, do not require phosphorylation.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Identify the three primary classes of Direct-Acting Antiviral (DAA) agents based on their targets in the Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) life cycle.
back:
• NS3/4A Protease Inhibitors (suffix '-previr').
• NS5A Inhibitors (suffix '-asvir').
• NS5B Polymerase Inhibitors (suffix '-buvir').

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Influenza agents like Oseltamivir and Zanamivir act as analogs of sialic acid to inhibit the viral enzyme [___].
back:
• Neuraminidase
• Prevents release of progeny virions from the host cell.
• Active against both Influenza A and B.
• Most effective when initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: A patient with HLA-B*5701 allele develops a life-threatening multi-organ hypersensitivity reaction after starting an NRTI. The specific drug responsible is [___].
back:
• Abacavir
• Screening for HLA-B*5701 is mandatory before initiation.
• Symptoms include fever, rash, and respiratory distress.
• Re-challenge is strictly contraindicated and potentially fatal.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Describe the physiological role of Ritonavir when used at low doses in combination with other Protease Inhibitors (PIs).
back:
• Acts as a pharmacokinetic 'booster'.
• Potently inhibits CYP3A4 metabolism of the co-administered PI.
• Increases drug exposure (AUC), prolongs half-life, and raises the genetic barrier to resistance.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Contrast the mechanism of action between Enfuvirtide and Maraviroc in the inhibition of HIV cell entry.
back:
• Enfuvirtide: Fusion inhibitor; binds to the gp41 subunit of the viral envelope.
• Maraviroc: Entry inhibitor; binds to the host CCR5 co-receptor to block gp120 binding.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Name the two primary classes of drugs used for the treatment of Chronic Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) infection.
back:
• Nucleoside/Nucleotide Analogs (e.g., Tenofovir, Entecavir).
• Interferons (e.g., Pegylated Interferon Alfa-2a).
• Nucleotide analogs suppress replication; Interferons provide immune modulation.

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: In HSV-infected cells, the initial phosphorylation of acyclovir to its monophosphate form is specifically catalyzed by the virus-specified enzyme [___].
back:
• Viral thymidine kinase
• Provides selective toxicity for infected cells
• Essential for subsequent conversion to active triphosphate metabolites by host kinases

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: An AIDS patient with a CD4 count of 40 presents with blurred vision and retinal hemorrhages. The prescribed agent requires activation by the viral phosphotransferase UL97. Identify the drug.
back:
• Ganciclovir
• Acts as a guanosine analog inhibiting DNA polymerase
• Used for CMV retinitis and end-organ disease
• Valganciclovir is the orally bioavailable prodrug

category: Classify antiviral drugs
front: Explain the role of Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors (INSTIs) in blocking the HIV replication cycle.
back:
• Bind directly to the viral integrase enzyme
• Inhibit the final step of provirus integration (strand transfer)
• Prevent the integration of reverse-transcribed HIV DNA into the host cell genome

category: Classify antiviral drugs
coreConcept: Comparison of HIV reverse transcriptase inhibitors
front: Contrast Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) with Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs) regarding their binding sites and phosphorylation requirements.
back:
• NRTIs: Bind at the catalytic site; require intracellular phosphorylation to active triphosphate forms
• NNRTIs: Bind to an allosteric pocket; do not require phosphorylation or activation

category: Classify antiviral drugs
