front: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4 count of 40 presents with blurred vision and floaters. The oral prodrug used as the standard for induction and maintenance of the resulting CMV retinitis is [___].
back:
• Valganciclovir
• L-valyl ester prodrug of ganciclovir
• High oral bioavailability (~60%)
• Rapidly hydrolyzed by intestinal and hepatic esterases

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the role of the UL97 phosphotransferase enzyme in the pharmacological activation of Ganciclovir within CMV-infected cells.
back:
• Catalyzes the first phosphorylation step
• Converts ganciclovir to ganciclovir monophosphate
• Mutations in UL97 are the primary cause of clinical CMV resistance
• Essential for subsequent viral DNA polymerase inhibition

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast Foscarnet and Acyclovir regarding their specific molecular requirements for intracellular activation and viral DNA polymerase inhibition.
back:
• Acyclovir: Requires viral thymidine kinase for initial phosphorylation
• Foscarnet: Directly inhibits DNA polymerase without requiring activation
• Foscarnet remains active against thymidine kinase-deficient (acyclovir-resistant) strains

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary electrolyte disturbances and mineral imbalances associated with the chelation of divalent cations during Foscarnet therapy.
back:
• Hypocalcemia (most common and dangerous)
• Hypomagnesemia and hypokalemia
• Hypo- or hyperphosphatemia
• Can lead to seizures and cardiac arrhythmias

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: To mitigate the risk of dose-dependent proximal tubular nephrotoxicity, intravenous [___] must be co-administered with high-dose probenecid and aggressive saline prehydration.
back:
• Cidofovir
• Cytosine nucleotide analog
• Probenecid blocks active tubular secretion of the drug
• Prevents Fanconi's syndrome and proteinuria

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient being treated for Herpes encephalitis with high-dose intravenous therapy develops an acute rise in serum creatinine and BUN. This renal impairment is primarily due to [___].
back:
• Crystalline nephropathy (Acyclovir)
• Occurs when drug solubility is exceeded in the tubules
• Prevented by adequate hydration and slow infusion rates
• Usually reversible upon drug discontinuation

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the two-fold mechanism by which Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral replication once it has been activated by viral and host kinases.
back:
• Competitive inhibition: Competes with dGTP for viral DNA polymerase
• Chain termination: Incorporation into the DNA template prevents further strand elongation
• Forms an irreversible complex with the DNA template

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast Valacyclovir and Acyclovir in terms of their pharmacokinetic profile after oral administration.
back:
• Bioavailability: Valacyclovir (54–70%) vs. Acyclovir (15–20%)
• Serum levels: Valacyclovir achieves 3–5x higher concentrations
• Valacyclovir allows for less frequent daily dosing due to superior absorption

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Which systemic antiviral is associated with dose-limiting myelosuppression, specifically manifesting as neutropenia and thrombocytopenia?
back:
• Ganciclovir (and Valganciclovir)
• Most common serious adverse effect
• Risk is additive with other myelosuppressive drugs like Zidovudine
• Requires frequent monitoring of complete blood counts

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Acyclovir is a guanosine analog that requires three phosphorylation steps; the initial rate-limiting step is specifically catalyzed by the virus-specified enzyme [___].
back:
• Viral thymidine kinase.
• This converts acyclovir to its monophosphate form.
• Ensures the drug is only activated within virus-infected cells.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: An HIV patient with a CD4 count <50 cells/μL is treated for CMV retinitis. A few weeks later, CBC reveals severe neutropenia. Which drug and primary mechanism are responsible?
back:
• Ganciclovir (or Valganciclovir).
• Dose-limiting myelosuppression is its hallmark side effect.
• Caused by inhibition of host cell DNA polymerase at high levels.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the role of Foscarnet as an inorganic pyrophosphate analog in inhibiting viral DNA synthesis.
back:
• Directly binds and blocks the pyrophosphate binding site of DNA polymerase.
• Inhibits cleavage of pyrophosphate from deoxynucleotide triphosphates.
• Requires no intracellular phosphorylation steps to be active.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast Acyclovir and Cidofovir regarding their dependence on viral enzymes for intracellular activation.
back:
• Acyclovir: Dependent on viral thymidine kinase for the first phosphorylation step.
• Cidofovir: Independent of viral enzymes; utilizes host cell kinases for phosphorylation.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the L-valyl ester prodrug of acyclovir and state its primary pharmacokinetic advantage.
back:
• Valacyclovir.
• Rapidly converted to acyclovir via first-pass metabolism.
• Advantage: Significantly higher oral bioavailability (54–70%) compared to oral acyclovir (15–20%).

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: To mitigate dose-dependent proximal tubular nephrotoxicity, intravenous Cidofovir must be administered concurrently with aggressive hydration and [___].
back:
• High-dose Probenecid.
• Probenecid blocks the active tubular secretion of the drug.
• Helps prevent accumulation in renal tubular cells.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient with thymidine kinase-deficient HSV is resistant to Acyclovir and Famciclovir. Which pyrophosphate analog should be used to treat this infection?
back:
• Foscarnet.
• Effective because it does not require phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase.
• Directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe how Acyclovir specifically achieves viral DNA chain termination during replication.
back:
• Acyclovir lacks a 3'-hydroxyl group on its acyclic sugar side chain.
• Once incorporated into viral DNA, no further nucleotides can be attached.
• Acts as a competitive inhibitor of dGTP.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the specific viral enzymes required for the initial phosphorylation of Acyclovir in HSV versus Ganciclovir in CMV.
back:
• HSV (Acyclovir): Thymidine kinase.
• CMV (Ganciclovir): Phosphotransferase encoded by the UL97 gene.
• Mutations in these specific genes lead to drug-specific resistance.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: What is the clinical indication for Trifluridine and why is its use restricted to topical application?
back:
• Indication: HSV keratoconjunctivitis and epithelial keratitis.
• Restriction: Non-selective incorporation into both viral and host DNA.
• Too toxic for systemic administration.

category: Discuss the main steps of viral replication that are targets for antiviral drugs
front: In the influenza A replication cycle, the class of drugs that specifically targets the M2 proton ion channel to prevent viral uncoating is [___].
back: Amantadine and Rimantadine. • Block the M2 channel to prevent acidification of the endosome. • Prevents the release of viral RNA into the host cytoplasm.

category: Discuss the main steps of viral replication that are targets for antiviral drugs
front: An HIV-infected patient is prescribed a regimen including Raltegravir. This drug class exerts its effect by blocking which specific step of the viral life cycle?
back: Integration. • Inhibits the integrase strand transfer enzyme. • Prevents the covalent insertion of proviral DNA into host cell chromosomes.

category: Discuss the main steps of viral replication that are targets for antiviral drugs
front: Explain how neuraminidase inhibitors like Oseltamivir carry out their biological function upon mature influenza virions.
back: Inhibits viral release. • Competitively blocks the neuraminidase enzyme site. • Prevents cleavage of sialic acid residues, causing newly formed virions to clump on the cell surface.

category: Discuss the main steps of viral replication that are targets for antiviral drugs
front: Contrast the molecular targets of the HIV entry inhibitors Maraviroc and Enfuvirtide.
back: • Maraviroc: Binds host CCR5 co-receptor (blocks binding). • Enfuvirtide: Binds viral gp41 subunit (blocks membrane fusion and entry).

category: Discuss the main steps of viral replication that are targets for antiviral drugs
front: Identify the critical replication step targeted by HIV protease inhibitors such as Darunavir and Atazanavir.
back: Maturation (Post-translational processing). • Prevents cleavage of the Gag-Pol polyprotein into functional proteins. • Results in the production of immature, noninfectious particles.

category: Discuss the main steps of viral replication that are targets for antiviral drugs
front: The conversion of single-stranded viral RNA into double-stranded DNA by viral enzymes is the pharmacological target of the [___] drug class.
back: NRTIs and NNRTIs. • Nucleoside/Nucleotide and Non-nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors. • Essential for inhibiting early proviral DNA synthesis.

category: Discuss the main steps of viral replication that are targets for antiviral drugs
front: A patient uses a topical 10% cream for recurrent orolabial herpes. The drug acts by inhibiting fusion between the host cell plasma membrane and the HSV envelope. Name the agent.
back: Docosanol. • Saturated 22-carbon aliphatic alcohol. • Prevents viral entry into the host cell before intracellular replication starts.

category: Discuss the main steps of viral replication that are targets for antiviral drugs
front: Describe the roles of the activated triphosphate form of Acyclovir in the inhibition of herpesvirus DNA replication.
back: Competitive inhibition and chain termination. • Competes with deoxyGTP for the viral DNA polymerase. • Incorporation into the DNA strand causes irreversible termination.

category: Discuss the main steps of viral replication that are targets for antiviral drugs
front: Distinguish between NRTIs and NNRTIs regarding their binding mechanism to the reverse transcriptase enzyme.
back: • NRTIs: Competitive inhibitors that require intracellular phosphorylation to activate. • NNRTIs: Noncompetitive allosteric inhibitors that do not require activation.

category: Discuss the main steps of viral replication that are targets for antiviral drugs
front: Name the specific viral enzyme targeted by the nucleotide analog Sofosbuvir in the treatment of chronic Hepatitis C.
back: NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. • Inhibits viral replication by acting as a chain terminator. • Potent activity across all HCV genotypes.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: The initial phosphorylation of acyclovir to its monophosphate form is selectively catalyzed in infected cells by the virus-specified enzyme [___].
back:
• Thymidine Kinase (TK)
• Host cell enzymes then convert it to di- and triphosphate forms
• TK-deficient strains exhibit cross-resistance to valacyclovir and famciclovir.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A transplant recipient develops chronic cutaneous lesions that fail to respond to high-dose acyclovir. Susceptibility testing confirms a thymidine kinase-deficient HSV strain. The systemic alternative that inhibits DNA polymerase directly without requiring viral activation is [___].
back:
• Foscarnet
• It is an inorganic pyrophosphate analog
• Directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase and RNA polymerase
• Useful for acyclovir-resistant HSV/VZV and ganciclovir-resistant CMV.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the role of the viral protein UL97 in the pharmacological action of Ganciclovir during Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection.
back:
• UL97 is a viral protein kinase (phosphotransferase)
• It performs the initial phosphorylation of ganciclovir to its monophosphate form
• Mutations in UL97 are the primary cause of ganciclovir resistance.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast Acyclovir and Cidofovir regarding their dependence on viral enzymes for intracellular activation.
back:
• Acyclovir: Requires viral Thymidine Kinase for the first phosphorylation step
• Cidofovir: A nucleotide analog phosphorylated solely by host cell kinases
• This allows Cidofovir activity against TK-deficient HSV/CMV strains.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary metabolic and electrolyte abnormalities associated with Foscarnet therapy that necessitate monitoring of ionized cations.
back:
• Renal impairment (nephrotoxicity)
• Symptomatic hypocalcemia (due to chelation of divalent cations)
• Hypomagnesemia and hypokalemia
• Potential for seizures due to electrolyte shifts.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: To improve oral bioavailability compared to acyclovir, the L-valyl ester prodrug [___] is utilized, achieving serum levels comparable to intravenous acyclovir.
back:
• Valacyclovir
• Undergoes rapid first-pass hydrolysis in the liver/intestines
• Bioavailability is 54–70% (vs. 15–20% for acyclovir)
• Preferred for VZV where higher drug levels are required.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: An AIDS patient treated for CMV retinitis develops severe, dose-limiting neutropenia. Which specific anti-CMV nucleoside analog is most likely responsible for this hematological toxicity?
back:
• Ganciclovir
• Most common adverse effect is reversible myelosuppression
• Risk increases when co-administered with other myelosuppressive drugs like Zidovudine (AZT).

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the physiological mechanism by which Trifluridine is restricted to topical use in herpetic keratitis.
back:
• It is a fluorinated pyrimidine nucleoside
• Triphosphate form incorporates into both viral and host cell DNA
• High systemic toxicity prevents internal administration
• Used topically for HSV-1 and HSV-2 keratoconjunctivitis.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the mechanism of action of Acyclovir versus Penciclovir regarding DNA chain termination.
back:
• Acyclovir: Causes obligate chain termination once incorporated into viral DNA
• Penciclovir: Competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase but does not cause immediate chain termination
• Both require viral TK for activation.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: State the standard pharmacological intervention required to mitigate the dose-dependent nephrotoxicity of Cidofovir.
back:
• Aggressive pre-hydration with Normal Saline
• Concomitant administration of high-dose Probenecid
• Probenecid blocks active tubular secretion of the drug, protecting proximal tubule cells.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: To become active, Acyclovir must first be monophosphorylated by the virus-specified enzyme [___].
back:
- Thymidine kinase
- Converts acyclovir to its monophosphate form
- Selective activation ensures the drug accumulates primarily in virus-infected cells
- Host kinases later complete the conversion to active triphosphate

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient receiving high-dose intravenous Acyclovir for herpes encephalitis develops a sudden rise in serum creatinine. This adverse effect is primarily due to [___].
back:
- Crystalline nephropathy
- Results from drug precipitation in the renal tubules
- Most common with rapid high-dose intravenous infusions
- Prevention involves aggressive pre-infusion hydration and slower delivery rates

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain how Foscarnet inhibits viral replication without requiring activation by viral or host kinases.
back:
- Inorganic pyrophosphate analog
- Directly binds to and inhibits viral DNA/RNA polymerase
- Does not require phosphorylation by thymidine kinase or UL97
- Acts at the pyrophosphate binding site to block nucleotide cleavage

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the initial phosphorylation step required for the activation of Acyclovir in HSV-infected cells versus Ganciclovir in CMV-infected cells.
back:
- Acyclovir: Initially phosphorylated by viral **thymidine kinase**
- Ganciclovir: Initially phosphorylated by viral **phosphotransferase UL97**
- Both drugs subsequently utilize host cell kinases to achieve active triphosphate forms
- CMV lacks thymidine kinase

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: State the primary pharmacological advantage of using Valacyclovir over Acyclovir for oral treatment of shingles.
back:
- Superior oral bioavailability (54–70%) compared to oral acyclovir
- Rapidly converted to acyclovir via first-pass intestinal/hepatic metabolism
- Provides serum levels equivalent to intravenous acyclovir dosing
- Allows for less frequent dosing intervals

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: The most common dose-limiting adverse effect of systemic Ganciclovir therapy is [___].
back:
- Myelosuppression (neutropenia and thrombocytopenia)
- Considered dose-limiting and usually reversible upon discontinuation
- Toxicity is additive when co-administered with other myelosuppressive drugs like zidovudine
- Monitoring of complete blood counts is mandatory

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient treated for ganciclovir-resistant CMV retinitis develops perioral paresthesias and a positive Chvostek sign. Identify the drug responsible and the underlying metabolic disturbance.
back:
- Foscarnet-induced symptomatic hypocalcemia
- Result of the drug chelating divalent metal cations
- Risk is significantly increased by concurrent use of pentamidine
- Requires careful monitoring of electrolytes and slow drug infusion

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the mechanism by which Cidofovir maintains its antiviral effect despite a short plasma half-life of 2.6 hours.
back:
- Rapid intracellular conversion to the active cidofovir diphosphate form
- Active metabolite possesses a significantly prolonged intracellular half-life (17–65 hours)
- Long-term storage in cidofovir phosphocholine reservoirs further extends action
- Enables effective weekly or bi-weekly induction/maintenance dosing

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the clinical application and systemic limitation of Trifluridine compared to Acyclovir.
back:
- Application: Trifluridine treats HSV keratoconjunctivitis and acyclovir-resistant keratitis
- Limitation: Incorporates into host DNA, making it too toxic for systemic use
- Mechanism: Does not require viral thymidine kinase for its initial activation

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the specific step in the HSV life cycle targeted by the over-the-counter topical agent Docosanol.
back:
- Blocks fusion between the host cell membrane and viral envelope
- Prevents viral entry into host cells and subsequent replication
- Effective only when applied within 12 hours of prodromal symptom onset
- Minimal risk of systemic absorption or adverse effects

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Acyclovir requires initial phosphorylation by the virus-specified enzyme [___] to be converted into its monophosphate form.
back:
• Thymidine kinase
• This ensures the drug is selectively activated only in virus-infected cells
• Host cell enzymes then perform subsequent phosphorylations.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient with HSV encephalitis treated with high-dose intravenous Acyclovir develops a rapid rise in serum creatinine. This 'crystalline nephropathy' can be prevented by [___].
back:
• Ensuring adequate hydration
• Maintaining a slow rate of drug infusion
• These measures prevent the precipitation of drug crystals in the renal tubules.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the two specific molecular mechanisms by which Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral replication after entering the DNA chain.
back:
• Competes with deoxyGTP for viral DNA polymerase
• Acts as a chain terminator, preventing further elongation of the viral DNA strand.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the initial activating enzymes required for Acyclovir (used in HSV) versus Ganciclovir (used in CMV).
back:
• Acyclovir: Virus-specified thymidine kinase
• Ganciclovir: Virus-specified protein kinase phosphotransferase UL97.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary pharmacological advantage of Valacyclovir over oral Acyclovir for treating Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV).
back:
• Valacyclovir is a prodrug with much higher oral bioavailability (54–70%)
• It achieves serum levels similar to intravenous acyclovir, which is necessary for less-susceptible VZV.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: The most common dose-limiting adverse effect associated with systemic Ganciclovir therapy is [___].
back:
• Myelosuppression (specifically neutropenia and thrombocytopenia)
• This effect is usually reversible upon drug discontinuation.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: An AIDS patient treated for ganciclovir-resistant CMV retinitis develops seizures and severe hypocalcemia. The most likely drug responsible for these electrolyte disturbances is [___].
back:
• Foscarnet
• It chelates divalent cations (Calcium, Magnesium) and is frequently associated with mineral imbalances and CNS toxicity.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain how Foscarnet carries out its biological function against viral DNA polymerase without requiring intracellular activation.
back:
• It is an inorganic pyrophosphate analog
• It binds directly to the pyrophosphate-binding site of DNA polymerase, blocking the cleavage of pyrophosphate from deoxynucleotide triphosphates.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast Cidofovir and Ganciclovir regarding their reliance on viral enzymes for intracellular activation.
back:
• Ganciclovir: Depends on the viral UL97 kinase for its first phosphorylation
• Cidofovir: Phosphorylated by host cell kinases independently of viral enzymes, bypassing viral resistance.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: State the primary clinical indication for Trifluridine and why its use is restricted to topical application.
back:
• Indication: HSV-1 and HSV-2 keratoconjunctivitis and keratitis
• Restriction: It is incorporated into host DNA as well as viral DNA, making it too toxic for systemic use.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Acyclovir is selectively activated only in virus-infected cells because the initial phosphorylation step requires the virus-specific enzyme [___].
back:
- Viral thymidine kinase
- It converts the drug to acyclovir monophosphate
- Host cell enzymes perform subsequent phosphorylations to the active triphosphate form.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: An HIV-positive patient being treated for Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis develops severe, dose-limiting neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. Identify the most likely causative agent.
back:
- Ganciclovir
- Myelosuppression is its primary dose-limiting toxicity
- This effect is typically reversible upon drug discontinuation.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain why Foscarnet maintains efficacy against thymidine kinase-deficient strains of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV).
back:
- It is an inorganic pyrophosphate analog
- It inhibits viral DNA polymerase directly
- It does not require activation/phosphorylation by viral or host kinases.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast Valacyclovir and Acyclovir regarding their oral bioavailability and pharmacological classification.
back:
- Valacyclovir is an L-valyl ester prodrug
- It has 3-5 times higher oral bioavailability than acyclovir
- It is rapidly converted to acyclovir via first-pass hepatic metabolism.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the pharmacological rationale for co-administering high-dose Probenecid with intravenous Cidofovir therapy.
back:
- Probenecid blocks active tubular secretion of cidofovir
- This prevents drug accumulation in the proximal renal tubules
- It significantly reduces the risk of dose-dependent nephrotoxicity.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: The topical pyrimidine nucleoside used for herpetic keratoconjunctivitis that is too toxic for systemic use due to incorporation into host DNA is [___].
back:
- Trifluridine
- It inhibits viral DNA synthesis but lacks selectivity for viral over host polymerase
- Systemic use is precluded by bone marrow toxicity.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A transplant recipient develops non-healing perianal ulcers. Cultures grow HSV-2 that is resistant to Acyclovir due to a thymidine kinase mutation. Specify the preferred systemic alternative.
back:
- Foscarnet
- It bypasses the need for viral kinase activation
- It directly targets the pyrophosphate binding site of DNA polymerase.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the specific biochemical role of the Cytomegalovirus UL97 gene product in relation to antiviral therapy.
back:
- UL97 encodes a viral phosphotransferase (kinase)
- It performs the essential first phosphorylation of ganciclovir
- Mutations in UL97 are the primary cause of ganciclovir resistance.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast Ganciclovir and Foscarnet regarding their primary cumulative toxicities during long-term CMV maintenance therapy.
back:
- Ganciclovir: Bone marrow suppression (leukopenia/anemia)
- Foscarnet: Nephrotoxicity and symptomatic electrolyte wasting (hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and seizures).

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary clinical intervention required to prevent Acyclovir-induced crystalline nephropathy during high-dose intravenous administration.
back:
- Vigorous intravenous hydration
- Maintains high urine flow rates
- Prevents drug precipitation and subsequent obstructive uropathy in the renal tubules.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: In the treatment of HSV and VZV, the initial phosphorylation of acyclovir to its monophosphate form is catalyzed by the virus-specified enzyme [___].
back:
* Viral thymidine kinase
* Selective activation occurs only in infected cells
* Host kinases perform subsequent phosphorylations to the active triphosphate.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: An AIDS patient treated for CMV retinitis develops a severe drop in absolute neutrophil count. The drug responsible most likely acts by inhibiting [___].
back:
* Viral DNA polymerase (Ganciclovir)
* Dose-limiting myelosuppression is its primary toxicity
* Toxicity is usually reversible upon drug discontinuation.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which acyclovir triphosphate causes cessation of viral DNA replication.
back:
* Competitive inhibition of viral DNA polymerase
* Incorporation into the viral DNA template
* Obligate chain termination due to lack of a 3' hydroxyl group.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast acyclovir and its prodrug valacyclovir regarding their oral bioavailability and metabolic conversion.
back:
* Acyclovir: Low bioavailability (15–20%); administered as active drug.
* Valacyclovir: High bioavailability (54–70%); converted to acyclovir via hepatic first-pass metabolism.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the unique mechanism of action of foscarnet that distinguishes it from nucleoside analog antivirals.
back:
* Inorganic pyrophosphate analog
* Binds directly to the pyrophosphate binding site of viral DNA polymerase
* Does not require intracellular phosphorylation for activity.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: The nucleotide analog [___] maintains activity against thymidine kinase-deficient HSV strains because its phosphorylation is independent of viral enzymes.
back:
* Cidofovir
* Relies entirely on host cell kinases for activation
* Primarily used for CMV retinitis and acyclovir-resistant HSV.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: A patient receiving intravenous foscarnet for resistant CMV develops perioral paresthesias and a positive Chvostek sign. Identify the electrolyte abnormality and its pathogenesis.
back:
* Hypocalcemia
* Pathogenesis: Foscarnet chelates divalent cations
* Risk is significantly increased by concomitant use of intravenous pentamidine.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the biochemical role of the CMV-specified protein kinase UL97 in the pharmacological activity of ganciclovir.
back:
* Catalyzes the initial, rate-limiting phosphorylation of ganciclovir
* Determines selective toxicity for CMV-infected cells
* Mutations in UL97 are the primary cause of ganciclovir resistance.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the primary dose-limiting toxicities of ganciclovir versus cidofovir.
back:
* Ganciclovir: Myelosuppression (neutropenia and thrombocytopenia).
* Cidofovir: Dose-dependent proximal tubular nephrotoxicity (requires aggressive pre-hydration and probenecid).

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary clinical indication for topical trifluridine and its major metabolic limitation for systemic use.
back:
* Indication: HSV keratoconjunctivitis and recurrent epithelial keratitis.
* Limitation: Incorporation into host DNA (lack of selectivity) causes severe systemic toxicity.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Acyclovir requires initial monophosphorylation by the virus-specified enzyme [___] before it can be further activated by host cell kinases.
back:
* Thymidine kinase (TK)
* Crucial for selective toxicity
* TK-deficient strains (most common mutants) are cross-resistant to Valacyclovir and Famciclovir

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: An AIDS patient treated for CMV retinitis presents with a significantly decreased absolute neutrophil count. Identify the most likely culprit drug and its primary adverse effect.
back:
* Ganciclovir
* Myelosuppression (Neutropenia)
* Reversible upon discontinuation; dose-limiting toxicity

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Explain the pharmacological mechanism that allows Cidofovir to remain effective against thymidine kinase-deficient Herpes Simplex Virus.
back:
* Nucleotide analog (contains phosphonate)
* Activation by host kinases is independent of viral thymidine kinase
* Competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast the therapeutic rationale for choosing Valacyclovir over Acyclovir in an outpatient with shingles (VZV), considering dosing frequency and systemic exposure.
back:
* Valacyclovir: Oral L-valyl ester prodrug; 54-70% bioavailability; tid dosing.
* Acyclovir: Low oral absorption (15-20%); requires 5x daily dosing for VZV efficacy.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the inorganic pyrophosphate analog used for CMV retinitis that inhibits DNA polymerase directly without requiring intracellular phosphorylation.
back:
* Foscarnet
* Directly blocks pyrophosphate binding site on polymerase
* Active against ganciclovir-resistant and acyclovir-resistant strains

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Docosanol, a non-nucleoside over-the-counter agent for orolabial herpes, works by inhibiting [___] between the viral envelope and the host cell membrane.
back:
* Fusion
* Prevents viral entry into host cells
* Only effective if applied within 12 hours of prodromal symptoms

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: An AIDS patient on Ganciclovir for CMV retinitis is also taking Zidovudine (AZT). Which hematological parameter must be monitored most closely due to this specific drug-drug interaction?
back:
* Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC)
* Both drugs are myelosuppressive
* Synergistic risk of life-threatening neutropenia

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Describe the specific intracellular step required to activate Ganciclovir against Cytomegalovirus (CMV) compared to its activation in HSV-infected cells.
back:
* CMV: Initial phosphorylation by protein kinase UL97
* HSV: Phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase
* Both require subsequent host cell kinases to triphosphate form

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Contrast Valganciclovir and Ganciclovir regarding their role in the long-term maintenance therapy of CMV retinitis.
back:
* Valganciclovir: Oral prodrug; high bioavailability; preferred for long-term maintenance.
* Ganciclovir: IV formulation used for acute induction; oral form is no longer available.

category: Describe drugs used in treatment of herpes simplex, varicella zoster, and cytomegalovirus virus infection with their pharmacological properties, mechanism of action and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary reason Trifluridine is restricted to topical ophthalmic use rather than systemic administration.
back:
* Non-selective toxicity
* Incorporates into host (human) DNA as well as viral DNA
* Systemic use causes severe host cell damage

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Acyclovir requires an initial phosphorylation step by the virus-specific enzyme [___] to be converted into its active monophosphate form.
back:
• Viral thymidine kinase (TK)
• This step ensures drug activation occurs only in infected cells
• Host cell enzymes then complete the triphosphorylation.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A patient being treated for herpes encephalitis with high-dose intravenous acyclovir develops an acute rise in serum creatinine. Identify the primary mechanism of this renal injury.
back:
• Crystalline nephropathy
• Caused by acyclovir precipitation in renal tubules
• Prevention requires adequate hydration and slow infusion rates.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Explain the dual mechanism by which acyclovir triphosphate halts viral DNA replication.
back:
• Competitive inhibition of viral DNA polymerase (competes with deoxyGTP)
• Chain termination following incorporation into the viral DNA strand.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the pharmacokinetic properties of valacyclovir and acyclovir regarding oral bioavailability.
back:
• Valacyclovir has 3–5 times higher bioavailability (54–70%)
• It is a prodrug rapidly converted to acyclovir via first-pass metabolism
• Achieves serum levels comparable to IV acyclovir.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Identify the most common genetic mutation that results in clinical resistance of Herpes Simplex Virus to acyclovir.
back:
• Deficiency or mutation in viral thymidine kinase (TK)
• Leads to cross-resistance with valacyclovir and famciclovir
• DNA polymerase mutations are a much less common cause.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Famciclovir is an oral prodrug that undergoes rapid deacetylation and oxidation to its active compound [___].
back:
• Penciclovir
• It is an acyclic guanosine analog
• It has a longer intracellular half-life than acyclovir.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: An AIDS patient receiving chronic high-dose valacyclovir (8g/day) presents with fever, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. This suggests the development of [___].
back:
• TTP/HUS (Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura/Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome)
• This is a rare, serious adverse effect specific to high-dose valacyclovir in immunosuppressed patients.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Distinguish the inhibitory action of penciclovir triphosphate on viral DNA from that of acyclovir triphosphate.
back:
• Penciclovir inhibits viral DNA polymerase but does NOT cause chain termination
• Acyclovir acts as a potent obligate chain terminator.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the requirement for viral enzymes in the activation of acyclovir compared to cidofovir.
back:
• Acyclovir: Requires viral thymidine kinase for the first phosphorylation
• Cidofovir: Phosphorylation is independent of viral enzymes (uses host kinases)
• Cidofovir remains active against TK-deficient strains.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: State the most common, non-serious adverse effects associated with oral administration of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir.
back:
• Nausea
• Diarrhea
• Headache
• Generally all three are well-tolerated in immunocompetent patients.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Acyclovir is selectively activated in infected cells because its initial phosphorylation to a monophosphate is catalyzed by the virus-specified enzyme [___].
back:
• Viral thymidine kinase (TK).
• This ensures the drug primarily accumulates in infected cells, sparing healthy host cells that lack the specific kinase.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A 45-year-old patient receiving high-dose intravenous acyclovir for HSV encephalitis develops a sudden rise in serum creatinine. This adverse effect is primarily caused by [___].
back:
• Crystalline nephropathy (obstructive renal failure).
• Caused by the precipitation of acyclovir crystals in the renal tubules.
• Prevention involves slow infusion and aggressive patient hydration.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Describe the two distinct ways acyclovir triphosphate blocks viral DNA synthesis after it is successfully activated by viral and host kinases.
back:
• Competitive inhibition: It competes with deoxyGTP for the viral DNA polymerase.
• Chain termination: Incorporation into the DNA template prevents further elongation because it lacks the necessary 3'-hydroxyl group.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
coreConcept: Mechanism difference between Acyclovir and Famciclovir
front: Contrast the molecular mechanism of action of penciclovir (derived from famciclovir) with acyclovir regarding its effect on the growing viral DNA chain.
back:
• Acyclovir: Acts as an obligate chain terminator upon incorporation.
• Penciclovir: Competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase but does NOT cause obligate chain termination.
• Intracellular Half-life: Penciclovir triphosphate remains active significantly longer (7–20 hours).

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Explain the pharmacodynamic advantage of using Valacyclovir over oral Acyclovir in the treatment of Herpes Zoster.
back:
• Bioavailability: Much higher (54–70%) compared to oral acyclovir (15–20%).
• Metabolism: L-valyl ester prodrug is rapidly converted to acyclovir, achieving serum levels equivalent to intravenous acyclovir administration.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Clinical resistance to acyclovir in HSV isolates is most commonly due to a deficiency in [___], which confers cross-resistance to both valacyclovir and famciclovir.
back:
• Viral thymidine kinase (TK) activity.
• TK-deficient strains cannot perform the rate-limiting first phosphorylation step.
• Often observed in immunocompromised patients (e.g., AIDS patients).

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A newborn is suspected of having neonatal HSV infection involving the central nervous system. Identify the preferred drug and the pharmacokinetic property that allows its efficacy here.
back:
• Drug: Intravenous Acyclovir.
• Pharmacokinetics: High tissue distribution; CSF concentrations reach 20–50% of plasma levels.
• Clinical: Requires high-dose therapy for 14–21 days to ensure neurodevelopmental protection.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: State the physiological basis for why acyclovir-resistant (thymidine kinase-deficient) strains usually remain susceptible to Foscarnet.
back:
• Foscarnet does not require activation by viral thymidine kinase or any phosphorylation steps.
• It directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase by blocking the pyrophosphate binding site.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the elimination half-lives of acyclovir and famciclovir in patients with normal renal function versus those with anuria.
back:
• Normal: Acyclovir half-life is ~2.5 hours; Famciclovir (penciclovir) is ~2 hours.
• Anuria: Acyclovir half-life increases to 20 hours.
• Clearance: Primarily renal for both, requiring significant dose reduction in kidney failure.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Identify the rare but life-threatening syndrome specifically associated with high-dose chronic valacyclovir (8g/day) therapy in AIDS patients.
back:
• Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP).
• Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS).
• Occurs at significantly higher doses than standard HSV/VZV suppression regimens.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: The high selectivity of acyclovir for herpesvirus-infected cells is primarily due to its initial phosphorylation step, which is catalyzed by the virus-specified enzyme [___].
back:
● Viral thymidine kinase
● This enzyme converts acyclovir to its monophosphate form
● Host cell kinases then complete the conversion to the active triphosphate metabolite

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A patient receiving high-dose intravenous acyclovir for HSV encephalitis develops a sudden rise in serum creatinine. This adverse effect is caused by [___].
back:
● Crystalline nephropathy
● Results from drug precipitation in the renal tubules
● Preventable by adequate hydration and slow infusion rates

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Explain the dual mechanism by which acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral DNA synthesis.
back:
● Competes with deoxyGTP for the viral DNA polymerase
● Acts as a chain terminator after being incorporated into the viral DNA template

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the oral bioavailability and metabolic activation of acyclovir and its prodrug valacyclovir.
back:
● Bioavailability: Acyclovir (15–20%) vs. Valacyclovir (54–70%)
● Activation: Valacyclovir is an L-valyl ester converted to acyclovir via first-pass hydrolysis in the liver and intestine

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Identify the primary molecular mechanism responsible for most clinical isolates showing resistance to acyclovir.
back:
● Deficiency or mutation of the viral thymidine kinase enzyme
● Leads to failure of the initial phosphorylation step required for drug activation

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Famciclovir is the diacetyl ester prodrug of the acyclic guanosine analog [___].
back:
● Penciclovir
● It is rapidly deacetylated and oxidized in the liver after oral administration

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A patient with advanced AIDS receiving high-dosage valacyclovir (8 g/d) for CMV prophylaxis develops microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. This suggests [___].
back:
● TTP/HUS (Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura/Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome)
● This rare but serious toxicity is specifically linked to high-dose valacyclovir in immunocompromised hosts

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Explain why penciclovir (the active form of famciclovir) differs from acyclovir in its effect on the viral DNA chain.
back:
● Penciclovir does not cause chain termination
● It inhibits DNA polymerase but allows continued elongation, albeit with lower affinity than acyclovir

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the standard therapeutic use of topical acyclovir cream versus oral acyclovir for recurrent genital herpes.
back:
● Topical: Substantially less effective; of no clinical benefit in recurrent disease
● Oral: Standard of care; reduces duration of symptoms and viral shedding

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Besides nausea and headache, identify two neurological adverse effects associated with high-dose intravenous acyclovir infusion.
back:
● Tremors and delirium
● Seizures may also occur in severe cases

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Acyclovir remains pharmacologically inactive until its first phosphorylation step is catalyzed by the virus-specified enzyme [___] in infected cells.
back:
● Thymidine Kinase (TK).
● Selective activation ensures the drug accumulates only in virus-infected cells.
● Subsequent phosphorylations are performed by host cell kinases.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A patient receiving high-dose intravenous acyclovir for herpes encephalitis develops rising serum creatinine and oliguria. This complication is primarily caused by [___].
back:
● Crystalline nephropathy (obstructive uropathy).
● Prevention includes adequate hydration and slow infusion rates.
● Characterized by drug precipitation in renal tubules.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Explain the role of Acyclovir triphosphate in inhibiting viral DNA synthesis once it is incorporated into the viral template.
back:
● Acts as a competitive inhibitor of viral DNA polymerase (competing with deoxyGTP).
● Functions as an obligate chain terminator, preventing further DNA strand elongation.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast Acyclovir and Valacyclovir regarding their oral bioavailability and metabolic relationship.
back:
● Acyclovir: Low oral bioavailability (15–20%).
● Valacyclovir: L-valyl ester prodrug with high bioavailability (54–70%).
● Valacyclovir is rapidly converted to acyclovir via first-pass hepatic hydrolysis.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Identify the active metabolite of Famciclovir and its specific pharmacodynamic effect on the viral DNA polymerase.
back:
● Active metabolite: Penciclovir.
● Effect: Competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase but, unlike acyclovir, does not cause immediate chain termination.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Acyclovir, Valacyclovir, and Famciclovir are all chemical analogs of the nucleoside [___].
back:
● Guanosine.
● They compete with natural deoxyguanosine triphosphate for incorporation by viral DNA polymerase.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: An AIDS patient receiving high-dose Valacyclovir (8g/day) presents with confusion, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. The clinician should immediately screen for which serious adverse syndrome?
back:
● Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura/Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (TTP/HUS).
● This specific toxicity is primarily associated with high-dose Valacyclovir in severely immunocompromised patients.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: How do HSV strains most commonly develop clinical resistance to Acyclovir therapy in immunocompromised hosts?
back:
● Deficiency or alteration in viral Thymidine Kinase (TK) activity.
● TK-deficient strains prevent the initial activation step required for drug efficacy.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the intracellular half-life and persistence of Penciclovir triphosphate with Acyclovir triphosphate.
back:
● Penciclovir triphosphate: Significantly longer intracellular half-life (7–20 hours).
● Acyclovir triphosphate: Shorter intracellular half-life (approximately 0.7–1 hour).

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Specify the primary physiological route of elimination for Acyclovir and the required clinical intervention in cases of uremia.
back:
● Route: Renal (glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion).
● Intervention: Dosage reduction based on calculated creatinine clearance.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: The initial and rate-limiting step in the pharmacological activation of acyclovir requires the specific viral enzyme [___].
back:
• Thymidine kinase (TK)
• Converts acyclovir to acyclovir monophosphate
• Ensures drug accumulation only in virus-infected cells

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A 40-year-old male with advanced AIDS receiving high-dosage valacyclovir (8g/day) develops confusion, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Identify the likely drug-associated syndrome.
back:
• Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura/hemolytic-uremic syndrome (TTP/HUS)
• Occurs primarily with high doses in immunocompromised hosts
• Necessitates immediate drug discontinuation

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Explain the dual mechanism by which acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral DNA synthesis.
back:
• Competitive inhibition: Competes with dGTP for viral DNA polymerase
• Chain termination: Acts as a substrate; incorporation stops DNA elongation (lacks 3' hydroxyl group)

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the molecular inhibitory actions of acyclovir versus penciclovir (the active metabolite of famciclovir) upon the viral DNA chain.
back:
• Acyclovir: Mandatory chain terminator (lacks 3' OH)
• Penciclovir: Competitive inhibitor of DNA polymerase; does NOT cause immediate chain termination

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Mention the primary pharmacokinetic advantage of valacyclovir over oral acyclovir.
back:
• Increased oral bioavailability (54–70% vs 15–20%)
• Rapidly converted to acyclovir via first-pass hepatic/intestinal esterases
• Achieves serum levels approximating IV acyclovir

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: To mitigate the risk of reversible crystalline nephropathy during high-dose intravenous acyclovir infusion, the patient must receive adequate [___].
back:
• Hydration (bolus fluid intake)
• Prevents drug precipitation in renal tubules
• Avoidance of rapid infusion rates is also required

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A transplant recipient develops a perianal ulcer. Viral isolate is an HSV strain deficient in thymidine kinase. Explain why acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir are all ineffective.
back:
• Cross-resistance occurs because all three require viral TK for initial phosphorylation
• TK-deficient mutants cannot activate the prodrugs
• Requires bypass agents (e.g., Foscarnet)

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Explain the role of 'suicide inactivation' in the pharmacodynamics of acyclovir.
back:
• Acyclovir triphosphate acts as a 'suicide substrate'
• Irreversibly binds the viral DNA polymerase-template complex after incorporation
• Permanently disables the enzyme molecule

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the dosing frequency and clinical utility of famciclovir versus acyclovir in the treatment of acute Herpes Zoster (Shingles).
back:
• Famciclovir: 500 mg tid; better patient compliance; faster reduction in post-herpetic neuralgia
• Acyclovir: 800 mg 5 times daily; shorter half-life; higher pill burden

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Identify the rare but serious neuropsychiatric adverse effects associated with acyclovir and valacyclovir.
back:
• Tremors, delirium, and seizures
• More common with intravenous administration or high doses
• Risk increased in patients with renal impairment

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Acyclovir's high selectivity for infected cells is maintained because its initial activation to a monophosphate derivative requires the virus-specified enzyme [___].
back:
• Thymidine kinase
• Host cell enzymes then perform subsequent phosphorylation steps
• Results in accumulation of the active drug only in HSV/VZV infected cells

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A patient with shingles receiving rapid intravenous infusion of high-dose acyclovir develops acute renal dysfunction. This is most likely caused by [___].
back:
• Crystalline nephropathy (obstructive uropathy)
• Avoided by ensuring adequate hydration and maintaining a slow infusion rate
• Reversible upon drug discontinuation and volume expansion

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Explain the dual inhibitory mechanisms by which acyclovir triphosphate halts viral replication.
back:
• Competitive inhibition: Competes with deoxyGTP for viral DNA polymerase
• Irreversible complex: Binds the DNA template-polymerase complex
• Chain termination: Incorporation into the DNA strand prevents further elongation

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the structural classification and prodrug nature of valacyclovir and famciclovir.
back:
• Valacyclovir: L-valyl ester prodrug of acyclovir; converted via first-pass hepatic/intestinal hydrolysis
• Famciclovir: Diacetyl ester prodrug of 6-deoxypenciclovir; converted to penciclovir
• Efficacy: Both provide higher bioavailability than oral acyclovir

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Identify the primary pharmacological advantage of prescribing valacyclovir over oral acyclovir for recurrent genital herpes.
back:
• Increased oral bioavailability (54–70% for valacyclovir vs. 15–20% for acyclovir)
• Results in serum levels approximating those achieved with intravenous acyclovir
• Allows for less frequent dosing intervals

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Resistance to the antiherpes class primarily develops through mutations in the viral gene encoding [___], which prevents drug phosphorylation.
back:
• Thymidine kinase (TK)
• TK-deficient strains are the most common clinical mutants
• Confers cross-resistance between acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A 30-year-old male with HIV on high-dose chronic valacyclovir therapy develops a syndrome characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. This represents [___].
back:
• Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)
• Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS)
• Typically associated with very high dosages (8 g/day) in immunocompromised patients

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Explain how the mechanism of penciclovir triphosphate (the active form of famciclovir) differs from that of acyclovir triphosphate during DNA synthesis.
back:
• Competitive inhibition: Penciclovir competes with deoxyGTP for viral DNA polymerase
• Non-terminator: Unlike acyclovir, penciclovir does NOT cause obligate chain termination
• Accumulation: Achieves higher intracellular concentrations with a longer half-life (7–20 hours)

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the utility of intravenous versus oral acyclovir formulations in clinical practice.
back:
• Intravenous: Preferred for herpes encephalitis, neonatal HSV, and severe VZV/HSV in immunocompromised patients
• Oral: Standard for genital herpes, orolabial herpes, and uncomplicated varicella or zoster

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: List the three central nervous system toxicities associated with high-dose intravenous acyclovir administration.
back:
• Tremors
• Delirium
• Seizures
• More common in patients with renal failure due to drug accumulation

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: The initial phosphorylation of acyclovir is selectively performed by the virus-specified enzyme [___], ensuring it accumulates primarily in cells infected with HSV or VZV.
back:
• Thymidine kinase (TK).
• Converts acyclovir to acyclovir monophosphate.
• Host cell enzymes perform subsequent di- and tri-phosphorylation.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A patient receiving high-dose IV acyclovir for herpes encephalitis develops an acute rise in serum creatinine. This nephrotoxicity is typically caused by [___].
back:
• Crystalline nephropathy.
• Occurs due to renal tubular precipitation of the drug.
• Prevented by adequate hydration and slow infusion rates.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Explain how acyclovir triphosphate specifically inhibits viral DNA synthesis once it is incorporated into the growing DNA strand.
back:
• Acts as a potent chain terminator.
• Lacks the 3' hydroxyl group required for further elongation.
• Competes with deoxyGTP for the viral DNA polymerase.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A patient with shingles prefers an oral regimen with less frequent dosing than the 5-times-daily acyclovir schedule. Contrast the pharmacokinetics of Valacyclovir that allow this change.
back:
• Valacyclovir is an L-valyl ester prodrug of acyclovir.
• It has much higher oral bioavailability (54–70% vs 15–20%).
• Serum levels are 3–5 times higher, approximating IV acyclovir levels.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Identify the most common mechanism of clinically significant resistance to acyclovir in immunocompromised patients.
back:
• Deficiency or alteration in viral thymidine kinase (TK).
• Less commonly, mutations in viral DNA polymerase.
• Results in cross-resistance to valacyclovir and famciclovir.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Famciclovir is a diacetyl ester prodrug that is rapidly converted by first-pass metabolism to its active form, [___].
back:
• Penciclovir.
• Acts as a competitive inhibitor of viral DNA polymerase.
• Reaches higher intracellular concentrations than acyclovir.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A 28-year-old with frequent genital herpes outbreaks is prescribed daily valacyclovir. Beyond reducing symptoms, what is the primary public health benefit of this suppressive therapy?
back:
• Decreases asymptomatic viral shedding.
• Lowers the rate of sexual transmission to partners.
• Reduces frequency and severity of symptomatic recurrences.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: How does the intracellular mechanism of penciclovir triphosphate differ fundamentally from acyclovir triphosphate regarding the viral DNA chain?
back:
• Acyclovir causes mandatory chain termination.
• Penciclovir inhibits viral DNA polymerase but does NOT cause chain termination.
• Both competitively inhibit dGTP binding.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the serious cumulative toxicities of high-dose valacyclovir (8g/d) in AIDS patients versus its use in transplant recipients.
back:
• AIDS: Risk of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura/hemolytic-uremic syndrome (TTP/HUS).
• Transplant: Risk of neurotoxicity (confusion, hallucinations, seizures).
• Gastrointestinal intolerance is common in both.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: What is the primary route of elimination for acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir?
back:
• Renal excretion.
• Occurs via both glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion.
• Dosage adjustment is mandatory in renal insufficiency.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
coreConcept: Selective Acyclovir Activation via Viral Enzymes
front: In the activation of acyclovir, the rate-limiting first step involving phosphorylation to acyclovir monophosphate is catalyzed by the virus-specified enzyme [___].
back:
Viral Thymidine Kinase (TK).
• Ensures drug activation occurs only in infected cells.
• Host cell kinases perform the subsequent phosphorylations to the active triphosphate form.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A 28-year-old male with HSV encephalitis receives high-dose intravenous acyclovir. Three days later, his serum creatinine rises significantly. The most likely mechanism for this renal injury is [___].
back:
Crystalline Nephropathy.
• Occurs due to drug precipitation in the renal tubules.
• Risk is minimized by adequate hydration and avoiding rapid infusion rates.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism by which acyclovir triphosphate halts viral replication once it is incorporated into the DNA template.
back:
DNA Chain Termination.
• Competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase.
• Lacks the 3' hydroxyl group necessary for further nucleotide attachment, preventing DNA strand elongation.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast Acyclovir and Valacyclovir regarding their pharmacokinetic profile and clinical utility in treating Herpes Zoster (shingles).
back:
Bioavailability Contrast:
• Valacyclovir is a prodrug with 3-5 times higher oral bioavailability than acyclovir.
• It achieves plasma levels comparable to IV acyclovir, allowing for simpler dosing in VZV infections.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Why do thymidine kinase-deficient HSV strains remain susceptible to Cidofovir or Foscarnet despite showing resistance to acyclovir and famciclovir?
back:
Activation Independence:
• Acyclovir and Famciclovir require viral TK for initial phosphorylation.
• Cidofovir and Foscarnet do not require viral TK for activation or binding to the polymerase.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: The oral prodrug of penciclovir, which is used for the treatment of herpes zoster and recurrent genital herpes, is [___].
back:
Famciclovir.
• Rapidly converted to penciclovir via first-pass metabolism.
• Highly effective against VZV due to higher intracellular concentrations and prolonged half-life.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A patient taking high-dose valacyclovir (8g/day) for CMV prophylaxis develops confusion, hallucinations, and abdominal pain. This presentation most likely indicates [___].
back:
CNS Toxicity / Neurotoxicity.
• Manifests at high doses or in patients with renal impairment.
• May also be associated with Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) in AIDS patients at this dosage.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Describe how penciclovir (from famciclovir) differs from acyclovir in its effect on the growing viral DNA chain.
back:
Non-Chain Termination:
