• Penciclovir triphosphate inhibits viral DNA polymerase competitively.
• Unlike acyclovir, it does not cause immediate chain termination upon incorporation.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the CNS adverse effects of acyclovir with its renal adverse effects regarding their clinical presentation.
back:
Toxicity Presentation:
• CNS: Manifests as tremors, delirium, or seizures, usually with high serum levels.
• Renal: Manifests as crystalline nephropathy and rising creatinine; associated with dehydration.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Identify the specific biochemical component of valacyclovir that is cleaved by intestinal and hepatic esterases to produce active acyclovir.
back:
L-valyl ester.
• This esterification improves intestinal absorption via peptide transporters.
• First-pass hydrolysis ensures rapid conversion to the parent acyclovir molecule.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: The selective activation of acyclovir within an infected host cell requires initial phosphorylation by the virus-specified enzyme [___].
back:
• Thymidine kinase (TK).
• It converts acyclovir into its monophosphate form.
• This ensures drug accumulation occurs strictly within virus-infected cells, protecting healthy host cells.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A 30-year-old male receiving rapid intravenous acyclovir for HSV encephalitis develops an acute rise in serum creatinine. Explain the likely pathophysiology.
back:
• Crystalline nephropathy.
• Acyclovir precipitates in the renal tubules when given rapidly or without adequate hydration.
• It is usually reversible with fluids and slowing the infusion rate.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Explain the dual mechanism by which acyclovir triphosphate halts viral DNA synthesis.
back:
• Competitive inhibition: It competes with deoxyGTP for the viral DNA polymerase.
• Chain termination: Once incorporated into the DNA template, it stops elongation because it lacks a 3'-hydroxyl group.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A patient with acyclovir-resistant HSV (thymidine kinase-deficient) requires therapy. Contrast the utility of Valacyclovir versus Foscarnet in this specific case.
back:
• Valacyclovir: Ineffective; it is an acyclovir prodrug still requiring viral thymidine kinase for activation.
• Foscarnet: Effective; it inhibits DNA polymerase directly without requiring phosphorylation by viral enzymes.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Describe the primary pharmacokinetic advantage of Valacyclovir over oral Acyclovir.
back:
• Enhanced Bioavailability: Oral bioavailability is 54–70% for valacyclovir compared to only 15–20% for acyclovir.
• Result: It achieves serum levels nearly equivalent to intravenous acyclovir with less frequent dosing.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Unlike acyclovir, the active metabolite of famciclovir, known as [___], inhibits viral DNA polymerase without causing immediate chain termination.
back:
• Penciclovir triphosphate.
• It has a longer intracellular half-life (7–20 hours) compared to acyclovir.
• It reaches much higher intracellular concentrations within the infected cell.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: An HIV-positive patient on high-dose Valacyclovir (8 g/day) presents with schistocytes on peripheral smear and renal failure. Identify the specific adverse syndrome.
back:
• Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura / Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (TTP/HUS).
• This is a rare, severe side effect seen specifically with high-dosage chronic therapy in immunocompromised hosts.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Detail the metabolic transformation steps required to convert oral Famciclovir into its pharmacologically active form.
back:
• Deacetylation/Oxidation: Rapid first-pass metabolism in liver and intestine to penciclovir.
• Viral Activation: Phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase to monophosphate.
• Host Activation: Converted to active triphosphate by cellular kinases.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the susceptibility and dosing requirements of Acyclovir for Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) versus Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV).
back:
• Potency: Acyclovir is ~10 times more potent against HSV than VZV.
• Dosing: Standard HSV doses are lower (e.g., 400mg); VZV requires significantly higher doses (e.g., 800mg) for efficacy.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: List the two most common categories of central nervous system (CNS) toxicity associated with high-dose intravenous Acyclovir.
back:
• Neuropsychiatric: Tremors, delirium, and hallucinations.
• Severe events: Seizures.
• Risk factors: Advanced age and underlying renal insufficiency.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Antiretroviral drugs such as Zidovudine and Lamivudine belong to the [___] class, acting via competitive inhibition of HIV reverse transcriptase to cause premature chain termination.
back: Nucleoside/nucleotide Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs).

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A 45-year-old HIV-positive male is considered for Maraviroc therapy. Before initiating this agent, a specific laboratory test must be performed to confirm [___].
back:
• Viral tropism.
• Specifically, infection must be exclusively CCR5-tropic.
• Maraviroc is ineffective against CXCR4 or mixed-tropic HIV.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Explain how Protease Inhibitors (PIs) carry out their biological function to prevent the maturation of HIV.
back:
• Inhibit the HIV protease enzyme.
• Prevent cleavage of the Gag-Pol polyprotein precursor.
• Block processing of proteins into functional forms.
• Result in immature, noninfectious virions.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) and Non-nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs) regarding their binding sites and requirement for intracellular activation.
back:
• NRTIs: Bind the enzyme active site; require intracellular phosphorylation (activation).
• NNRTIs: Bind allosteric sites (near active site); do not require phosphorylation.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Describe the primary pharmacological rationale for using low-dose Ritonavir in combination with other Protease Inhibitors (PIs).
back:
• Acts as a pharmacokinetic 'booster.'
• Potently inhibits CYP3A4-mediated metabolism.
• Increases PI half-life and plasma exposure.
• Allows for lower/less frequent dosing.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Antiretrovirals such as Raltegravir and Dolutegravir target the viral enzyme [___], which is essential for the third step of provirus integration into the host genome.
back: Integrase (specifically Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors).

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A patient starting a regimen containing Abacavir is closely monitored for fever, rash, and respiratory symptoms. Screening for which specific genetic marker is mandatory to prevent this syndrome?
back:
• HLA-B*5701 allele.
• Marker for high risk of Abacavir hypersensitivity reaction.
• Positive test contraindicates the use of Abacavir.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Explain the role of the viral glycoprotein gp41 in the mechanism of action of the fusion inhibitor Enfuvirtide.
back:
• Enfuvirtide binds to the gp41 subunit.
• Blocks conformational changes required for membrane fusion.
• Prevents viral entry into the host cell cytoplasm.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF) with Tenofovir Alafenamide (TAF) regarding systemic toxicity profiles.
back:
• TDF: Associated with proximal renal tubulopathy (Fanconi syndrome) and bone density loss.
• TAF: Lower plasma levels with higher intracellular delivery; significantly reduced renal and bone toxicity.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Identify the primary black-box toxicity associated with the entire class of Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) resulting from mitochondrial damage.
back:
• Lactic acidosis.
• Hepatic steatosis.
• Most common with older agents like Stavudine or Zidovudine.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: The NRTI agent [___] is unique among nucleosides because it requires screening for the HLA-B*5701 allele prior to initiation to prevent a potentially fatal multi-organ hypersensitivity reaction.
back:
• Abacavir
• Guanosine analog
• Prevents multi-organ hypersensitivity syndrome
• Screening identifies patients at 100% negative predictive risk

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A 32-year-old HIV-positive patient recently started on a new regimen presents with vivid dreams, nightmares, and dizziness. Identify the specific agent and its drug class responsible for these neuropsychiatric symptoms.
back:
• Agent: Efavirenz
• Class: NNRTI
• Side effects typically resolve within 4–6 weeks
• Should be taken on an empty stomach at bedtime

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Explain the role of HIV integrase and how agents like Raltegravir or Dolutegravir interrupt the viral replication cycle.
back:
• Integrase inserts reverse-transcribed HIV DNA into host chromosomes
• INSTIs bind to the integrase enzyme
• Blocks the specific 'strand transfer' step
• Prevents viral genome integration into host DNA

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast the requirement for intracellular activation between Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) and Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs).
back:
• NRTIs: Require intracellular phosphorylation by cellular kinases to active triphosphate forms.
• NNRTIs: Do not require intracellular activation or phosphorylation to inhibit reverse transcriptase.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Identify the primary pharmacological rationale for including low-dose Ritonavir in a Protease Inhibitor-based regimen.
back:
• Acts as a pharmacokinetic 'booster'
• Potently inhibits the CYP3A4 enzyme
• Increases plasma concentrations and half-life of primary PIs
• Allows for lower doses and reduced pill burden

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: The entry inhibitor [___] acts as a CCR5 co-receptor antagonist, but requires a tropism assay to ensure the patient's HIV strain does not use the CXCR4 receptor.
back:
• Maraviroc
• Binds host CCR5 protein on CD4 cells
• Prevents viral gp120 binding and entry
• Ineffective against CXCR4-tropic or mixed-tropic virus

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A patient on HIV therapy for five years presents with central obesity, 'buffalo hump' fat accumulation, and thinning of the limbs. Which drug class is most classically associated with this metabolic syndrome?
back:
• Protease Inhibitors (PIs)
• Syndrome: Lipodystrophy (fat redistribution)
• Often associated with hyperglycemia and insulin resistance
• Dyslipidemia is a common metabolic consequence

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Describe how the inhibition of the HIV protease enzyme specifically leads to the production of non-infectious viral particles.
back:
• Protease cleaves the Gag-Pol polyprotein precursor
• Cleavage is required for maturation into structural proteins
• Inhibition results in immature, budding particles
• Prevents formation of the infectious virion core

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast the mechanisms of renal injury associated with Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF) and Indinavir.
back:
• TDF: Causes proximal renal tubulopathy (Fanconi's Syndrome) and acute/chronic renal failure.
• Indinavir: Causes nephrolithiasis (kidney stones) due to drug crystallization in acidic urine.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Name the specific thymidine analog NRTI that is the drug of choice for reducing the risk of vertical transmission of HIV during pregnancy and labor.
back:
• Zidovudine (AZT)
• Prevents perinatal and transplacental transmission
• Administered during pregnancy, labor, and to the neonate
• Major dose-limiting toxicity is macrocytic anemia

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: The mechanism of action of echinocandins, such as caspofungin, involves the non-competitive inhibition of the enzyme [___], which is essential for fungal cell wall synthesis.
back:
• 1,3-beta-glucan synthase.
• Disrupts the structural integrity of the fungal cell wall.
• Leads to osmotic instability and cell death.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
coreConcept: Voriconazole Clinical Use and Drug Interactions
front: A 45-year-old transplant recipient on cyclosporine requires treatment for invasive aspergillosis. Why is Voriconazole preferred over Amphotericin B, and what pharmacokinetic interaction must be monitored?
back:
• Preferred for superior efficacy and reduced toxicity in aspergillosis.
• Interaction: Voriconazole inhibits CYP3A4.
• Result: Significantly increases cyclosporine levels, requiring dose reduction and monitoring.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain how Flucytosine selectively targets fungal cells while minimizing toxicity to human host cells.
back:
• Fungi use cytosine permease for drug uptake.
• Fungal cytosine deaminase converts Flucytosine to toxic 5-fluorouracil.
• Human cells lack cytosine deaminase, avoiding this toxic conversion.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the renal toxicity profiles of conventional Amphotericin B deoxycholate with its liposomal formulations like AmBisome.
back:
• Conventional: Causes reversible (decreased perfusion) and irreversible (tubular injury) azotemia.
• Liposomal: Lipid vehicles serve as reservoirs to reduce nonspecific binding to human renal membranes.
• Result: Significantly lower nephrotoxicity with liposomal forms.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the specific biochemical step inhibited by Terbinafine and the resulting intracellular consequence for the fungal cell.
back:
• Step: Inhibition of squalene epoxidase.
• Consequence: Prevents ergosterol synthesis.
• Leads to accumulation of toxic squalene and membrane disruption.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: To minimize the risk of 'shake and bake' infusion-related reactions during Amphotericin B administration, patients are often pre-medicated with [___].
back:
• Antipyretics (Acetaminophen).
• Antihistamines or Corticosteroids.
• Meperidine (specifically to abort rigors).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: An HIV-positive patient with Cryptococcal meningitis is treated with Amphotericin B and Flucytosine. What is the pharmacological rationale for this combination?
back:
• Rationale: Synergistic interaction.
• Amphotericin B forms pores in the membrane.
• This facilitates enhanced Flucytosine entry to inhibit DNA/RNA synthesis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Describe the primary molecular mechanisms by which Candida species develop clinical resistance to azole antifungals.
back:
• Mutations in the ERG11 gene (14-alpha-demethylase target).
• Increased expression of MDR or CDR efflux pumps.
• Alterations in ergosterol biosynthetic pathways to bypass inhibition.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast Fluconazole and Itraconazole regarding their penetration into the Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) and primary clinical indications.
back:
• Fluconazole: High CSF penetration (>70%); drug of choice for Cryptococcal meningitis.
• Itraconazole: Poor CSF penetration; used for dimorphic fungi like Histoplasma and Blastomyces.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the specific antifungal agent most associated with transient visual disturbances, such as altered color perception or blurring, immediately following dosing.
back:
• Voriconazole.
• Occurs in approximately 30% of patients.
• Symptoms are typically dose-related and resolve within 30 minutes.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: The class of antiretrovirals that acts by binding directly to the HIV-1 reverse transcriptase enzyme to cause allosteric inhibition is [___].
back:
Nonnucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs).
• Examples: Efavirenz, Nevirapine.
• Do not require intracellular phosphorylation.
• Bind to a site distinct from the active site.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A patient on long-term HIV therapy develops central obesity, a 'buffalo hump,' and insulin resistance. These metabolic and morphologic derangements are most characteristic of the [___] class.
back:
Protease Inhibitors (PIs).
• Part of the lipodystrophy syndrome.
• Includes hyperglycemia and hyperlipidemia.
• Atazanavir is less likely to cause these effects than other PIs.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Explain the difference in the requirement for intracellular activation between NRTIs and NNRTIs.
back:
• NRTIs: Prodrugs requiring host cell kinases for triple phosphorylation to active triphosphate forms.
• NNRTIs: Direct inhibitors that require no intracellular activation or phosphorylation to be active.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast the viral targets of Enfuvirtide and Maraviroc in preventing HIV entry into the host cell.
back:
• Enfuvirtide: Binds to the gp41 subunit of the viral envelope to block membrane fusion.
• Maraviroc: Binds host cell CCR5 co-receptor to block viral attachment.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Identify the primary pharmacological interaction common to all Protease Inhibitors (PIs) regarding hepatic metabolism.
back:
All PIs are substrates for and inhibitors of the CYP3A4 enzyme system.
• Leads to numerous drug-drug interactions.
• Ritonavir is the most potent inhibitor in this class.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: The pharmacological practice of using a low dose of [___] to inhibit CYP3A4 and increase the plasma exposure of another Protease Inhibitor is known as 'boosting.'
back:
Ritonavir.
• Functions as a pharmacokinetic enhancer.
• Decreases pill burden and increases the genetic barrier to resistance.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A clinician screens a patient for the HLA-B*5701 allele before initiating therapy. Identify the specific NRTI being prescribed and the purpose of this test.
back:
Abacavir.
• Screening prevents a potentially fatal systemic hypersensitivity reaction.
• Symptoms include fever, rash, and multi-organ involvement.
• Positive test contraindicates its use.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Detail the mechanism by which Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors (INSTIs) like Raltegravir halt HIV replication.
back:
They bind to viral integrase.
• Specifically inhibit 'strand transfer.'
• Prevents integration of reverse-transcribed viral DNA into the host cell chromosome.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF) with Tenofovir Alafenamide (TAF) regarding systemic exposure and toxicity.
back:
• TDF: Higher plasma levels; associated with renal tubulopathy (Fanconi's) and decreased bone mineral density.
• TAF: 90% lower plasma levels; more efficient intracellular delivery with reduced renal/bone toxicity.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Identify the serious metabolic side effect that constitutes a 'class warning' for all Nucleoside/Nucleotide Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs).
back:
Lactic acidosis with hepatic steatosis.
• Result of mitochondrial toxicity via DNA polymerase-gamma inhibition.
• Most common with older agents like Stavudine and Zidovudine.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Unlike nonnucleoside analogs (NNRTIs), nucleoside and nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) require intracellular activation via [___] by cellular enzymes to the triphosphate form to be active.
back: ● Phosphorylation. ● Acts by competitive inhibition of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase. ● Incorporation into the growing viral DNA chain causes premature chain termination.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A patient starting a new antiretroviral regimen is screened for the HLA-B*5701 allele to prevent a potentially fatal hypersensitivity reaction characterized by fever, rash, and respiratory symptoms. Identify the drug.
back: ● Abacavir. ● Screening identifying patients at high risk for hypersensitivity is mandatory. ● Rechallenge is strictly contraindicated after a reaction. ● Class: Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor (NRTI).

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Explain the primary difference between the binding sites and activation requirements of NNRTIs compared to NRTIs.
back: ● Binding: NNRTIs bind allosterically near the reverse transcriptase active site; NRTIs compete at the catalytic site. ● Activation: NNRTIs do not require phosphorylation; NRTIs must be triphosphorylated by host cell kinases.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast the systemic exposure and toxicity profiles of Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF) with the newer formulation Tenofovir Alafenamide (TAF).
back: ● TAF maintains 90% lower plasma levels than TDF, concentrating more in lymphoid cells. ● TAF is associated with significantly less renal impairment and less reduction in bone mineral density.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Identify the antiretroviral class that prevents the processing of viral polyproteins into functional conformations, resulting in the production of immature, noninfectious virions.
back: ● Protease Inhibitors (PIs). ● Inhibit the proteolytic cleavage of Gag-Pol polyproteins. ● Examples include Atazanavir, Darunavir, and Lopinavir. ● Often associated with metabolic side effects like dyslipidemia.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: In modern antiretroviral therapy, low-dose Ritonavir is frequently used as a pharmacokinetic booster because it is a potent inhibitor of the [___] enzyme system.
back: ● CYP3A4 (Cytochrome P450 3A4). ● Increases systemic exposure and half-life of co-administered protease inhibitors. ● Allows for reduced dosing frequency and improves efficacy against resistant virus strains.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A physician orders a coreceptor tropism assay for an HIV patient before starting a specific entry inhibitor. If the virus uses the CXCR4 receptor, this drug will be ineffective. Name the drug.
back: ● Maraviroc. ● Class: CCR5 co-receptor antagonist. ● Specifically blocks gp120 binding to the CCR5 host protein on CD4+ cells. ● Ineffective against CXCR4-tropic or mixed-tropic HIV strains.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Explain how Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors (INSTIs) like Raltegravir or Dolutegravir interfere with the biological replication of the HIV provirus.
back: ● Bind to viral integrase enzymes. ● Specifically inhibit the strand transfer step. ● Blocks the integration of reverse-transcribed viral DNA into the host cell genome.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast the specific stages of the HIV entry process targeted by Enfuvirtide versus Maraviroc.
back: ● Enfuvirtide: Binds to the gp41 subunit to block the fusion of viral and host membranes. ● Maraviroc: Binds to the host CCR5 receptor to block initial viral attachment and entry.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Identify the antiretroviral nucleotide analog that is uniquely licensed for the treatment of both HIV-1 and chronic Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) infection.
back: ● Tenofovir (available as TDF or TAF). ● Potently inhibits both HIV reverse transcriptase and HBV DNA polymerase. ● Mainstay of treatment for patients co-infected with both viruses.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: To be converted to its active monophosphate form, acyclovir requires initial phosphorylation by the virus-specified enzyme [___].
back:
* **Viral thymidine kinase (TK)**
* Ensures acyclovir is selectively activated and accumulated only in cells infected by the virus.
* Host cell kinases perform the subsequent two phosphorylations to the active triphosphate.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: A patient receiving high-dose intravenous acyclovir for herpes encephalitis develops a sudden rise in serum creatinine. To prevent this "crystalline nephropathy," the clinician should ensure [___].
back:
* **Adequate hydration** and avoidance of rapid infusion.
* This prevents crystalline nephropathy caused by drug precipitation in renal tubules.
* Reversible upon drug cessation but can be fatal if ignored.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Explain the two specific biochemical mechanisms by which acyclovir triphosphate halts viral DNA synthesis.
back:
* **Competitive inhibition:** Triphosphate form competes with deoxyGTP for the viral DNA polymerase.
* **Chain termination:** Incorporation into the viral DNA template acts as an irreversible complex, stopping strand elongation.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the mechanism of action of penciclovir (derived from famciclovir) with that of acyclovir regarding DNA strand elongation.
back:
* **Acyclovir:** Causes obligate chain termination once incorporated into the DNA strand.
* **Penciclovir:** Competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase but lacks the obligate chain-terminating property.
* Both require viral thymidine kinase for activation.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: State the primary pharmacokinetic advantage that makes valacyclovir the preferred oral choice for treating Zoster (shingles) over oral acyclovir.
back:
* **Superior oral bioavailability** (approx. 54–70% compared to 15–20% for acyclovir).
* It is an L-valyl ester prodrug that undergoes rapid first-pass metabolism to achieve serum levels comparable to IV acyclovir.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Most clinical isolates of HSV that are resistant to acyclovir are cross-resistant to valacyclovir and famciclovir due to a deficiency in [___].
back:
* **Viral thymidine kinase (TK) activity**
* TK-deficient mutants cannot perform the initial phosphorylation step.
* This confers cross-resistance to other TK-dependent analogs; foscarnet bypasses this enzyme entirely.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: An AIDS patient treated with high-dose chronic valacyclovir (8 g/d) presents with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. Identify the most likely drug-induced complication.
back:
* **Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)** or **Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS)**.
* This rare but serious complication occurs primarily in AIDS patients receiving chronically high doses (e.g., 8 g/day).
* Requires immediate drug discontinuation.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Describe the stepwise phosphorylation sequence required for acyclovir to reach its pharmacologically active state.
back:
* **First phosphorylation:** Performed by viral thymidine kinase (the rate-limiting step).
* **Subsequent steps:** Two phosphorylations by host cell enzymes convert the monophosphate into the active, triphosphorylated form required for efficacy.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Contrast the primary clinical indications for the administration of intravenous versus oral acyclovir.
back:
* **Intravenous:** Indicated for herpes encephalitis, neonatal HSV, and severe/disseminated HSV or VZV in immunocompromised patients.
* **Oral:** Standard for uncomplicated primary or recurrent genital herpes, orolabial herpes, and varicella.

category: Explain the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics and adverse effects of acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir
front: Identify the virus against which acyclovir is approximately 10 times more potent than it is against Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV).
back:
* **Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1 and HSV-2)**
* Because VZV is less susceptible, it clinically requires significantly higher dosages for treatment compared to standard genital herpes management.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) act by [___] inhibition of the HIV-1 reverse transcriptase enzyme.
back:
• Competitive inhibition of the enzyme
• Acts as a substrate for incorporation into viral DNA
• Causes premature DNA chain termination
• Requires intracellular phosphorylation for activation

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A patient scheduled to begin an antiretroviral regimen is screened for the HLA-B*5701 allele. This diagnostic precaution is taken to prevent a systemic hypersensitivity reaction to [___].
back:
• Abacavir
• Characterized by fever, rash, and GI distress
• Fatal on re-challenge
• Reaction usually occurs within first 6 weeks

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Explain the role of the HIV protease enzyme and how Protease Inhibitors (PIs) interfere with the production of infectious virions.
back:
• HIV protease cleaves Gag-Pol polyproteins
• PIs prevent cleavage into functional proteins
• Results in production of immature, noninfectious particles
• Acts at the budding and maturation stage

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF) with Tenofovir Alafenamide (TAF) regarding plasma drug levels and specific organ toxicities.
back:
• TAF has 90% lower plasma levels than TDF
• TAF reaches higher concentrations in lymphoid cells
• TAF has significantly reduced renal toxicity
• TAF causes less bone mineral density loss

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Identify the mandatory pre-treatment assessment required before prescribing the entry inhibitor Maraviroc.
back:
• Co-receptor tropism assay
• Determines if virus is CCR5-tropic
• Maraviroc is ineffective against CXCR4 or mixed-tropic strains
• Targets the host CCR5 receptor

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Unlike NRTIs, Nonnucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs) bind to a(n) [___] site on the reverse transcriptase, requiring no intracellular phosphorylation.
back:
• Allosteric binding site
• Near but distinct from the NRTI site
• Results in non-competitive inhibition
• Highly susceptible to rapid single-mutation resistance

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A patient with advanced HIV is prescribed a combination of Lopinavir and low-dose Ritonavir. Identify the primary pharmacological purpose of the Ritonavir in this regimen.
back:
• Pharmacokinetic 'booster'
• Potent inhibitor of CYP3A4
• Increases systemic exposure and half-life of Lopinavir
• Allows for lower doses and reduced pill burden

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Describe how the 36-amino-acid peptide Enfuvirtide prevents the HIV virion from entering the host CD4+ T cell.
back:
• Binds to the gp41 subunit of the viral envelope
• Prevents conformational changes required for membrane fusion
• Administered only via subcutaneous injection
• Lacks cross-resistance with other antiretroviral classes

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast Emtricitabine and Lamivudine regarding their spectrum of activity beyond HIV-1 and their primary resistance profile.
back:
• Both are active against HBV
• Both select for the M184V resistance mutation
• Emtricitabine has a longer half-life (once-daily dosing)
• Both are generally well-tolerated cytosine analogs

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Name the specific viral replication step inhibited by agents such as Raltegravir and Dolutegravir.
back:
• Strand transfer (Integration)
• Prevents integration of viral DNA into host chromosomes
• Targets the HIV Integrase enzyme
• Blocks the third step of provirus integration

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: The [___] class of antiretrovirals, which includes Zidovudine and Lamivudine, acts by competitive inhibition of reverse transcriptase and requires intracellular phosphorylation to be active.
back:
Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs).

*   Competitively inhibit HIV reverse transcriptase.
*   Cause premature DNA chain termination.
*   Require host cell kinases for activation.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A 28-year-old HIV patient is tested for the HLA-B*5701 allele before starting a new regimen to avoid a life-threatening hypersensitivity reaction. This screening is mandatory for the drug [___].
back:
Abacavir.

*   Belongs to the NRTI class.
*   Screening identifies risk for severe hypersensitivity.
*   Rechallenge is strictly contraindicated after a reaction.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Explain the role of the HIV protease enzyme and how Protease Inhibitors (PIs) like Darunavir interfere with this process.
back:
Protease cleaves Gag-Pol polyproteins into functional structural proteins.

*   PIs block this cleavage step.
*   Results in immature, noninfectious virion production.
*   Does not require intracellular activation.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast the binding sites of Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) and Nonnucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs) on the reverse transcriptase enzyme.
back:
NRTIs bind to the catalytic site (competitive inhibition).

*   NNRTIs bind to a distinct allosteric site (noncompetitive inhibition).
*   NNRTIs do not require phosphorylation or compete with nucleotides.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Identify the primary mechanism of action for Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors (INSTIs) such as Raltegravir and Dolutegravir.
back:
They inhibit the strand transfer step of viral integration.

*   Prevent HIV DNA from incorporating into host chromosomes.
*   Target the viral integrase enzyme specifically.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: The [___] antiretroviral class is most notorious for causing metabolic side effects including lipodystrophy, hyperglycemia, and insulin resistance.
back:
Protease Inhibitors (PIs).

*   Associated with 'buffalo hump' and central obesity.
*   Commonly cause hyperlipidemia.
*   Atazanavir has the lowest risk among PIs.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A patient with HIV is prescribed Maraviroc. For this drug to be effective, the patient's viral population must exclusively demonstrate [___] tropism.
back:
CCR5 co-receptor tropism.

*   Maraviroc is a CCR5 co-receptor antagonist.
*   Prevents viral entry into CD4+ cells.
*   Ineffective against CXCR4-tropic or mixed-tropic strains.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Describe the physiological rationale for including low-dose Ritonavir in combination with other Protease Inhibitors (e.g., Lopinavir).
back:
Pharmacokinetic 'boosting'.

*   Ritonavir inhibits CYP3A4 enzymes.
*   Increases plasma concentrations of the companion PI.
*   Allows for lower doses and reduced pill burden.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast the delivery methods and targets of the fusion inhibitor Enfuvirtide and the CCR5 antagonist Maraviroc.
back:
Enfuvirtide: Subcutaneous injection; targets viral gp41.

*   Maraviroc: Oral administration; targets host CCR5 receptor.
*   Both prevent viral entry but at different fusion/attachment steps.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Which specific NRTI is uniquely classified as a nucleotide analog, requiring only two intracellular phosphorylations instead of three?
back:
Tenofovir (TDF or TAF).

*   It is an acyclic nucleoside phosphonate.
*   Activated to the active diphosphate form.
*   Maintains activity against many HBV strains.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Unlike other agents in its class that require three separate phosphorylation steps, [___] is classified as a nucleotide analog (NtRTI) because it is administered as a monophosphate and requires only two host phosphorylations.
back:
* Tenofovir (Disoproxil or Alafenamide)
* Bypasses the initial viral-mediated phosphorylation step
* Acts as a potent DNA chain terminator
* Potent activity against both HIV and HBV

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: An HIV patient started on a guanosine analog NRTI develops a multisystem hypersensitivity reaction including fever and rash. This reaction is a genetically linked classification risk associated with the [___] allele.
back:
* Abacavir
* HLA-B*5701 allele
* Mandatory screening required before initiation
* Re-challenge is strictly contraindicated due to risk of fatal anaphylaxis

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Explain the essential laboratory classification step required before a patient can be prescribed the CCR5 antagonist Maraviroc.
back:
* Co-receptor tropism assay (e.g., Trofile assay)
* Maraviroc only works against CCR5-tropic HIV
* Ineffective against CXCR4-tropic or mixed-tropic (dual-tropic) virus
* Prevents gp120 binding to the CCR5 host receptor

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast the genetic barrier to resistance between first-generation NNRTIs (e.g., Nevirapine) and second-generation NNRTIs (e.g., Etravirine).
back:
* 1st Generation: Low genetic barrier; single mutation (K103N) causes class-wide resistance
* 2nd Generation: High genetic barrier; effective against many 1st-gen resistant strains
* 2nd Gen: Requires multiple cumulative mutations for significant loss of efficacy

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Name the two pharmacological agents classified as 'boosters' used to increase the systemic exposure of Protease Inhibitors (PIs) and their primary target.
back:
* Ritonavir and Cobicistat
* Target: Cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) inhibition
* Cobicistat: No intrinsic antiviral activity
* Ritonavir: Potent antiviral PI and potent CYP inhibitor

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Agents like Raltegravir and Dolutegravir are classified as [___] because they inhibit the final step of provirus integration into host cell chromosomes.
back:
* Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors (INSTIs)
* Specifically block the 'strand transfer' step
* Prevent HIV DNA integration into the human genome
* Generally have low metabolic side effects

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A pregnant HIV-positive patient on a zidovudine-containing regimen develops severe macrocytic anemia. This side effect is a classic classification toxicity of [___] analogs.
back:
* Zidovudine (AZT)
* Thymidine analog (NRTI)
* Key toxicity: Dose-limiting bone marrow suppression
* Causes characteristic elevated Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Describe the unique biological classification and route of administration for the agent Enfuvirtide.
back:
* Fusion Inhibitor (biomimetic peptide)
* Binds to the gp41 subunit of HIV envelope
* Route: Subcutaneous injection only
* Reason: Large peptide structure is degraded if given orally

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast Nevirapine and Delavirdine regarding their primary impact on the Cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme system.
back:
* Nevirapine: Potent CYP3A4 inducer; requires dose escalation to counter auto-induction
* Delavirdine: CYP3A4 inhibitor; increases levels of co-administered drugs
* Implication: Significant drug-drug interaction risks for both agents

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Protease Inhibitors (PIs) are classified as acting at the final stage of the viral life cycle because they specifically inhibit viral [___].
back:
* Maturation
* Prevent cleavage of Gag-Pol polyproteins
* Result in production of immature, non-infectious virions
* Act after the budding process is complete

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: [___] is the primary antiretroviral agent classified as a CCR5 co-receptor antagonist that prevents HIV entry by blocking the host cell chemokine receptor.
back:
• Maraviroc
• Mechanism: Prevents binding of HIV gp120 to the host CCR5 receptor.
• Note: Requires tropism testing before initiation.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A patient on a long-term regimen including Stavudine presents with abdominal pain and deep rapid breathing. Labs show lactic acidosis and hepatic steatosis. This condition is a class effect of NRTIs caused by [___].
back:
• Mitochondrial toxicity
• Pathophysiology: Inhibition of host mitochondrial DNA polymerase-gamma
• Common with: Thymidine analogs (Stavudine, Zidovudine).

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Explain the role of second-generation NNRTIs, such as Etravirine, in patients with established resistance to first-generation agents like Efavirenz.
back:
• Overcomes resistance: Effective against strains with K103N or Y181C mutations.
• High genetic barrier: Requires multiple mutations to lose clinical efficacy.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast the pharmacological interaction between Zidovudine and Stavudine that renders their combination contraindicated.
back:
• Competitive Antagonism: Both are thymidine analogs.
• Mechanism: Zidovudine inhibits the intracellular phosphorylation required to activate Stavudine.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Identify the pharmacological rationale for adding low-dose Ritonavir to a Protease Inhibitor (PI) regimen.
back:
• Pharmacokinetic boosting: Potently inhibits CYP3A4 enzymes.
• Effect: Increases drug exposure, prolongs half-life, and allows for reduced dosing frequency.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Before initiating treatment with the NRTI [___], patients must be screened for the HLA-B*5701 allele to prevent severe hypersensitivity reactions.
back:
• Abacavir
• Screening significance: Negative predictive value approaches 100%.
• Presentation: Fever, rash, and respiratory/GI symptoms.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A 30-year-old patient reports vivid nightmares and symptoms of depression two weeks after starting a regimen containing an NNRTI. Identify the agent responsible.
back:
• Efavirenz
• Class: Nonnucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor (NNRTI)
• Management: Bedtime dosing typically helps reduce these CNS side effects.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Differentiate the intracellular activation of Tenofovir from that of other nucleoside analogs like Lamivudine.
back:
• Tenofovir (Nucleotide): Requires only two intracellular phosphorylations to reach the active diphosphate form.
• Nucleoside analogs: Require three phosphorylations to reach the active triphosphate form.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF) with Tenofovir Alafenamide (TAF) regarding their risk for renal and bone toxicity.
back:
• TDF: Associated with proximal renal tubulopathy (Fanconi's) and bone density loss.
• TAF: Lower systemic plasma levels result in significantly reduced renal and bone toxicity.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Which specific NRTI is associated with the unique adverse effect of hyperpigmentation on the palms or soles?
back:
• Emtricitabine
• Incidence: Approximately 3%, occurring most frequently in African American patients.
• Mechanism: Cytosine analog closely related to Lamivudine.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Unlike triazoles, the imidazole [___] is rarely used systemically today because it significantly inhibits mammalian cytochrome P450, interfering with human steroid hormone synthesis.
back: Ketoconazole

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient being treated for invasive aspergillosis reports seeing flashes of light and blurred vision shortly after each intravenous dose. Identify the antifungal agent most likely responsible for these transient visual disturbances.
back: Voriconazole

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain the clinical precaution regarding the concurrent administration of Caspofungin and the immunosuppressant Cyclosporine.
back:
*   Risk of elevated liver enzymes (transaminitis).
*   The combination should generally be avoided unless benefit outweighs risk.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient with refractory invasive aspergillosis is switched from Voriconazole to a newer triazole prodrug with a 130-hour half-life. Contrast this new agent with Voriconazole regarding its activity against the agents of Mucormycosis.
back:
*   Voriconazole: Has no activity against Mucoraceae (Zygomycetes).
*   Isavuconazole (the new agent): Possesses significant activity against both Aspergillosis and Mucormycosis.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Specify the expected effect of Micafungin co-administration on the serum concentrations of Nifedipine and Sirolimus.
back: It increases the blood levels/concentrations of both medications.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: The allylamine Terbinafine is clinically distinguished as being [___] against dermatophytes, whereas Griseofulvin is only fungistatic.
back: Fungicidal

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: A patient on Itraconazole capsules for Histoplasmosis is started on Omeprazole for acid reflux. Predict the impact on the efficacy of the antifungal therapy.
back: Reduced efficacy; Itraconazole capsules require an acidic gastric environment for absorption. Proton pump inhibitors raise pH, significantly decreasing bioavailability.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Explain the biochemical reason why infections caused by Candida krusei cannot be managed with Fluconazole.
back:
*   Candida krusei displays intrinsic (innate) resistance to Fluconazole.
*   Management requires alternative agents like Voriconazole or Echinocandins.

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Contrast the 'reversible' and 'irreversible' components of renal toxicity caused by systemic Amphotericin B therapy.
back:
*   Reversible: Prerenal failure due to decreased renal perfusion (responsive to sodium loading).
*   Irreversible: Renal tubular injury/dysfunction (typically occurs after cumulative doses >4g).

category: Discuss mechanisms of action and resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, adverse effects of antifungal drugs
front: Identify the two specific electrolytes that are most commonly depleted due to the renal tubular wasting caused by systemic Amphotericin B therapy.
back: Potassium (K+) and Magnesium (Mg2+).

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Beta-lactam antibiotics, which are structural analogs of the natural d-Ala-d-Ala substrate, exert their bactericidal effect by covalently binding to the active site of [___].
back:
Penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)

* Inhibits the transpeptidation reaction.
* Halts peptidoglycan synthesis.
* Triggers autolysin activity resulting in cell death.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 45-year-old male with MRSA bacteremia experiences intense flushing and pruritus over his face and neck shortly after starting a rapid intravenous antibiotic infusion. This reaction is primarily mediated by the release of [___].
back:
Histamine

* Diagnosis: "Red man" syndrome.
* Causative agent: Rapid infusion of Vancomycin.
* Prevention: Prolong infusion time to 1-2 hours or antihistamine pretreatment.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the synergistic mechanism by which cell wall-active agents (like penicillins) enhance the efficacy of aminoglycosides against enterococci.
back:
Increased drug uptake

* Penicillins disrupt the cell wall peptidoglycan.
* Facilitates aminoglycoside penetration into the cytoplasm.
* Allows access to the 30S ribosomal target in otherwise resistant cells.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the mechanism of penicillin resistance in standard Staphylococcus aureus with the mechanism found in Methicillin-resistant strains (MRSA).
back:
Enzymatic Inactivation vs. Target Modification

* S. aureus: Produces β-lactamase (penicillinase) that hydrolyzes the β-lactam ring.
* MRSA: Possesses the *mecA* gene, encoding an altered PBP2a with low affinity for β-lactams.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Describe the specific interaction between tetracyclines and divalent/trivalent cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, Al3+) that impacts their clinical pharmacology.
back:
Chelation and reduced absorption

* Drugs form insoluble complexes in the gut.
* Significantly decreases oral bioavailability.
* Requires 1-2 hours separation from dairy, antacids, or iron.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Before initiating therapy with [___] for the radical cure of P. vivax, patients must be screened for G6PD deficiency to prevent acute hemolytic anemia.
back:
Primaquine

* MOA: Eliminates dormant liver hypnozoites.
* Clinical Use: Prevention of relapse in P. vivax and P. ovale.
* Cautions: Contraindicated in pregnancy.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 68-year-old patient on chronic corticosteroids for COPD is treated with Levofloxacin for pneumonia. He suddenly experiences acute pain and swelling in his heel. Identify the complication likely occurring.
back:
Achilles Tendon Rupture (Tendinitis)

* Drug Class: Fluoroquinolones.
* Risk Factors: Age >60, corticosteroids, and renal insufficiency.
* Clinical Action: Discontinue drug immediately.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Detail the intracellular biochemical step required for Metronidazole to exhibit its bactericidal effect against anaerobic organisms.
back:
Non-enzymatic Reduction

* Reacts with reduced ferredoxin in anaerobic cells.
* Forms toxic, highly reactive thiyl radicals.
* radicals bind to DNA, causing strand breakage and helical disruption.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the specific metabolic enzymes targeted by Sulfonamides versus Trimethoprim in the synthesis of bacterial folic acid.
back:
Dihydropteroate Synthase vs. Dihydrofolate Reductase

* Sulfonamides: Inhibit Dihydropteroate Synthase (PABA analog).
* Trimethoprim: Inhibits Dihydrofolate Reductase.
* Outcome: Sequential blockade providing synergistic activity.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary parasitic indication for Albendazole in Pakistan and its specific administration requirement to maximize efficacy for this condition.
back:
Hydatid Disease (Echinococcosis)

* Requirement: Must be taken with a fatty meal.
* Effect: Enhances systemic absorption for tissue parasites.
* MOA: Inhibits microtubule synthesis.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: [___] is a newer phosphonoamidate prodrug of Tenofovir that achieves higher intracellular levels of the active diphosphate in lymphoid cells and hepatocytes while maintaining 90% lower plasma concentrations than the older disoproxil fumarate form.
back:
* Tenofovir Alafenamide (TAF).
* Benefits: Reduced renal and bone toxicity compared to Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF).
* Classification: Nucleotide Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor (NtRTI).

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A treatment-naive HIV patient is found to have the K103N mutation on baseline genotypic testing. Identify the antiretroviral class that is rendered ineffective by this specific polymorphism and should be avoided in the initial regimen.
back:
* First-Generation NNRTIs.
* Affected Drugs: Efavirenz, Nevirapine, and Delavirdine.
* Clinical Significance: A single mutation confers high-level class resistance.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Explain the role of host cell enzymes in the mechanism of action for Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) prior to their interaction with HIV-1 reverse transcriptase.
back:
* Intracellular Phosphorylation: Requires host cell kinases.
* Activation: Converted into an active triphosphate form.
* Action: Triphosphates compete with endogenous nucleotides for incorporation into viral DNA.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A patient on Raltegravir requires therapy for tuberculosis with Rifampin, while another patient on Darunavir/ritonavir requires the same. Contrast the management of these two antiretrovirals based on their primary metabolic pathways.
back:
* Raltegravir: Dose is increased; metabolized via UGT1A1 glucuronidation which Rifampin induces.
* Darunavir: Generally contraindicated; PIs are CYP3A4 substrates heavily induced by Rifampin, leading to subtherapeutic levels.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Identify the specific Protease Inhibitors (PIs) that contain a sulfonamide moiety, which mandates caution in patients with known sulfa allergies.
back:
* Darunavir.
* Fosamprenavir.
* Tipranavir.
* Clinical Note: Associated with higher risk of hypersensitivity and skin rashes.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: The use of the entry inhibitor Maraviroc is strictly limited to patients harboring HIV strains that are [___], as determined by specific tropism testing.
back:
* CCR5-tropic.
* Mechanism: Maraviroc binds specifically to host CCR5 receptors.
* Limitation: Ineffective against CXCR4-tropic or dual-tropic HIV strains.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: A 28-year-old HIV+ woman starting Abacavir develops fever, malaise, and a maculopapular rash within 3 weeks. Explain the standard diagnostic prerequisite used to prevent this specific reaction.
back:
* HLA-B*5701 Allele Screening.
* Prerequisite: Mandatory testing before Abacavir initiation.
* Management: Immediate drug discontinuation if hypersensitivity occurs; rechallenge is strictly contraindicated.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
coreConcept: PI vs INSTI Mechanism of Action
front: Explain the mechanism by which Protease Inhibitors (PIs) prevent HIV maturation, differentiating this from the step inhibited by Integrase inhibitors.
back:
* PIs: Inhibit HIV aspartyl protease; blocks cleavage of Gag-Pol polyproteins.
* Effect: Prevents production of mature structural proteins; progeny are non-infectious.
* Contrast: Integrase inhibitors block DNA strand transfer into the host genome.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Contrast the binding sites and inhibition type of NNRTIs versus NRTIs on the HIV Reverse Transcriptase (RT) enzyme.
back:
* NRTIs: Bind to the catalytic active site (Competitive inhibition).
* NNRTIs: Bind to an allosteric site near the active site (Non-competitive inhibition).
* Result: NNRTIs cause conformational changes that halt DNA synthesis.

category: Classify antiretroviral agents
front: Identify the two 'second-generation' Nonnucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs) designed to maintain activity against viral strains resistant to older agents like Efavirenz.
back:
* Etravirine.
* Rilpivirine.
* Key Feature: Higher genetic barrier to resistance; active against common K103N mutants.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: The primary mechanism of action for penicillins involves covalent binding to [___], which are enzymes essential for the transpeptidation reaction in bacterial cell wall synthesis.
back:
• Penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)
• Binding inhibits the final cross-linking of peptidoglycan chains
• Leads to cell wall weakening and subsequent osmotic lysis
• Only effective against actively growing bacteria

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 45-year-old burn victim in the ICU develops a systemic infection. The physician initiates high-dose Gentamicin once daily. What pharmacodynamic property of aminoglycosides justifies this dosing interval to maximize efficacy?
back:
• Concentration-dependent killing: Efficacy increases with higher peak concentrations
• Postantibiotic effect (PAE): Antibacterial activity persists even after serum levels drop
• Once-daily dosing provides a drug-free interval, reducing nephrotoxicity risk

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the role of the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the peptidoglycan pentapeptide as a target for Vancomycin.
back:
• Vancomycin binds firmly to the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus
• Sterically hinders transglycosylase and transpeptidase enzymes
• Prevents elongation and cross-linking of the peptidoglycan polymer
• Resistance occurs via modification of the target to D-Ala-D-Lactate

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the ribosomal target and binding site of Linezolid with those of the Macrolide class (e.g., Erythromycin).
back:
• Linezolid: Binds 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit; prevents formation of the initiation complex
• Macrolides: Bind the 50S subunit near the exit tunnel; block translocation and elongation
• Linezolid inhibits protein synthesis at an earlier stage than macrolides

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Describe the primary mechanism of action of fluoroquinolones like Ciprofloxacin in Gram-negative versus Gram-positive bacteria.
back:
• Gram-negative: Primarily inhibits DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II), preventing DNA supercoiling
• Gram-positive: Primarily inhibits topoisomerase IV, interfering with daughter cell DNA separation
• Both actions result in rapid bactericidal death by disrupting DNA replication

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Tetracyclines are contraindicated in pregnant women and children under age 8 because they bind to [___] in developing teeth, causing permanent discoloration and enamel dysplasia.
back:
• Calcium (chelation)
• Deposited in newly formed bone and dentin
• Can lead to fluorescence, discoloration, and growth inhibition
• Doxycycline is the preferred agent in adults due to better absorption

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 28-year-old female presents with a severe maculopapular rash and fever after starting Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole for a UTI. This reaction is likely a result of which sulfonamide-associated dermatologic emergency?
back:
• Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)
• Can progress to Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)
• Often presents with mucosal involvement and systemic symptoms
• Requires immediate discontinuation of the offending sulfonamide

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain how Metronidazole achieves selective toxicity against anaerobic bacteria and certain protozoa.
back:
• Intracellular reduction by ferredoxin in anaerobic organisms
• Reduction generates reactive intermediates that damage microbial DNA
• Human cells and aerobic bacteria lack the low-potential reductases necessary for activation
• Results in unstable DNA molecules and cell death

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the anatomical preference for utilizing Clindamycin versus Metronidazole in the empiric treatment of anaerobic infections.
back:
• Clindamycin: Preferred for anaerobes "above the diaphragm" (e.g., lung abscesses, dental infections)
• Metronidazole: Preferred for anaerobes "below the diaphragm" (e.g., intra-abdominal and pelvic infections)
• Metronidazole also covers C. difficile, whereas Clindamycin is a risk factor for it

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary dose-limiting toxicity of Isoniazid (INH) and the vitamin supplement routinely co-administered to prevent it.
back:
• Peripheral neuropathy (due to interference with B6 metabolism)
• Hepatitis (age-dependent risk, increased in alcohol users)
• Supplement with Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) to alleviate neurotoxicity
• Sideroblastic anemia can also occur if B6 is not supplied

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: To exert its bactericidal effect, Isoniazid must be activated by the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase enzyme known as [___].
back:
• KatG enzyme
• Activated form inhibits mycolic acid synthesis
• Target is AcpM and KasA proteins
• Essential for mycobacterial cell wall integrity

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 28-year-old female being treated for Trichomonas vaginalis presents with severe nausea, vomiting, and flushing after consuming a glass of wine. This reaction occurs because the prescribed drug inhibits [___].
back:
• Aldehyde dehydrogenase
• Drug: Metronidazole (or Tinidazole)
• Causes accumulation of acetaldehyde
• Results in a Disulfiram-like reaction

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain how chloroquine effectively targets Plasmodium falciparum within the erythrocyte's acidic food vacuole.
back:
• Blocks biocrystallization of heme into non-toxic hemozoin
• Leads to buildup of toxic free heme
• Free heme causes parasite membrane damage
• Only effective against blood schizonts

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the pharmacokinetic interaction between dexamethasone and the two primary agents used for neurocysticercosis: Albendazole and Praziquantel.
back:
• Dexamethasone increases albendazole sulfoxide serum levels
• Dexamethasone decreases praziquantel bioavailability by 50%
• Albendazole preferred due to better subarachnoid penetration
• Steroids reduce inflammation from dying parasites

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the enzyme and specific intracellular environment required for the conversion of Pyrazinamide to its active form, pyrazinoic acid.
back:
• Enzyme: Mycobacterial pyrazinamidase (pncA gene)
• Environment: Acidic (pH 5.5)
• Location: Macrophage lysosomes
• Action: Disrupts mycobacterial cell membrane metabolism

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Patients receiving high-dose Ethambutol for tuberculosis require regular monitoring for [___], as it may cause dose-dependent retrobulbar neuritis.
back:
• Visual acuity and red-green color discrimination
• Occurs in ~2% of patients
• Usually reversible if drug stopped promptly
• Contraindicated in children too young for assessment

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A patient with HIV/TB co-infection is on a Protease Inhibitor-based regimen. Substitution of Rifampin with [___] is recommended to minimize Cytochrome P450 induction.
back:
• Rifabutin
• Less potent inducer of CYP3A4 than Rifampin
• Prevents subtherapeutic concentrations of Protease Inhibitors
• Requires dosage adjustment based on concomitant PI use

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Describe the neuro-muscular mechanism by which Ivermectin induces paralysis in nematodes like Onchocerca volvulus.
back:
• Intensifies GABA-mediated signal transmission
• Activates glutamate-gated chloride channels
• Leads to hyperpolarization and muscle paralysis
• Causes rapid death of microfilariae

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the stages of the Plasmodium life cycle targeted by Chloroquine versus those targeted by Primaquine.
back:
• Chloroquine: Blood schizonts (asexual erythrocytic forms) only
• Primaquine: Hepatic stages (hypnozoites) and Gametocides
• Primaquine prevents relapse in P. vivax/ovale
• Neither is reliably causal prophylactic

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the metabolic pathway inhibited by Dapsone and the specific enzyme deficiency that predisposes patients to drug-induced hemolysis.
back:
• Pathway: Folate synthesis (PABA antagonist)
• Enzyme Deficiency: G6PD (Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase)
• Used for: Leprosy and Pneumocystis prophylaxis
• Side effect: Methemoglobinemia and hemolysis

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: To overcome bacterial resistance caused by penicillinases (beta-lactamases), amoxicillin is often co-formulated with [___], which acts as a suicide inhibitor of the enzyme.
back:
• Clavulanic acid
• It prevents the hydrolysis of the beta-lactam ring
• Restores antibiotic activity against strains like S. aureus and H. influenzae.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A patient being treated for MRSA bacteremia and secondary pneumonia is started on Daptomycin. Despite blood culture clearance, his lung infection fails to improve. This occurs because [___] in the lungs antagonizes the drug.
back:
• Pulmonary surfactant
• Daptomycin binds to surfactant, preventing its interaction with bacterial cell membranes
• Clinical Rule: Never use daptomycin to treat pneumonia.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the physiological requirement for the active transport of Aminoglycosides (e.g., Gentamicin) across the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane.
back:
• Oxygen-dependent process
• Requires an electrochemical gradient coupled to a proton pump
• Absence of this system makes aminoglycosides ineffective against anaerobic bacteria.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the molecular binding target of Vancomycin in susceptible strains with the specific modification found in Vancomycin-resistant Enterococci (VRE).
back:
• Susceptible: D-Alanyl-D-Alanine terminus of peptidoglycan
• VRE: D-Alanyl-D-Lactate modification
• The D-Ala-D-Lac change results in the loss of a critical hydrogen bond, reducing drug affinity.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the specific mycobacterial enzyme required to convert the prodrug Isoniazid (INH) into its active form to inhibit mycolic acid synthesis.
back:
• KatG (Catalase-peroxidase)
• Mutation or deletion of this enzyme is a primary mechanism of high-level Isoniazid resistance.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Fluoroquinolones like Ciprofloxacin are generally contraindicated in pregnant women and children under 18 years because they may cause damage to [___].
back:
• Growing cartilage (Arthropathy)
• In adults, they are associated with an increased risk of tendinitis or tendon rupture.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: An HIV-positive patient on a stable regimen including Protease Inhibitors and Warfarin begins Rifampin for tuberculosis. Why is there a significant risk of virologic failure and subtherapeutic anticoagulation?
back:
• Potent induction of Cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP3A4)
• Rifampin significantly increases the metabolic clearance of both PIs and Warfarin
• Rifabutin is the preferred alternative for tuberculosis in these patients.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain how Echinocandins carries out its biological function differently compared to polyene and azole antifungals.
back:
• Targets the fungal cell wall (not the membrane)
• Inhibits β(1,3)-D-glucan synthase
• Leads to osmotic instability and cell lysis by blocking glucan polysaccharide synthesis.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the specific ribosomal subunits targeted by Tetracyclines and Macrolides during the inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis.
back:
• Tetracyclines: 30S subunit (blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding to the A site)
• Macrolides: 50S subunit (blocks the polypeptide exit tunnel and prevents translocation).

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Why must patients taking Metronidazole strictly avoid alcohol consumption during and for 48 hours after therapy?
back:
• Disulfiram-like reaction
• Inhibition of hepatic aldehyde dehydrogenase leads to acetaldehyde accumulation
• Symptoms: Severe flushing, tachycardia, palpitations, and nausea.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: The primary mechanism of action for ̢̢-lactam antibiotics involves binding to [̢̢̢], which inhibits the transpeptidation reaction of bacterial cell wall synthesis.
back:
* **Penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)**.
* PBPs are membrane enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan.
* Binding inhibits cell wall rigidity and triggers autolysins, leading to bacterial lysis and death.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A patient being treated for a Bacteroides fragilis infection experiences severe nausea and flushing after drinking a glass of wine. Identify the most likely drug and its unique biochemical trigger in anaerobic cells.
back:
* **Metronidazole**.
* Requires non-enzymatic reduction by **ferredoxin** in anaerobes.
* Reduced metabolites cause DNA destabilization.
* Inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing a **disulfiram-like reaction** with alcohol consumption.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the role of the d-Ala-d-Ala terminus in the mechanism of action of Vancomycin.
back:
* Vancomycin binds firmly to the **d-Ala-d-Ala terminus** of nascent peptidoglycan.
* This sterically inhibits **transglycosylase**, preventing chain elongation.
* Resistance involves replacing terminal d-Ala with **d-lactate**, losing a critical hydrogen bond.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the clinical application of Albendazole in Hydatid disease versus its use in Neurocysticercosis regarding the role of corticosteroids.
back:
* **Hydatid Disease:** Primary medical therapy; corticosteroids are not standardly required.
* **Neurocysticercosis:** Corticosteroids are essential to minimize inflammation from dying larvae.
* Dexamethasone **increases** albendazole sulfoxide levels, unlike its effect on praziquantel.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Why is cilastatin co-administered with imipenem in clinical practice?
back:
* Imipenem is rapidly inactivated by **dehydropeptidase I** in renal tubules.
* This results in low urinary drug levels and potential nephrotoxicity.
* **Cilastatin** inhibits this enzyme, ensuring therapeutic concentrations and preventing toxicity.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: The anti-influenza agent [̢̢̢] acts by inhibiting the viral M2 proton ion channel, but is currently not recommended due to widespread resistance (>99%) in H3N2 strains.
back:
* **Amantadine** (or Rimantadine).
* Prevents viral uncoating within host cells.
* Effective only against Influenza A.
* Significant adverse effects include **CNS toxicities** like delirium and hallucinations.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 30-year-old female treated with Nitrofurantoin for an uncomplicated UTI presents with sudden-onset cough and dyspnea. Identify the pathophysiology behind this adverse effect.
back:
* **Nitrofurantoin-induced pulmonary toxicity**.
* Caused by non-specific reactive intermediates from bacterial reductases.
* Can manifest as acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis or chronic fibrosis.
* Requires immediate drug discontinuation and avoidance in renal impairment.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the mechanism by which Oseltamivir prevents the spread of Influenza A and B within the respiratory tract.
back:
* Competitively inhibits **viral neuraminidase**.
* Prevents cleavage of sialic acid residues on host cells.
* Causes newly released virions to **clump** together and stick to the host membrane, blocking viral spread.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the mechanisms of action for sulfonamides versus trimethoprim within the folate synthesis pathway.
back:
* **Sulfonamides:** PABA analogs that inhibit **dihydropteroate synthase**.
* **Trimethoprim:** Inhibits **dihydrofolate reductase**.
* Together (TMP-SMZ), they provide **sequential blockade**, creating synergistic bactericidal activity against susceptible organisms.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary mechanism of resistance developed by staphylococci against Nafcillin.
back:
* **Modification of target PBPs**.
* Strains produce an altered protein (**PBP2a**) with extremely low binding affinity for ̢̢-lactams.
* This characterizes Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), rendering all traditional penicillins ineffective.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Beta-lactam antibiotics are structural analogs of the natural D-Ala-D-Ala substrate and function by covalently binding to the active site of [___].
back:
• Penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)
• Inhibits the transpeptidation reaction
• Halts peptidoglycan synthesis leading to cell death by osmotic pressure and autolysins.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 45-year-old male on treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis develops symmetrical numbness and paresthesia in his feet. This condition is most likely caused by a deficiency in [___] induced by his medication.
back:
• Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
• Isoniazid promotes its excretion, causing peripheral neuropathy
• Most common in slow acetylators or patients with malnutrition
• Managed by co-administering 25–50 mg of pyridoxine daily.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the three simultaneous ways Aminoglycosides interfere with bacterial protein synthesis upon binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit.
back:
• Interference with the initiation complex of peptide formation
• Misreading of mRNA causing incorporation of incorrect amino acids
• Breakup of polysomes into nonfunctional monosomes
• These effects lead to irreversible cell death.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast Ceftazidime and Cefepime regarding their stability against chromosomal Beta-lactamases and their activity against penicillin-non-susceptible streptococci.
back:
