• Due to the inherent pigment properties of the drug and its metabolites
• Can permanently stain soft contact lenses.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the specific synergistic mechanism utilized by the combination of Trimethoprim and Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ) in treating bacterial infections.
back:
• Sequential blockade of folate synthesis
• Sulfonamides: Compete with PABA to inhibit dihydropteroate synthase.
• Trimethoprim: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the ribosomal targets and effects of Tetracyclines versus Macrolides during bacterial protein synthesis.
back:
• Tetracyclines: Bind 30S subunit; block entry of aminoacyl-tRNA to the A-site.
• Macrolides: Bind 50S subunit; block the polypeptide exit tunnel/translocation step.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the most significant musculoskeletal adverse effect associated with the use of Fluoroquinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin) in elderly patients or those on corticosteroids.
back:
• Tendonitis and Achilles tendon rupture
• Risk increases with age >60 and concurrent steroid use
• Requires immediate discontinuation of the drug.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: In the synthesis of the bacterial cell wall, Beta-lactam antibiotics act as structural analogs of the [___] substrate, covalently binding to the active site of penicillin-binding proteins.
back:
• D-alanyl-D-alanine (D-Ala-D-Ala)
• This binding inhibits the transpeptidation reaction
• Halts peptidoglycan synthesis, leading to cell death

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A strain of *Staphylococcus aureus* isolated from a skin abscess is found to be resistant to methicillin. Describe the molecular pathophysiology of this specific resistance mechanism.
back:
• Production of altered target proteins (PBP2a)
• Results in low affinity for binding Beta-lactam drugs
• Mediated by the acquisition of the *mecA* gene

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain how Daptomycin carries out its bactericidal function differently from Vancomycin in treating resistant Gram-positive infections.
back:
• Binds membrane via calcium-dependent lipid tail insertion
• Causes rapid depolarization and potassium efflux
• Vancomycin inhibits cell wall synthesis at the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the clinical utility of Cefazolin and Ceftriaxone in a patient presenting with suspected bacterial meningitis who has a history of a mild non-anaphylactic rash to Amoxicillin.
back:
• Cefazolin: First-generation; lacks CNS penetration; inappropriate for meningitis
• Ceftriaxone: Third-generation; excellent CNS penetration; drug of choice
• Allergy: Low cross-reactivity (<1%); safe to use Ceftriaxone cautiously

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Describe the pharmacological rationale for once-daily dosing of Aminoglycosides despite their relatively short serum half-lives of 2-3 hours.
back:
• Concentration-dependent killing (higher peak increases kill rate)
• Significant Postantibiotic Effect (PAE) persists after drug clearance
• Lower troughs reduce accumulation in renal/vestibular tissues

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: For the systemic treatment of hydatid disease or neurocysticercosis, the therapeutic effectiveness of oral Albendazole is significantly enhanced when administered with [___].
back:
• A fatty meal (increases oral bioavailability)
• Corticosteroids (e.g. dexamethasone)
• Minimizes inflammatory response to dying tissue parasites

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 56-year-old hospitalized patient develops copious diarrhea after a course of Ceftriaxone. Stool tests confirm *C. difficile*. Explain the pharmacological intervention of choice if this is a severe case.
back:
• Oral Vancomycin (first-line for severe cases)
• Poorly absorbed = high intraluminal gut concentration
• Fidaxomicin is a narrow-spectrum alternative with low relapse rates

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 7-year-old child is treated with a drug from the Tetracycline class. Explain the biochemical mechanism underlying the specific dental adverse effect associated with this drug class.
back:
• Chelation with calcium in newly formed bone/teeth
• Deposition as a drug-calcium-orthophosphate complex
• Causes permanent brown discoloration and enamel dysplasia

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the metabolic handling of Sulfonamides in adults with the physiological risk they pose to neonates when administered near the end of pregnancy.
back:
• Adults: Hepatic acetylation/glucuronidation and renal excretion
• Neonates: Sulfonamides displace bilirubin from albumin
• Leads to Kernicterus (bilirubin-induced brain damage)

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the specific bacterial enzymes targeted by Fluoroquinolones like Ciprofloxacin to inhibit DNA synthesis during replication.
back:
• DNA Gyrase (Topoisomerase II): Prevents DNA relaxation
• Topoisomerase IV: Interferes with daughter cell separation
• Results in bactericidal action against aerobic Gram-negatives

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: The broad-spectrum antihelminthic drug Albendazole acts primarily by inhibiting [___] synthesis, which prevents the assembly of structural elements in nematodes.
back:
• Microtubule synthesis inhibition
• Binds to β-tubulin specifically
• Prevents glucose uptake, resulting in glycogen depletion and parasite death

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 28-year-old female being treated for Trichomonas vaginalis experiences severe nausea and flushing after consuming a glass of wine. Identify the drug responsible and its specific biochemical contraindication.
back:
• Drug: Metronidazole
• Effect: Disulfiram-like reaction
• Mechanism: Inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase enzyme
• Patient must avoid alcohol for 72 hours after therapy

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the role of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) in the antiparasitic mechanism of Ivermectin.
back:
• Intensifies GABA-mediated neurotransmission
• Targets glutamate-gated chloride channels
• Leads to hyperpolarization and tonic paralysis of the parasite
• Selective because human GABA receptors are in the protected CNS

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the clinical rationale for choosing Albendazole over Praziquantel in a patient with symptomatic parenchymal neurocysticercosis who requires concomitant corticosteroid therapy.
back:
• Corticosteroids increase Albendazole plasma levels/bioavailability
• Corticosteroids decrease Praziquantel levels by up to 50%
• Albendazole has superior subarachnoid penetration and lower cost

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the specific enzymatic target altered in high-level Mupirocin resistance (MIC > 1000 mcg/mL) during the treatment of S. aureus colonization.
back:
• Isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase
• Resistance is mediated by a plasmid-encoded gene (mupA)
• Prevents binding of the drug to the amino acid synthesis site

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Praziquantel effectively treats Schistosomiasis by increasing the cell membrane permeability to [___], resulting in rapid paralysis and dislodgement of the worm.
back:
• Calcium ions (Ca2+)
• Causes rapid tetanic contraction
• Induces tegumental vacuolization and subsequent parasite destruction by host immune cells

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 70-year-old patient with a Creatinine Clearance of 25 mL/min presents with an uncomplicated UTI. Explain why Nitrofurantoin is contraindicated in this clinical scenario.
back:
• Inadequate renal excretion prevents effective urinary concentrations
• Increased serum accumulation leads to systemic toxicities
• High risk of peripheral neuropathy and pulmonary fibrosis

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Describe the specific intracellular biochemical step required to activate Metronidazole into its toxic, DNA-damaging form within anaerobic bacteria.
back:
• Nonenzymatic reduction of the nitro group
• Reaction involves the electron transport protein ferredoxin
• Generates reactive oxygen species/intermediates that induce DNA strand breakage

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the therapeutic utility of Diethylcarbamazine and Ivermectin in the management of Onchocerca volvulus (Onchocerciasis).
back:
• Ivermectin: Drug of choice; kills microfilariae slowly over months
• Diethylcarbamazine: Avoided due to risk of severe Mazzotti reactions
• Neither drug is reliably macrofilaricidal (kills adult worms)

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: State the molecular target of Fidaxomicin and the primary reason for its low systemic toxicity.
back:
• Target: Sigma subunit of RNA polymerase
• Inhibits bacterial protein synthesis
• Low toxicity due to negligible systemic absorption following oral administration

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Beta-lactam antibiotics act as structural analogs of the natural d-Ala-d-Ala substrate and covalently bind to the active site of [___].
back:
• Penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)
• Inhibits the transpeptidation reaction in cell wall synthesis
• Halts peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to cell death by lysis.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 45-year-old burn patient is started on Gentamicin. After 7 days, he complains of tinnitus and dizziness. Identify the target of this toxicity and its usual clinical prognosis.
back:
• Target: Cranial Nerve VIII (Vestibulocochlear nerve)
• Type: Aminoglycoside-induced ototoxicity
• Prognosis: Often irreversible vestibular or auditory damage.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which Tetracyclines exert their bacteriostatic effect.
back:
• Bind reversibly to the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome
• Block binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to the mRNA-ribosome acceptor site
• Prevents addition of amino acids to growing peptide chains.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the mechanism of resistance in Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) with typical beta-lactamase producing Staphylococci.
back:
• Typical Staphylococci: Produce beta-lactamase enzymes that hydrolyze the antibiotic ring.
• MRSA: Possess mecA gene encoding PBP 2a, which has very low affinity for most beta-lactams.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary mechanism of action of Vancomycin and its specificity for Gram-positive organisms.
back:
• Binds firmly to D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of nascent peptidoglycan
• Inhibits transglycosylase, preventing chain elongation and cross-linking
• Too large to penetrate Gram-negative outer membranes.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: An agent used for anaerobic infections and C. difficile that causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol and produces toxic reactive intermediates is [___].
back:
• Metronidazole
• Reduced by parasite ferredoxin to form toxic metabolites
• Targets bacterial DNA; highly active against Bacteroides and Clostridium.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 65-year-old patient on Ciprofloxacin for a UTI develops sudden ankle pain. Identify the associated black-box warning and high-risk concurrent medications.
back:
• Effect: Tendonitis or Achilles tendon rupture
• Risk Factors: Age >60, renal failure, and concurrent corticosteroid use
• Mechanism: Direct toxicity to articular cartilage.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the selective toxicity of Amphotericin B and the common electrolyte disturbances associated with its chronic use.
back:
• Mechanism: Binds to fungal ergosterol to form transmembrane pores
• Selectivity: Higher affinity for ergosterol than human cholesterol
• Toxicity: Renal tubular acidosis with potassium and magnesium wasting.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast Sulfonamides and Trimethoprim regarding their specific inhibitory targets in the bacterial folate pathway.
back:
• Sulfonamides: Dihydropteroate synthase (competes with PABA)
• Trimethoprim: Dihydrofolate reductase
• Result: Sequential blockade leads to synergistic bactericidal activity.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: The primary drug used for both the radical cure of P. vivax malaria and as an alternative for primary prevention is [___].
back:
• Primaquine
• Targets: Hepatic hypnozoites and gametocytes
• Critical Precaution: Must screen for G6PD deficiency to prevent hemolysis.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: [___] are the primary membrane-bound enzymes targeted by Beta-lactam antibiotics, which, when inhibited, prevent the final transpeptidation step of bacterial cell wall synthesis.
back:
• Penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs).
• Inhibition halts peptidoglycan cross-linking.
• Leads to cell wall weakening and osmotic lysis.
• Active only against growing bacteria.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 40-year-old patient on Fluoxetine is treated for Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) with Linezolid. He suddenly develops tremors, hyperreflexia, and hyperthermia. This drug-drug interaction is known as [___].
back:
• Serotonin Syndrome.
• Linezolid acts as a nonselective monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI).
• Causes accumulation of serotonin when combined with SSRIs.
• Requires immediate discontinuation of the offending agents.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the synergistic mechanism by which the combination of Sulfonamides and Trimethoprim inhibits bacterial growth.
back:
• Sequential blockade of the folic acid pathway.
• Sulfonamides compete with PABA for dihydropteroate synthase.
• Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase.
• Results in more complete inhibition of DNA synthesis than single agents.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the pharmacodynamics of Aminoglycosides with Penicillins regarding their bacterial killing patterns.
back:
• Aminoglycosides: Concentration-dependent killing and significant post-antibiotic effect (PAE).
• Penicillins: Time-dependent killing; efficacy relies on duration serum levels remain above MIC.
• Clinical implication: Aminoglycosides allow for high-dose, once-daily dosing.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary hepatic metabolic pathway for Isoniazid (INH) and the clinical relevance of genetic polymorphism in this pathway.
back:
• N-acetylation by N-acetyltransferase.
• Slow acetylators: Increased risk of peripheral neuropathy and toxicity.
• Fast acetylators: May require higher doses for efficacy.
• Genetic variation is common in different populations.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: The anti-tuberculous drug [___] is unique because it requires activation by the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase enzyme, KatG, to inhibit mycolic acid synthesis.
back:
• Isoniazid (INH).
• Mutation in KatG is a primary mechanism of high-level resistance.
• Activated form targets the inhA and kasA gene products.
• It is bactericidal for actively dividing tubercle bacilli.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 28-year-old pregnant woman requires treatment for a respiratory infection. Tetracyclines are strictly avoided because they cross the placenta and bind to [___] in the fetus.
back:
• Calcium in newly formed bone and teeth.
• Causes permanent tooth discoloration (yellow-brown).
• Leads to enamel dysplasia and potential bone growth inhibition.
• Contraindicated throughout pregnancy and in children under 8.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Describe the intracellular chemical event required to trigger the antimalarial activity of the Artemisinin derivatives.
back:
• Iron-catalyzed cleavage of the endoperoxide bridge.
• Occurs within the parasite's food vacuole.
• Leads to the production of toxic free radicals.
• These radicals damage parasite proteins and lipids, causing rapid death.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the antifungal mechanisms of Amphotericin B and the Azole group (e.g., Fluconazole).
back:
• Amphotericin B: Binds directly to ergosterol, forming pores that cause cell leakage.
• Azoles: Inhibit cytochrome P450 enzymes to block the synthesis of ergosterol from lanosterol.
• Result: Amphotericin B is fungicidal; Azoles are generally fungistatic.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Name the specific drug required for the 'radical cure' of Plasmodium vivax malaria and identify its target stage.
back:
• Primaquine.
• Targets the dormant hepatic stage (hypnozoites).
• Prevents clinical relapses of the infection.
• Mandatory requirement: Must screen for G6PD deficiency before administration.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: The first antiviral agent to receive FDA approval for the treatment of hospitalized COVID-19 patients, which acts by inhibiting viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, is [___].
back:
* Remdesivir.
* Mechanism: Adenosine nucleotide analog.
* Action: Competes with ATP to cause premature termination of viral RNA transcription.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A 65-year-old male is hospitalized with COVID-19 pneumonia requiring supplemental oxygen. To reduce mortality in this patient with severe inflammatory response, the most high-yield corticosteroid to add is [___].
back:
* Dexamethasone.
* Role: Reduces systemic cytokine storm.
* Efficacy: Indicated specifically for patients requiring oxygen or mechanical ventilation to improve survival rates.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Explain the mechanism by which Nirmatrelvir (a component of Paxlovid) inhibits the replication of SARS-CoV-2.
back:
* Main Protease (Mpro) Inhibition: Selectively inhibits the 3CL protease.
* Effect: Prevents cleavage of viral polyproteins into functional units.
* Result: Halts viral assembly and maturation.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Contrast the primary administration routes and molecular targets of Remdesivir and Molnupiravir in the management of coronavirus.
back:
* Route: Remdesivir is intravenous; Molnupiravir is oral.
* Mechanism: Remdesivir causes chain termination; Molnupiravir induces 'lethal mutagenesis' via RNA error accumulation.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Identify the clinical role and specific molecular target of monoclonal antibodies like Sotrovimab in treating early-stage coronavirus infection.
back:
* Role: Prevents disease progression in high-risk outpatients.
* Target: Spike (S) protein of the virus.
* Effect: Blocks viral attachment and entry into host cells.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: In the combination drug Paxlovid, [___] is added not for its antiviral activity against SARS-CoV-2, but to act as a pharmacological booster.
back:
* Ritonavir.
* Function: Inhibits CYP3A4 enzymes.
* Effect: Increases and sustains therapeutic plasma concentrations of the active protease inhibitor, Nirmatrelvir.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: An obese 50-year-old female tests positive for COVID-19 with mild symptoms. She is at high risk for progression. The oral antiviral combination considered first-line for outpatient treatment is [___].
back:
* Paxlovid (Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir).
* Timing: Must be initiated within 5 days of symptom onset.
* Outcome: Significant reduction in the risk of hospitalization and death.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Describe the mechanism by which the monoclonal antibody Tocilizumab assists in the treatment of hospitalized COVID-19 patients with progressive respiratory failure.
back:
* IL-6 Receptor Antagonist.
* Mechanism: Blocks binding of Interleukin-6 to its receptor.
* Clinical Effect: Mitigates the hyper-inflammatory 'cytokine storm' associated with severe lung injury.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Contrast the pharmacological targets of Baricitinib and Dexamethasone when used as adjunctive therapies in severe COVID-19 cases.
back:
* Baricitinib: Inhibits Janus Kinase (JAK) 1/2 signaling pathways.
* Dexamethasone: Broadly suppresses pro-inflammatory gene transcription.
* Application: Both treat host immune-mediated damage rather than the virus itself.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: What is the primary pharmacological class and biochemical classification for Molnupiravir?
back:
* Class: Nucleoside analog (specifically a cytidine analog).
* Classification: Mutagenic ribonucleoside.
* Action: Acts as a substrate for viral RNA polymerase to induce catastrophic viral mutation.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: The first antiviral drug to receive FDA approval for the treatment of hospitalized COVID-19 patients is [___], which acts as a nucleotide analog that inhibits viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
back:
• Remdesivir
• Mechanism: Competes with ATP for incorporation into the viral RNA chain, causing premature chain termination.
• High-yield fact: Primarily used in patients requiring supplemental oxygen to reduce recovery time.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A 65-year-old male with diabetes and mild COVID-19 is prescribed Paxlovid. The regimen includes Nirmatrelvir and [___], which is added solely to inhibit CYP3A4 and boost the therapeutic levels of the primary antiviral.
back:
• Ritonavir
• Role: Pharmacokinetic enhancer (booster).
• Mechanism: Inhibits cytochrome P450 3A4, slowing the metabolic breakdown of Nirmatrelvir to maintain effective plasma concentrations.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which Nirmatrelvir prevents the replication of the SARS-CoV-2 virus.
back:
• Nirmatrelvir is a Main Protease (Mpro) inhibitor.
• It blocks the 3CL protease enzyme.
• This prevents the cleavage of viral polyproteins into functional units necessary for viral assembly.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Contrast the molecular mechanisms of Molnupiravir and Remdesivir in the inhibition of SARS-CoV-2 replication.
back:
• Molnupiravir: Induces 'lethal mutagenesis' (error catastrophe) by causing broad mutations during viral RNA synthesis.
• Remdesivir: Acts as a direct chain terminator of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) complex.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
coreConcept: Viral Entry and Host Response Modulation
front: Identify the cellular receptor required for SARS-CoV-2 entry and the class of drugs used to treat the hyperinflammatory 'cytokine storm' in severe cases.
back:
• Receptor: ACE2 (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2).
• Drug Classes: Systemic corticosteroids (e.g., Dexamethasone) and IL-6 receptor antagonists (e.g., Tocilizumab).

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: In patients with severe COVID-19 who require high-flow oxygen or mechanical ventilation, the corticosteroid [___] is the treatment of choice to reduce systemic inflammation and mortality.
back:
• Dexamethasone
• Clinical Use: Indicated only in patients requiring respiratory support.
• Effect: Dampens the exaggerated host immune response in late-stage disease.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A hospitalized patient with COVID-19 shows rapidly increasing oxygen requirements and significantly elevated IL-6 levels. The most appropriate monoclonal antibody to block this cytokine's receptor is [___].
back:
• Tocilizumab
• Class: IL-6 receptor antagonist.
• Indication: Used in hospitalized patients with systemic inflammation and respiratory decline despite receiving corticosteroids.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Describe the mechanism by which Baricitinib aids in the treatment of hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia.
back:
• Baricitinib is a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor.
• It blocks the Janus kinase-STAT signaling pathway.
• This reduces cytokine-mediated inflammation and may inhibit viral endocytosis into host cells.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Contrast the clinical timing and goals of administering Paxlovid versus Tocilizumab in COVID-19 management.
back:
• Paxlovid: Administered early (within 5 days) to prevent viral replication and hospitalization.
• Tocilizumab: Administered late in hospitalized patients to manage severe systemic inflammation/cytokine storm.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Mention the specific safety concern regarding the use of Remdesivir in patients with significantly impaired kidney function.
back:
• Risk of accumulation of the sulfobutylether-beta-cyclodextrin (SBECD) carrier vehicle.
• Generally avoided if eGFR is <30 mL/min.
• Potential for nephrotoxicity with carrier accumulation.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: The essential 6-carbon heterocyclic nucleus required for the biologic activity of all penicillin derivatives is [___].
back:
• 6-aminopenicillanic acid (ring A + B)
• Consists of a thiazolidine ring fused to a β-lactam ring
• Hydrolysis of the β-lactam ring by bacterial enzymes yields inactive penicilloic acid.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 24-year-old male presents with a painless, indurated genital ulcer (chancre). Serological testing confirms Treponema pallidum. Identify the first-line treatment of choice.
back:
• Benzathine penicillin G (intramuscular)
• Provides long-acting repository drug levels
• Drug of choice for syphilis due to high spirochete sensitivity and lack of resistance.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Describe the molecular mechanism of action for Beta-lactam antibiotics during bacterial cell wall synthesis.
back:
• Act as structural analogs of the D-Ala-D-Ala substrate
• Covalently bind to Penicillin-Binding Proteins (PBPs)
• Inhibit transpeptidation reactions to prevent peptidoglycan cross-linking
• Results in osmotic lysis of actively growing cells.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast Penicillin G and Nafcillin regarding their susceptibility to staphylococcal β-lactamase and their primary route of elimination.
back:
• Penicillin G: Highly susceptible to hydrolysis; primary renal elimination (tubular secretion)
• Nafcillin: Resistant to staphylococcal β-lactamase; primary biliary excretion (requires no dose adjustment in renal failure).

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the pharmacological rationale for co-administering Probenecid with natural penicillin derivatives.
back:
• Probenecid competes for the organic acid secretory carrier in renal tubules
• Impairs renal tubular secretion of β-lactams
• Significantly increases and prolongs therapeutic drug concentrations in the blood.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Resistance to antistaphylococcal penicillins (MRSA) is mediated by the acquisition of the mecA gene, which encodes an altered target known as [___].
back:
• PBP2a (Penicillin-Binding Protein 2a)
• Possesses extremely low binding affinity for β-lactam antibiotics
• Allows peptidoglycan synthesis to continue despite high drug concentrations.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A patient with hospital-acquired pneumonia develops an infection with β-lactamase-producing Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Identify the role of adding Tazobactam to Piperacillin for this patient.
back:
• Tazobactam acts as a suicide inhibitor of many bacterial β-lactamases
• Protects hydrolyzable Piperacillin from enzymatic destruction
• Extends the antibacterial spectrum to include resistant Gram-negative bacilli.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the synergistic resistance mechanism involving porin channels and the periplasmic space found specifically in Gram-negative bacteria.
back:
• Porins: Down-regulation reduces drug entry into the periplasm
• Periplasmic β-lactamases: Hydrolyze drug molecules that pass the membrane
• Synergy: Reduced penetration ensures concentration remains below the lethal threshold.

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast oral Amoxicillin and Ampicillin regarding their pharmacokinetics and the effect of food on bioavailability.
back:
• Amoxicillin: Superior oral absorption; serum levels are unaffected by food intake
• Ampicillin: Lower oral bioavailability; absorption significantly impaired by food (must be taken 1-2 hours before or after meals).

category: Discuss their mechanism of action, resistance, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the specific dipeptide structural analog that Beta-lactam antibiotics mimic to inhibit bacterial cell wall transpeptidases.
back:
• D-alanyl-D-alanine (D-Ala-D-Ala)
• Mimicry allows binding to Penicillin-Binding Proteins (PBPs)
• Mimics the terminal peptide of the pentapeptide linked to N-acetylmuramic acid.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: The nucleoside analog that inhibits viral replication by targeting the SARS-CoV-2 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) in hospitalized patients is [___].
back: Remdesivir.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A 60-year-old male with COVID-19 presents with a respiratory rate of 28/min and oxygen saturation of 88%. Clinical guidelines recommend the initiation of [___] to provide a mortality benefit in this oxygen-dependent phase.
back: Dexamethasone (Corticosteroids).

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Explain the pharmacokinetic role of Ritonavir when administered as part of the Paxlovid combination for COVID-19.
back:
• Potent CYP3A4 inhibitor
• Acts as a "booster" by slowing Nirmatrelvir metabolism
• Maintains therapeutic antiviral drug concentrations

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Contrast the molecular mechanisms and administration routes of Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir versus Remdesivir.
back:
• Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir: Oral 3CL protease inhibitor; targets polyprotein cleavage
• Remdesivir: Intravenous RdRp inhibitor; targets viral RNA synthesis and causes chain termination

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Identify the Interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptor antagonist indicated for hospitalized COVID-19 patients exhibiting rapid respiratory failure and systemic inflammation.
back: Tocilizumab.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: The mutagenic ribonucleoside analog that induces "error catastrophe" in the SARS-CoV-2 genome is [___].
back: Molnupiravir.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A high-risk 70-year-old patient presents with 2 days of mild COVID-19 symptoms. Identify the first-line oral antiviral therapy that requires careful screening for drug-drug interactions due to CYP3A4 inhibition.
back: Paxlovid (Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir).

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Explain how the clinical application of neutralizing monoclonal antibodies (e.g., Sotrovimab) differs from that of Tocilizumab in COVID-19 management.
back:
• Monoclonal Antibodies: Early use in high-risk outpatients to prevent viral entry
• Tocilizumab: Late use in hospitalized patients to block host inflammatory signaling

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Contrast the intracellular signaling pathway inhibited by Baricitinib with the extracellular target of Tocilizumab.
back:
• Baricitinib: Inhibits intracellular Janus Kinase (JAK) 1/2 signaling
• Tocilizumab: Competitively binds the extracellular IL-6 receptor

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Identify the specific viral enzyme inhibited by Nirmatrelvir that is essential for processing polyproteins into functional viral units.
back: Main Protease (Mpro), also known as 3C-like protease (3CLpro).

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: The primary nucleotide analog administered intravenously to inhibit the SARS-CoV-2 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase is [___].
back:
* Remdesivir.
* Functionally acts as a prodrug of an adenosine nucleotide analog.
* Specifically inhibits the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) to stop replication.
* Causes delayed chain termination, preventing the synthesis of functional viral RNA strands.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A hospitalized COVID-19 patient develops sudden respiratory failure with a massive spike in interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels. The monoclonal antibody used to target this receptor is [___].
back:
* Tocilizumab.
* Recombinant monoclonal antibody that binds to both soluble and membrane-bound IL-6 receptors.
* Utilized to manage the cytokine storm or hyper-inflammatory phase of the disease.
* Proven to reduce the risk of mechanical ventilation and mortality in severe cases.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism by which Nirmatrelvir inhibits the replication of the coronavirus.
back:
* Nirmatrelvir acts as an inhibitor of the 3CL protease (main protease or Mpro).
* It prevents the cleavage of viral polyproteins into functional units necessary for assembly.
* This blockade halts the formation of the viral replication complex within the host cell.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Contrast the molecular mechanisms of Remdesivir and Molnupiravir in the treatment of SARS-CoV-2.
back:
* Remdesivir: A nucleotide analog that acts as a chain terminator during RNA synthesis.
* Molnupiravir: A ribonucleoside analog that introduces multiple genetic errors, known as 'lethal mutagenesis.'
* Remdesivir requires intravenous administration, whereas Molnupiravir is an oral agent for high-risk outpatients.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Identify the pharmacological role of Ritonavir when co-formulated with Nirmatrelvir for COVID-19 treatment.
back:
* Ritonavir acts as a pharmacokinetic enhancer or 'booster' for Nirmatrelvir.
* It potently inhibits the hepatic CYP3A4 enzyme system.
* This prevents the rapid metabolism of Nirmatrelvir, maintaining therapeutic plasma concentrations for a longer duration.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: In hospitalized COVID-19 patients requiring supplemental oxygen, the high-yield corticosteroid proven to reduce 28-day mortality is [___].
back:
* Dexamethasone.
* A potent glucocorticoid that suppresses the host's systemic inflammatory response.
* Indicated specifically for patients who are hypoxic or require mechanical ventilation.
* Use in the early viral phase without respiratory distress may be counterproductive or harmful.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A 65-year-old obese patient tests positive for COVID-19 and is within 3 days of symptom onset. The most effective oral antiviral combination to prevent hospitalization is [___].
back:
* Paxlovid (Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir).
* Must be initiated as soon as possible, ideally within 5 days of symptom onset.
* It reduces the risk of hospitalization or death by nearly 89% in high-risk adults.
* Targets the intracellular viral main protease to stop post-translational processing.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Describe the intracellular signaling pathway targeted by Baricitinib in the treatment of severe COVID-19 pneumonia.
back:
* Baricitinib is a Janus Kinase (JAK) inhibitor, targeting JAK1 and JAK2 proteins.
* It interrupts the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, which prevents the transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
* By modulating the immune response, it reduces lung injury and systemic inflammatory markers.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Contrast the mechanism of action of Sotrovimab with that of Nirmatrelvir in neutralizing the coronavirus.
back:
* Sotrovimab: A monoclonal antibody that binds the viral spike protein to block entry.
* Nirmatrelvir: A protease inhibitor that prevents viral replication after the virus has entered the cell.
* Sotrovimab provides passive immunity, while Nirmatrelvir acts as a direct-acting antiviral enzyme inhibitor.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Mention the specific oral ribonucleoside analog that introduces viral errors but is avoided in pregnancy due to potential teratogenicity.
back:
* Molnupiravir.
* Converted intracellularly to its triphosphate form and incorporated into the viral RNA genome.
* Highly contraindicated in pregnancy due to the risk of embryo-fetal toxicity and developmental harm.
* Recommended only for mild-to-moderate COVID-19 when other treatments are not available.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: The primary intravenous antiviral agent used for SARS-CoV-2 that acts as a nucleotide analog to inhibit RNA-dependent RNA polymerase is [___].
back: • Remdesivir • Inhibits viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) • Acts as an adenosine analog to cause premature termination of viral RNA transcription.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A 72-year-old hospitalized patient with COVID-19 requires supplemental oxygen and shows signs of systemic inflammation. The corticosteroid indicated to reduce the risk of mortality is [___].
back: • Dexamethasone • Suppresses the hyper-inflammatory 'cytokine storm' • Indicated only for patients requiring supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Explain the role of Nirmatrelvir within the combination drug Paxlovid for treating COVID-19.
back: • Acts as a main protease (Mpro) inhibitor • Blocks the 3C-like protease (3CLpro) enzyme • Prevents the cleavage of viral polyproteins into functional units for replication.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Contrast the molecular mechanisms of action of Remdesivir and Molnupiravir in inhibiting SARS-CoV-2.
back: • Remdesivir: Nucleotide analog causing delayed chain termination • Molnupiravir: Ribonucleoside analog inducing 'lethal mutagenesis' or error catastrophe during RNA synthesis.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Identify the pharmacological purpose of co-administering Ritonavir with Nirmatrelvir in Paxlovid.
back: • Potent inhibitor of cytochrome P450 (CYP3A4) • Serves as a pharmacokinetic 'booster' • Maintains therapeutic plasma levels of Nirmatrelvir by slowing its hepatic metabolism.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: The Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor used for hospitalized COVID-19 patients requiring high-flow oxygen to modulate the immune response is [___].
back: • Baricitinib • Inhibits JAK1 and JAK2 signaling pathways • Reduces cytokine-mediated systemic inflammation and lung injury.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A hospitalized COVID-19 patient exhibits rapidly rising inflammatory markers and high oxygen needs. Identify the Interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptor antagonist appropriate for this patient.
back: • Tocilizumab • Monoclonal antibody targeting IL-6 receptors • Blocks downstream inflammatory signaling to prevent disease progression to mechanical ventilation.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Describe how Molnupiravir facilitates the termination of SARS-CoV-2 despite being incorporated into the viral RNA genome.
back: • Induces viral 'error catastrophe' • The viral RNA polymerase reads incorporated Molnupiravir as either cytidine or uridine • Resulting mutations render the viral genome non-functional.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Contrast the standard route of administration and patient selection for Paxlovid versus Remdesivir.
back: • Paxlovid: Oral route; used for non-hospitalized mild-to-moderate high-risk patients • Remdesivir: Intravenous route; used for both high-risk outpatients and hospitalized patients.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Identify the primary viral enzyme targeted by the protease inhibitor Nirmatrelvir.
back: • Main Protease (Mpro) • Also known as 3C-like protease (3CLpro) • Cleaves viral polyproteins pp1a and pp1ab into essential non-structural proteins.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Benzimidazole drugs like albendazole and mebendazole exert their primary antihelminthic effect by inhibiting [___].
back:
* Microtubule synthesis
* Binds to parasitic β-tubulin with high affinity
* Prevents polymerization of tubulin dimers

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: A 45-year-old farmer with chronic steroid use develops abdominal pain and larva currens. Ivermectin is initiated. Explain the mechanism by which this drug paralyzes the parasite.
back:
* Intensifies GABA-mediated transmission
* Acts as a GABA receptor agonist in peripheral nerves
* Induces flaccid paralysis of the nematode

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Describe the specific ion-channel related mechanism by which Praziquantel induces paralysis in schistosomes and cestodes.
back:
* Increases cell membrane permeability to calcium
* Triggers rapid intracellular calcium influx
* Results in spastic paralysis and tegumental damage

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Contrast the effects of concomitant corticosteroid administration on the systemic bioavailability of Praziquantel versus Albendazole.
back:
* Praziquantel: Bioavailability is significantly decreased (up to 50%)
* Albendazole: Bioavailability (active sulfoxide metabolite) is increased by dexamethasone

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Identify the primary pathophysiology behind the acute febrile reactions and lymphangitis seen during Diethylcarbamazine therapy for filariasis.
back:
* Host immune response to dead parasites
* Triggered by proteins released from dying microfilariae
* Often necessitates adjunctive corticosteroid therapy

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Pyrantel pamoate acts as a [___] agent that induces release of acetylcholine and inhibits cholinesterase, leading to spastic paralysis in worms.
back:
* Neuromuscular blocking agent
* Persistent activation of nicotinic receptors
* Worms are expelled from the lumen by peristalsis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: A hospital identifies an outbreak of S. aureus with high-level mupirocin resistance (MIC >1000 mcg/mL). What is the genetic basis for this drug failure?
back:
* Acquisition of a second gene
* Encodes an altered isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase
* Usually plasmid-encoded and transmissible

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Detail the metabolic pathway targeted by Nitazoxanide in protozoal organisms like Giardia lamblia and Cryptosporidium parvum.
back:
* Inhibits the pyruvate-ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) enzyme
* Disrupts anaerobic energy metabolism
* Blocks essential electron transfer reactions

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Distinguish the clinical indications of Bithionol from those of Praziquantel regarding fluke (trematode) species coverage.
back:
* Bithionol: Alternative for Fasciola hepatica (sheep liver fluke)
* Praziquantel: Broad fluke coverage (Schistosoma) but ineffective against Fasciola

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Why must patients be strictly cautioned against ethanol consumption while receiving Metronidazole for amebic colitis?
back:
* Disulfiram-like reaction
* Inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase
* Causes accumulation of toxic acetaldehyde

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: The primary antiviral agent used in hospitalized COVID-19 patients that functions by inhibiting the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) is [___].
back:
Remdesivir. 
• Mechanism: Functions as an adenosine nucleotide analog.
• Action: Causes premature termination of viral RNA transcription.
• Administration: Given intravenously to hospitalized patients with severe disease.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A 65-year-old COVID-19 patient with bilateral lung infiltrates requires supplemental oxygen. The pharmacological intervention shown to decrease 28-day mortality by targeting the hyper-inflammatory phase is [___].
back:
Dexamethasone. 
• Class: Glucocorticoid (Corticosteroid).
• Indication: Hypoxic patients requiring oxygen or mechanical ventilation.
• Note: Not recommended for mild cases not requiring respiratory support.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism by which Nirmatrelvir halts the SARS-CoV-2 replication cycle.
back:
Nirmatrelvir is a Protease Inhibitor.
• Target: Specifically inhibits the Main Protease (Mpro), also known as 3CL protease.
• Result: Prevents the cleavage of viral polyproteins into functional proteins needed for viral assembly.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Contrast the functional roles of Nirmatrelvir and Ritonavir when administered together as the co-formulated drug Paxlovid.
back:
Nirmatrelvir is the active antiviral that inhibits viral protease.
Ritonavir acts as a pharmacokinetic booster by inhibiting the host enzyme CYP3A4, which prevents the rapid metabolism of Nirmatrelvir, maintaining its therapeutic levels.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Identify the specific biochemical mechanism by which Molnupiravir induces viral 'error catastrophe.'
back:
Lethal Mutagenesis.
• Mechanism: As a ribonucleoside analog, it is incorporated into viral RNA by RdRp.
• Effect: It causes widespread random mutations during replication, rendering the viral progeny non-viable.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: In patients with severe COVID-19 demonstrating a 'cytokine storm' and elevated inflammatory markers, the monoclonal antibody [___] is used to target IL-6 receptors.
back:
Tocilizumab.
• Class: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptor antagonist.
• Utility: Reduces the risk of progression to mechanical ventilation and death in severe systemic inflammation.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A 70-year-old high-risk outpatient presents with mild COVID-19 symptoms for 3 days. The most effective oral antiviral regimen to prevent hospitalization, which must be started within 5 days, is [___].
back:
Paxlovid (Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir).
• Timing: Must be initiated within 5 days of symptom onset.
• Contraindications: Significant due to many drug-drug interactions via the CYP3A4 pathway.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Describe how neutralizing monoclonal antibodies (e.g., Sotrovimab) prevent the cellular entry of the SARS-CoV-2 virus.
back:
Spike Protein Neutralization.
• Binding: The antibodies bind to the Receptor Binding Domain (RBD) of the viral Spike (S) protein.
• Blockade: This physically prevents the virus from docking with host ACE2 receptors.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Contrast the administration routes and primary clinical settings for the use of Remdesivir versus Molnupiravir.
back:
Remdesivir is administered Intravenously (IV) and is primarily utilized in inpatient/hospitalized settings.
Molnupiravir is an Oral medication suitable for outpatient use in patients with mild-to-moderate disease at high risk of progression.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Identify the pharmacological class and clinical application of Baricitinib in the context of COVID-19 therapy.
back:
Janus Kinase (JAK) Inhibitor.
• Application: Used in hospitalized patients requiring oxygen.
• Action: Blocks intracellular signaling of pro-inflammatory cytokines to modulate the immune-mediated lung injury.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Beta-lactam antibiotics, which are structural analogs of the natural d-Ala-d-Ala substrate, covalently bind to the active site of [___], thereby inhibiting the transpeptidation reaction.
back:
* Penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)
* Inhibition halts peptidoglycan synthesis
* Results in bacterial cell wall weakening and osmotic lysis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: A 40-year-old patient being treated for a severe methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) infection with Vancomycin develops sudden onset of flushing, chills, and a rash on the upper body during the infusion. Identify the primary physiological trigger for this reaction.
back:
* Non-immunologic histamine release from mast cells
* Known as 'Red Man' syndrome
* Prevented by slowing infusion rate or using antihistamines

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Describe the biochemical mechanism by which Daptomycin induces rapid cell death in Gram-positive bacteria.
back:
* Binds to the cell membrane via calcium-dependent lipid tail insertion
* Causes membrane depolarization and potassium efflux
* Arrests DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis without cell lysis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Contrast the mechanisms of resistance to Tetracyclines mediated by the Tet(AE) efflux pump versus the Tet(M) ribosomal protection protein.
back:
* Tet(AE): Actively pumps older tetracyclines out of the cell; Tigecycline is not a substrate.
* Tet(M): Ribosomal protein that prevents drug binding; Tigecycline overcomes this via steric hindrance.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Identify the primary mechanism of action and the major dose-limiting toxicity of Chloramphenicol in newborns.
back:
* Mechanism: Reversibly binds the 50S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting peptide bond formation.
* Toxicity: 'Gray baby' syndrome due to inadequate hepatic glucuronic acid conjugation.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Aminoglycosides are transported into the bacterial cytoplasm via an [___]-dependent process, which is why they lack activity against anaerobic organisms.
back:
* Oxygen-dependent
* Requires a transmembrane electrochemical gradient
* Transport is inhibited by low extracellular pH and anaerobic conditions

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: A 65-year-old patient on Warfarin therapy is started on Rifampin for a mycobacterial infection. Within a week, his INR drops significantly below the therapeutic range. Explain the pharmacological basis for this finding.
back:
* Potent induction of cytochrome P450 isoforms (especially CYP3A4)
* Increases the metabolic clearance of Warfarin
* Results in reduced anticoagulant effect

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Explain the synergistic mechanism of action of the combination drug Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMZ).
back:
* Sequential blockade of folate synthesis
* Sulfonamides: Inhibit dihydropteroate synthase (compete with PABA)
* Trimethoprim: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, preventing tetrahydrofolate formation

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Contrast the renal toxicity profiles of conventional Amphotericin B deoxycholate with its liposomal formulations.
back:
* Conventional: High risk of renal tubular injury and potassium/magnesium wasting.
* Liposomal: Reduced nonspecific binding to human membranes decreases nephrotoxicity while maintaining potency.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Identify the primary mechanism of action of the benzimidazole antihelminthic, Albendazole.
back:
* Inhibits microtubule synthesis in nematodes
* Active metabolite (albendazole sulfoxide) distributes widely into tissues
* Effectively kills both larvae and adult worms

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: The antihelminthic agent [___] acts by increasing the cell membrane permeability to calcium, resulting in rapid contraction and subsequent paralysis of trematodes and cestodes.
back:
• Praziquantel
• Leads to dislodgement and death of the parasite
• Effective against all Schistosoma species and most tapeworms.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: A 29-year-old patient on long-term therapy for a liver hydatid cyst presents with alopecia, fatigue, and pancytopenia. These toxicities are most commonly associated with [___].
back:
• Albendazole
• Occurs primarily during long-term use (e.g., for Echinococcus)
• Requires regular monitoring of blood counts and liver enzymes.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Explain the mechanism by which Ivermectin induces paralysis in nematodes and arthropods.
back:
• Acts as a GABA agonist
• Intensifies inhibitory signaling in peripheral nerves
• Paralyzes the parasite by opening glutamate-gated chloride channels.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Contrast the clinical preference and risk of systemic inflammatory reactions between Diethylcarbamazine and Ivermectin in the treatment of Onchocerciasis.
back:
• Ivermectin: Drug of choice; safer profile as it blocks microfilarial release.
• Diethylcarbamazine: No longer preferred; high risk of severe Mazotti reactions (fever, hypotension) due to rapid microfilarial killing.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Identify the primary dose-dependent adverse effect of Ribavirin that necessitates frequent monitoring of hemoglobin levels during Hepatitis C therapy.
back:
• Hemolytic anemia
• Occurs in 10–20% of patients
• Can exacerbate underlying cardiac disease; contraindicated in significant anemia.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: The antiviral agent [___] is often limited by symptomatic electrolyte imbalances including hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and a unique risk of genital ulcerations.
back:
• Foscarnet
• Directly inhibits viral DNA/RNA polymerase without phosphorylation
• Major toxicities: Nephrotoxicity and ionized calcium chelation.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: A patient with CMV retinitis is prescribed Cidofovir. Describe the mandatory adjunctive pharmacological measures required to prevent its characteristic proximal tubular nephrotoxicity.
back:
• High-dose Probenecid: Blocks active tubular secretion
• Aggressive Pre-hydration: Intravenous normal saline
• Prevents Fanconi-like syndrome and metabolic acidosis.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Detail the three distinct functions of the Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) DNA polymerase that are competitively inhibited by Entecavir.
back:
• Base priming
• Reverse transcription of the negative strand
• Synthesis of the positive strand of HBV DNA.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Contrast the dietary instructions for Albendazole when treating intraluminal parasites versus tissue-invasive helminths (e.g., Hydatid disease).
back:
• Intraluminal: Taken on an empty stomach to limit absorption.
• Tissue-invasive: Taken with a fatty meal to significantly increase systemic bioavailability.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Describe the specific biochemical target and the resultant viral effect of Oseltamivir on Influenza A and B virions.
back:
• Target: Viral neuraminidase enzyme
• Effect: Prevents release of progeny virions from the host cell
• Causes clumping of viruses to the infected cell membrane.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Beta-lactam antibiotics exert their bactericidal effect by inhibiting the [___] reaction, which is the final step in peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis.
back:
- Targets the Transpeptidation reaction.
- Covalently binds to the active site of Penicillin-Binding Proteins (PBPs).
- Halts peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to bacterial cell lysis.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
coreConcept: Metronidazole Adverse Effects and Drug Interactions
front: A 35-year-old patient being treated for an anaerobic infection with metronidazole consumes alcohol and presents with severe nausea, flushing, and palpitations. Explain the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
- Metronidazole causes a Disulfiram-like reaction.
- Inhibits the enzyme acetaldehyde dehydrogenase.
- Leads to toxic accumulation of acetaldehyde following ethanol ingestion.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Describe the specific biochemical target and the subsequent inhibitory effect of Vancomycin on the bacterial cell wall.
back:
- Binds firmly to the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of nascent peptidoglycan.
- Inhibits the enzyme transglycosylase.
- Prevents further elongation and cross-linking of the peptidoglycan polymer.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Contrast the structural toxicities of Tetracyclines in pediatric populations with the unique musculoskeletal risk associated with Fluoroquinolones.
back:
- Tetracyclines: Chelate calcium in growing bone/teeth; causes enamel dysplasia, permanent discoloration, and growth inhibition.
- Fluoroquinolones: Damage growing cartilage (arthropathy); causes tendinitis and risk of tendon rupture in adults.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Identify the non-antimicrobial physiological effect of Macrolides (e.g., Erythromycin) on the gastrointestinal tract that causes common side effects.
back:
- Direct stimulation of motilin receptors.
- Increases gastrointestinal motility (prokinetic effect).
- Causes anorexia, nausea, and vomiting independent of microbial flora changes.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Aminoglycosides like Gentamicin are notorious for [___] toxicity, which is usually reversible, and [___] toxicity, which is frequently irreversible.
back:
- Nephrotoxicity (reversible); Ototoxicity (irreversible).
- Ototoxicity includes both vestibular damage (vertigo) and auditory damage (tinnitus/hearing loss).

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: A patient on high-dose Sulfadiazine presents with hematuria and renal colic. Microscopic examination shows sulfonamide crystals. What is the management strategy to prevent this drug-induced renal injury?
back:
- Condition: Crystalluria due to low solubility of sulfonamides in acidic urine.
- Management: Aggressive hydration and alkalinization of urine (e.g., via sodium bicarbonate).

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Explain the three concurrent ways Aminoglycosides inhibit protein synthesis after entering the bacterial cytoplasm through oxygen-dependent transport.
back:
- Interference with the initiation complex of peptide formation.
- Misreading of mRNA, leading to the incorporation of incorrect amino acids.
- Breakup of polysomes into nonfunctional monosomes.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Contrast the mechanism of Sulfonamides with that of Trimethoprim in the context of bacterial folate metabolism.
back:
- Sulfonamides: PABA analogs that inhibit Dihydropteroate synthase.
- Trimethoprim: Inhibits Dihydrofolate reductase.
- Combined use results in sequential blockade and synergistic bactericidal activity.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Identify the specific enzyme inhibited by Fluoroquinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin) in Gram-negative organisms to prevent DNA relaxation.
back:
- Inhibits DNA Gyrase (Topoisomerase II).
- Prevents the relaxation of positively supercoiled DNA required for normal transcription and replication.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Beta-lactam antibiotics act by covalently binding to [___], which inhibits the transpeptidation reaction essential for peptidoglycan cross-linking and bacterial cell wall integrity.
back:
● Penicillin-Binding Proteins (PBPs)
● Prevents final step of cell wall synthesis
● Leads to osmotic instability and cell lysis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: A patient receiving a rapid infusion of a glycopeptide antibiotic for MRSA develops intense flushing and pruritus of the face and upper torso. Identify the likely drug and the causative mechanism.
back:
● Drug: Vancomycin
● Mechanism: "Red man" syndrome
● Triggered by non-immunologic histamine release due to rapid intravenous infusion

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Explain the role of calcium-dependent binding in the mechanism of action of Daptomycin.
back:
● Lipid tail inserts into cell membrane in a calcium-dependent manner
● Causes rapid depolarization and potassium efflux
● Results in arrest of DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis leading to death

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Contrast the susceptibility of Ceftriaxone (3rd gen) and Cefepime (4th gen) regarding hydrolysis by chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamases produced by organisms like Enterobacter.
back:
● Ceftriaxone: Readily hydrolyzed by constitutively produced AmpC; avoided in Enterobacter infections
● Cefepime: Highly resistant to AmpC hydrolysis; preferred for these organisms

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Describe the unique toxicities associated with cephalosporins containing a methylthiotetrazole (MTT) group, such as Cefotetan.
back:
● Hypoprothrombinemia: Causes bleeding disorders (prevented by Vitamin K)
● Disulfiram-like reaction: Occurs if ingested with alcohol
● Inhibits Vitamin K epoxide reductase

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Fosfomycin exerts its antibacterial effect by covalently binding to the cysteine residue of [___], blocking the first step in the formation of UDP-N-acetylmuramic acid.
back:
● Enolpyruvate transferase
● Blocks addition of phosphoenolpyruvate to UDP-N-acetylglucosamine
● Inhibits very early stage of cell wall synthesis

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: A patient with renal failure is prescribed Imipenem/Cilastatin for a serious infection and subsequently develops generalized seizures. Explain the pharmacological rationale for this adverse event.
back:
● Excessive imipenem accumulation due to impaired renal clearance
● High concentrations reduce seizure threshold
● Cilastatin used to prevent imipenem degradation by renal dehydropeptidase

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: How does the substitution of D-lactate for the terminal D-alanine in peptidoglycan precursors affect Vancomycin activity?
back:
● Modification occurs at D-Ala-D-Ala binding site
● Results in loss of critical hydrogen bond
● Prevents high-affinity binding of Vancomycin to its target

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Contrast the primary elimination routes of Nafcillin and Penicillin G.
back:
● Nafcillin: Primarily cleared by biliary excretion; no dose adjustment in renal failure
● Penicillin G: Rapidly excreted by kidneys (90% tubular secretion, 10% filtration)

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Name the specific beta-lactam class that exhibits a spectrum limited to aerobic Gram-negative bacilli and lacks cross-allergenicity with most penicillins.
back:
● Monobactams (Aztreonam)
● Active against Pseudomonas
● Tolerated by most penicillin-allergic patients due to distinct chemical nucleus

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Vancomycin inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding firmly to the [___] terminus of nascent peptidoglycan pentapeptide.
back:
• D-alanyl-D-alanine (D-Ala-D-Ala)
• Inhibits the transglycosylase enzyme, preventing peptidoglycan elongation
• Interferes with cross-linking of the cell wall
• Leads to cell death via osmotic lysis and autolysin activation

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: A patient receiving a rapid intravenous infusion of vancomycin develops intense flushing, pruritus, and an erythematous rash on the face and neck. Identify the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
• Histamine release (Infusion-related)
• Often called "Red Man Syndrome"
• Result of non-immunologic histamine release from mast cells due to rapid infusion rate
• Managed by slowing the infusion or pre-treating with antihistamines

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Explain the role of the 30S ribosomal subunit in the mechanism of action of Tetracyclines.
back:
• Reversible binding to the 30S subunit
• Blocks the binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to the A-site on the mRNA-ribosome complex
• Prevents addition of new amino acids to the growing peptide
• Results in bacteriostatic protein synthesis inhibition

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Contrast the primary mechanism of resistance to beta-lactams in MRSA with the mechanism of intermediate resistance in Vancomycin-Intermediate S. aureus (VISA).
back:
• Altered Target vs. False Target
• MRSA: Production of PBP2a with low affinity for beta-lactams
• VISA: Thickened cell walls with decoy D-Ala-D-Ala residues
• Sequesters vancomycin in the outer cell wall, preventing it from reaching the membrane

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Identify the primary pharmacological reason why Daptomycin is ineffective for the treatment of bacterial pneumonia.
back:
• Antagonism by Pulmonary Surfactant
• Daptomycin binds to and is inactivated by surfactant in the alveoli
• Prevents the drug from achieving therapeutic concentrations in lung parenchyma
• Use is restricted to skin, soft tissue, and endovascular infections

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Patients prescribed Metronidazole must be strictly cautioned against consuming alcohol to avoid a severe [___] reaction.
back:
• Disulfiram-like reaction
• Inhibits acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, leading to acetaldehyde accumulation
• Symptoms include flushing, nausea, vomiting, and headache
• Metronidazole also causes a metallic taste and peripheral neuropathy with long-term use

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: A 65-year-old patient on Gentamicin for 10 days develops tinnitus and persistent dizziness. Describe the specific site of damage and the expected clinical prognosis.
back:
• Irreversible Ototoxicity (Vestibular/Auditory)
• Direct damage to sensory hair cells in the inner ear
• Toxicity is dose-related and time-dependent
• Prognosis: Damage is usually permanent and may result in deafness or ataxia

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Describe the molecular steps by which Amphotericin B creates lethal defects in fungal cells.
back:
• Ergosterol Binding
• Binds to ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane
• Forms transmembrane pores or channels
• Causes leakage of intracellular ions (K+) and macromolecules, leading to cell death

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Contrast the effect of divalent cations on the absorption of Doxycycline versus older tetracyclines.
back:
• Chelation Interaction
• Older Tetracyclines: Absorption significantly impaired by dairy products and antacids (Ca2+, Mg2+, Fe2+)
• Doxycycline: Absorption is not significantly affected by food or dairy
• Doxycycline has improved oral bioavailability and a longer half-life

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Name the most significant dose-related adverse effect of Ethambutol that necessitates monthly visual screening.
back:
• Retrobulbar Neuritis
• Symptoms: Decreased visual acuity and red-green color blindness
• Monitoring: Baseline and monthly testing of vision and color discrimination
• Usually reversible if the drug is discontinued immediately upon detection

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: The first antiviral drug approved for COVID-19 that acts by inhibiting the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) is [___].
back:
* Remdesivir.
* It is an adenosine nucleotide analog.
* Administered intravenously for hospitalized patients with COVID-19 pneumonia.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A 65-year-old high-risk diabetic patient with early COVID-19 is prescribed Paxlovid. This combination therapy works by inhibiting the [___], which is essential for processing viral polyproteins.
back:
* Main Protease (Mpro or 3CLpro).
* Prevents the cleavage of viral polyproteins into functional units.
* Halts viral replication and maturation.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Explain the role of lethal mutagenesis in the mechanism of action of Molnupiravir against SARS-CoV-2.
back:
* It is a ribonucleoside (cytidine) analog.
* Incorporated into viral RNA by the RdRp.
* Induces a high frequency of genetic mutations during replication, leading to 'error catastrophe.'

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A patient with COVID-19 requires supplemental oxygen but is not yet intubated. Contrast the indications for adding Dexamethasone versus Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir in this clinical scenario.
back:
* Dexamethasone: Indicated to modulate the late-stage inflammatory response and reduce mortality.
* Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir: Generally not indicated for hospitalized severe cases; intended for early mild-to-moderate disease in outpatients.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Identify the oral Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor that is frequently used in combination with Dexamethasone to treat hospitalized COVID-19 patients with systemic inflammation.
back:
* Baricitinib.
* Blocks the JAK-STAT signal transduction pathway.
* Modulates the cytokine storm seen in severe coronavirus infection.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: In patients with severe COVID-19 showing rapid respiratory decline, the humanized monoclonal antibody used to block Interleukin-6 (IL-6) signaling is [___].
back:
* Tocilizumab.
* Competitively binds to both soluble and membrane-bound IL-6 receptors.
* Reduces the incidence of invasive mechanical ventilation and mortality.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: A hospitalized patient with COVID-19 is failing Dexamethasone and has significantly elevated C-reactive protein. You initiate a drug that prevents IL-6 from binding to its receptor. Identify the underlying pathology this drug targets.
back:
* Cytokine Release Syndrome (Cytokine Storm).
* Characterized by hyper-inflammation and multi-organ damage.
* TOCILIZUMAB is the indicated IL-6 receptor blocker.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Describe the intracellular mechanism by which Remdesivir stops the replication of the SARS-CoV-2 viral genome.
back:
* Acts as a nucleoside triphosphate analog.
* Competes with ATP for the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
* Results in delayed chain termination of the viral RNA transcript.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Contrast the administration routes and primary settings for the use of Remdesivir and Paxlovid (Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir).
back:
* Remdesivir: Intravenous (IV) infusion; primarily used in hospitalized patients.
* Paxlovid: Oral tablets; primarily used in the outpatient setting for early infection.

category: Enumerate the drugs used to treat coronavirus
front: Identify the specific clinical contraindication for the use of Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir (Paxlovid) related to renal function.
back:
* Severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min).
* Dose adjustment is required for moderate impairment (eGFR 30–60).
* Nirmatrelvir is primarily cleared by the kidneys.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Penicillins and other beta-lactam antibiotics exert their bactericidal effect by covalently binding to [___], which inhibits the transpeptidation reaction essential for peptidoglycan cross-linking.
back:
• Penicillin-Binding Proteins (PBPs).
• Inhibits final cross-linking of the cell wall.
• Triggers membrane-bound autolytic enzymes.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: During a rapid intravenous infusion of a glycopeptide for a MRSA infection, a patient develops intense flushing and pruritus of the face and upper torso. Identify the most likely pharmacological mediator of this reaction.
back:
• Histamine release.
• Known as "Red Man Syndrome."
• Prevented by slowing infusion rate or antihistamine pretreatment.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Explain how tetracyclines inhibit bacterial protein synthesis at the ribosomal level.
back:
• Bind reversibly to the 30S ribosomal subunit.
• Block binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to the mRNA-ribosome acceptor site.
• Prevents addition of new amino acids to the peptide chain.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Contrast the killing kinetics of aminoglycosides with those of beta-lactam antibiotics regarding concentration versus time dependence.
back:
• Aminoglycosides: Concentration-dependent killing (higher peak/MIC ratio increases rate).
• Beta-lactams: Time-dependent killing (efficacy depends on time above MIC).
• Aminoglycosides also exhibit a significant post-antibiotic effect (PAE).

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Identify the pharmacological rationale for administering Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) concurrently with Isoniazid therapy.
back:
• Isoniazid promotes the excretion of pyridoxine.
• Prevents peripheral neuropathy and CNS toxicity.
• Essential in slow acetylators or malnourished patients.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: For acyclovir to become active against HSV, the first phosphorylation step must be catalyzed by the virus-specified enzyme [___].
back:
• Thymidine kinase.
• Converts acyclovir to monophosphate.
• Ensures selective activation only in infected cells.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: An African-American patient being treated for P. vivax malaria or leprosy presents with jaundice and dark urine. Investigation reveals Heinz bodies in erythrocytes. Identify the underlying mechanism of this drug reaction.
back:
• Oxidative stress in G6PD deficiency.
• Caused by Primaquine or Dapsone.
• Leads to acute hemolytic anemia.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Describe the distinct enzymatic targets of fluoroquinolones and the specific stage of DNA processing each target regulates.
back:
• Topoisomerase II (DNA Gyrase): Prevents relaxation of supercoiled DNA for transcription.
• Topoisomerase IV: Inhibits separation of replicated chromosomal DNA into daughter cells.

category: Describe their mechanism of action and their adverse effects
front: Differentiate the targets of sulfonamides and trimethoprim within the bacterial folate synthesis pathway.
back:
